Text: I think I see generative AI being used in a lot of different ways-at university, in day-to-day life, and at work. Since this is mostly about university, I’ll focus on that first. First off, there's assistance with assignments, like summarizing notes or legal cases. You’ll get a 30-page case filled with jargon from the 1950s and they’ll say, "Here’s some light reading before your tutorial." What? I’m not reading all that. Even if you try, it’s really hard to understand. So I’ve heard of people using generative AI to summarize it. I’m not saying you just type "Tell me the case" into ChatGPT-that’s dumb, it makes up stuff. But if you upload documents, it can sometimes summarize key points for you. There are going to be a lot of empty pauses in here, I hope you're ready. I’ll probably move on to other examples and maybe circle back to uni when I think of more. Oh wait-at uni, I’ve seen teachers using it too, mostly the ones who talk about generative AI. They make images for PowerPoints. I think we’re meant to talk about our feelings, so I’ll do that. I’m not really a big fan of using generative AI for drawings or images. I don’t understand the need-there are perfectly good images out there. I feel like it’s more ethical to use existing images from the internet. But instead, we’re wasting a whole lot of water [possibly referring to environmental costs of AI training?], and I think I just have some weird.. I struggle, maybe ethically, with the way these images are made. It just gives me an icky feeling. A lot of videos or pictures have an unnatural quality about them. Even if they don’t, and even if they look exactly like the real thing, I just don’t like it. I don’t like that it’s taking over art forms and photography. It’s stealing art to create its own, and that makes me feel like the arts are being devalued. If it were up to me-well, it is up to me, I guess that was a bad sentence start-but ideally, I feel generative AI should be used for more practical things, more assistance-based tasks. I don’t really like it when it’s used for creative stuff like that. That said, I do enjoy the occasional AI-generated meme. I think they’re funny. The fact that they’re AI-generated adds a layer of humour. But what I don’t like is seeing AI-generated content in advertisements. I don’t like that at all. I don’t know what kind of image brands are trying to project by using generated ads, but I’ll tell you what message comes across: it feels cheap. It makes the product seem cheap and the company seem untrustworthy. Like, you couldn’t pay a couple bucks to a graphic designer? Anyway, back to uni. In my other degree-information technology-I’ve seen people use AI to help with coding. If there’s a bug you can’t figure out, you upload the code to ChatGPT or Copilot or whatever you use. There’s another AI tool that’s pretty good with coding-let me try to find it. Anyway, you’d say, "This is the error that’s coming up with my code. What’s the issue?" And it’s actually pretty helpful. Oh-Claude.ai! That’s the one. It helps a lot. Saves so much time trying to figure out why your code isn’t working. Like, "Oh, it was a missing full stop the whole time." I don’t think that’s cheating at all. As long as AI is being used to assist rather than do the job for you in a university context, I don’t think it’s cheating. Okay, well, my alarm went off halfway through that-I forgot why. Yeah, that’s what I was going to say. I was finishing up anyway. I was going to say: why shouldn’t you use the tools that you have? It’s like being asked to build a table, and you have a hammer, but the university expects you not to use the hammer because it’ll make it easier. You’re meant to saw it carefully and just put it together like a Lego piece. But you know you have a hammer. You know you can use it, and you’re still building the table. It’s just a lot easier and quicker than trying to etch out the pieces of wood and stick them together like Lego. Why do that when you have a hammer?

Text: I've become increasingly more aware of AI in my everyday life, from observing it through personal use, the media, and apps I use daily on my phone and computer. I've noticed the integration of AI pretty much everywhere; it seems as though more people are using it now than not. In one of my classes, I've even noticed my tutor using AI to prepare the activities we participate in during the tutorials. She hands us a piece of paper each class detailing what we will be participating in, and I recognise the structure being written by AI in the way it's laid out on the page. I don’t see anything wrong with it being used. It is really helpful in many aspects, but I do believe it is taking away our ability to think independently. Though I do see AI being used for many innovative things. For example, Spotify incorporating Spotify DJ, which I do use on a daily basis as it predicts songs I would like based on what I listen to. I've also seen the integration of AI in my law classes with the introduction of Socrates. I think Socrates is a great study tool as it doesn’t take away independent thinking but instead teaches and helps you get to the answer without giving it away.3

Text: Recently my family have been planning a trip to Japan. When I would ask family members to send me things they wanted to do or places they wanted to go, I’d later find out that they had asked ChatGPT to make them itineraries. My dad pays for Abacus and it would even provide links and offer to make bookings for him, but I don’t trust any of it. I agree it’s a good way to get ideas about activities or ask it about the best times to travel, but I would never let it book anything for me. I don’t like it giving links, handling personal details or dealing with anything involving money. A version of Copilot has been introduced for use at work recently, and I work in a huge law firm. I’m interested to see how it gets incorporated into my job going forward, but I don’t know how clients would feel if they knew that for the rates they pay and trust they place in a firm / their lawyer, parts of their case or even their details could have been discussed with AI (no matter how secure it is). Copilot is also being used as part of one of my classes right now. While it does seem useful now, I was very disappointed when it was first announced because it is intended to be used for 20min of each hour-long class. I also found it ironic that it would not work on our laptops unless we disabled several privacy and security features on our browser. While I see benefits from incorporating AI into our classes, I feel like I’d prefer it creates quizzes for us and asks us questions rather than being used to answer questions and teach content. I personally in recent weeks have found that it is best used to edit and refine and also correct grammar and spelling for written works I do think it’s very good at doing this because it’s very good at using existing information that I provided to kind of clean it up whereas whenever I ask it a question or it needs to generate or find an answer for me I am Either never completely happy with the response. I feel like the response is entirely wrong or it’s missing key information on that note. I do think it is generally very good at recognising and summarising cases for me especially copilot. ChatGPT is awful at summarising cases and guaranteed it gets it wrong almost every time, however I’m confident when I ask copilot to give me a case summary it generally is correct and aligns with what I have either heard in a PowerPoint lecture scene on a textbook or just know from speaking with others. In terms of speaking with others I actually just thought about group assignments and the connection with AI. I have a lot of problems with group assignments but one of them is that when someone uses AI in their group assignment often no one else in the group can really notice or if they do, it’s really hard to address it with the person I’ve known many people who have been marked down in the past because someone in their group has used AI and that is just not their fault. I do wonder There is such a strong push for students to not collaborate not speak about assignments not speak about content not speak about anything at all related to uni however I feel that this is why students resort to speaking to AI it feels safer. It feels like it can’t be traced And it just feels like you are getting reassurance for your thought process and your understanding. I wonder what might happen if there was more opportunities to not necessarily have group assignments but work together and encourage people to do their assignments together rather than potentially getting the answers wrong in its entirety because people have used AI in their learning. It is really difficult to not to use AI. It also depends what type of AI were talking about because like I mentioned in the prompt about what my friends use, some of my friends use ChatGPT or the Snapchat AI or copilot or something else and everyone has a different experience depending on what they say generally the consensus is the same and it’s that people are asking questions I feel like especially at university there has become such a culture where you actually can’t ask questions it might just be QUT specific but when there is no discussion board, no email replies from some tutors and an overall deterrent from speaking with peers about assessment content. I do feel like this is why people resort to asking AI for clarification. I wonder whether it is less about telling students not to use AI and more about showing them how to use other methods to find the answer. I personally love a collaborative approach and I really see that in my psychology degree. Some of my best units and best assessment pieces have been because they involve other students whether it is a reflection on a tutorial where I was in a group or it was a conversations with other students in the class when we’re sitting in a circle that have allowed me to really understand the content on a different level. I think when I don’t understand a concept in law, or maybe I watch the tutorial online, I am significantly more likely to ask AI to confirm a concept for me and I am still very doubtful that it is even correct so I end up just feeling worse in some cases. I think at this stage my biggest issue with AI is that I don’t trust it and I don’t always trust that it’s responses are real and we don’t know always where that information that it’s providing is coming from however I do think that’s because AI is still relatively new and I think that it will learn and grow so fast That eventually my distaste for it will actually change. If I knew that AI responses were going to be fully referenced very accurate which I do believe it will be one day depending on where it draws this information. I think I would 100% use it more often because it is so efficient and it is so easily accessed. I don’t want to because when I’m paying for uni I want more of a connection with my tutors lecturers and my peers but especially in law I feel like that has been going downhill ever since I started my degree years ago. It’s very disappointing to see AI used as a teacher, but our other methods of learning are slowly becoming less effective due to the fear of AI.

Text: I don’t know whether it is part of the growing media coverage over the use of AI or whether I am just a bit naïve, but it seems that GenAI has been receiving more and more backlash. When I think of GenAI several things come to mind, namely the way AI seems to be uprooting me and my peers’ ability to extend our learning. This is because AI seems to take all the hard thinking out of the process. But to be honest, my experience with GenAI is rather limited. I have used it once in my first year of law to map out the sections of the Australian Constitution. Not feeling satisfied with the answer provided, I checked the Constitution and found that CoPilot had given me false information. However, I have seen interesting methods of using AI to assist with studying. Some include uploading lecture materials and readings to a GenAI bot which then formats your notes for you when you ask the bot a question. Overall, my current stance is moulded by the increasing negativity in the media. I would be interested in experimenting with AI to see if it can be used for good.6

Text: I might come back to it later as part of future entries, but on the way home from work tonight on my 30-odd minute drive, I was pondering the use of Gen AI-or more specifically, the rules that higher education institutions are trying to implement about the use of Gen AI-from a justice perspective. From an educational and assessment position, I have no problems at all with higher education institutions limiting the use of Gen AI by students. The ‘why’ of this statement will also likely be a topic for future entries, but for now, the simplest way of putting it is that Gen AI is fundamentally bad for learning something, and worse for its assessment. While it’s appropriate for higher education institutions to dissuade students from using Gen AI, one can’t help but notice the hypocrisy of higher education institutions implementing a bunch of policies and rules regarding the academic conduct (or misconduct, depending on one’s perspective), including the use of Gen AI, when the same institutions appear to have no interest in having policies, rules, and more importantly, transparency, about the quality and standards of the education and assessment provided by the institution’s own academic ‘teaching’ staff to the same set of students. Before coming to the LLB degree as an undergraduate, I spent nearly two decades involved in the assessment of high-stakes Fellowship examinations. The majority was in the operationalisation of an in-person practical examination including several years as the practical exam co-ordinator for the state of Queensland, along with the associated national level executive commitments that were part of that position, and then as a core member of a national taskforce to redesign that exam to make it COVID-safe. Everything was done to ensure that the two theory and one practical exams (and indeed, each question in each exam) was statistically reliable, using gold-standard assessment methods like the modified Angoff method for standard setting each and every question on each and every exam. While I was primarily involved in assessment, I was also involved in the complementary side of education, including training Quality Assurance examiners, regular examiners, and the candidates, as well as general education of undergraduate students and post-graduate registrars. Coming from this experience in the painstakingly meticulous level of attention, professionalism and drive for continuous improvement in education and high-stakes assessment, back to an undergraduate degree, was a bit of a rude awakening. The quality of teaching, especially from the tutors running the tutorials (which are the heart of education in each subject) was, to put it nicely, ‘variable’. The content of assessments was often unrelated to the core learning objectives each week, and the core learning objectives overall, while the consistency of marking of each assessment was not consistent at all. One specific example involved a subject which some of the central principles being taught related to cognitive biases and using specific techniques to overcome these biases. That the unit’s assessments and their grading were clearly riddled with bias was absolutely dripping with irony. Both assessments were policy submissions on electric vehicles. What’s that got to do with law, I hear you ask? Nothing. Nothing at all. It was an LLB elective devoid of any legal application. And, why electric vehicles? Why not pick something really important to jurisprudence, like the fact that Judges are more likely to give different sentences depending on the time of day, or the day of the week, or whether the accused was First Nations? That puzzled me too, until I learned that the unit co-ordinator’s pet research topic just happened to be electric vehicles … somehow unlikely to be a coincidence. The systemic biases that pervaded assessment grading were also painfully obvious. The unit co-ordinator put an article on Canvas at the beginning of the term to explain how to write policy submissions. The article literally said ‘… there is no set way to write a policy submission … Policy submissions can take any form you want.’ Yet the very first comment by the person grading my paper was ‘This is not how policy submissions are written.’ Ah … did you not read the article on Canvas that was specifically provided by the unit co-ordinator which said there was no set way to write a policy submission? The grading only got worse from there, with multiple examples of the well-known assessment bias of the ‘halo/horns effect’ amongst many others. Despite raising these very significant problems in grading and the comically sad irony of the grader being unaware of his own assessment biases, the unit co-ordinator was blind to her own academic and personal biases. In the end, my significant, legitimate concerns regarding the unit’s assessment were neither recognised nor respected. Instead, they were invalidated. The response I received was that my concerns were illegitimate, for no other reason than I was a first year student in an undergraduate course. The implication was that I was ignorant, and for good measure, also quite impudent for daring to question a professor … or associate professor … or whatever level of ivory tower academia was involved. Sure, I’m an undergraduate in QUT law. I also happen to be an academic Senior Lecturer in a different-though equally prestigious-university, not that it was worth raising in the swirling arrogant indifference. I am really terrible with names, and for the life of me, I can’t remember the names of the academic staff involved … shit. Oh, bugger it, it’s not important. All I remember was that he was a moron and she was a fucking bitch. This wasn’t the only subject where the teaching of the unit was woeful and its assessment and grading was deeply flawed, but my story-my ethnographic narrative, if you will-of that particular experience was sadly the most memorable, for all the wrong reasons. Which brings me back to Gen AI. The prevalence of fundamental flaws in education and assessment across the LLB subjects I’ve undertaken has affected my GPA, though thankfully not fatally so. I’m a crotchety old man with accumulated academic and life experience. I know how to write technical papers, use footnotes effectively, use EndNote referencing software and have been using AGLC4 in my work writing independent expert witness reports for several years. But what of the genuine first year student, a millennial fresh out of high school with no academic or life experience, trying to make the daunting transition from secondary to tertiary education? I’d imagine that in a cohort of hundreds of first year law students, there would be a lot of very scared, very stressed, perfectionist and previously high-performing 18-year-olds whose frontal lobes and concepts of adulthood are still maturing, with no idea of how to effectively understand, let alone study, the often dense legal content, adapt to the formal language of law, and try and navigate the convoluted-though-pedantic rules of AGLC4 … all while perpetually hung over. For that particular subgroup, the confusion and frustration of the systemic short-comings in teaching and assessment would be magnified, though they wouldn’t know how to navigate the academic systems or be brave enough to question their grades, even if they thought they’d been disadvantaged. - Enter Gen AI. Sure, every subject, and every assessment in those subjects, categorically forbids the use of Gen AI, but in the haze of partial understanding, performance pressure, ethanol withdrawal and pure desperation, Gen AI can become all too tempting, while their immature frontal lobes assure them that they’ll get away with it. Some might. Most won’t. Then a university committee, armed with some policy about Gen AI that was thought up by some other ivory tower academic with no concept of reality-let alone an understanding of what Gen AI actually is-will descend on those caught using Gen AI with a God-like wrath, righteously chastening them for their individual Gen AI policy transgressions. Having meted out the requisite punishment to each miscreant, the committee will return to their ivory tower and the university will bask in a smug self-congratulatory sense of success. It’s such a nice view from the ivory tower. It’s so high up that the systemic failings of education and assessment are too small to see … so high up to see the impact of those failings on those caught using Gen AI out of desperation … so high up to see the outcome of confusion and disappointment from the sub-standard education and assessment for those who didn’t use Gen AI, but really wanted to, because they had no fucking idea of what they were supposed to learn. Yes, Gen AI is fundamentally bad for learning something, and worse for its assessment. Yes, higher education institutions must limit the use of Gen AI by students. But higher education institutions-QUT included-need to take the tree-sized log out of their own eye before self-righteously castigating the Gen AI specks in the eyes of students. Having policies against student use of Gen AI is necessary, but the dearth of policies, rules, standards and transparency of their own education and assessment is sanctimonious arrogance of the highest order. Gen AI use by university students is not done in a vacuum. Until the academic elite come down from their ivory tower and implement better standards of education, statistically robust benchmarking of assessment, and transparency most important of all, universities are no better than those students who use Gen AI. We don’t need more policy submissions on electric vehicles. We need policies which promote universal fairness and justice, the beating heart of practical jurisprudence.

Text: I want to start this diary note by outlining that I am generally against the us of gen AI. My preexisting opinions are that it is not a tool that is helping humanity, but one that is more so harming it. I have the strong concern that we are degrading into a society that is decommissioning thought and logical opinion. Disincentivizing deep thought and actual considered opinion. I see GenAI being used in the same way as much of technology is - reducing topics that should be considered and well researched to 15 second bites - think about what TikTok has done to the collective attention span of young people. I see GenAI being used to deliver complicated information in an overly simplified and oftentimes incorrect fashion. I see students relying upon this (less so in law - because it simply does not work) to their detriment. In other use cases, I see GenAI replacing artists. Stealing copyrighted work. Countries around the world deciding not to legislate against the copyright theft in order to not see a dip in their GDP. I see GenAI as a non surprising result of a system that attempts to reward infinite growth on a planet that has limited resources. I see GenAI using extensive amounts of water and power. I see the predictions that the amount of resources that GenAI will grow to use will be equivalent to the rate of countries. I see the investors pouring billions into the technology with little understanding of what it actually is. I see all of this and hope that it is a bubble. I see all of this and hope that it is something that we can forget and move on from as a society, another tech-bro fad that conned wall street into funding it because of the promise that they would have to pay fewer salaries. I see all of this and hope that it will simply be another metaverse or crypto 2.0. I see all of this and worry. I know that this comes across as being doomsday-ey, but know that I did try to think about what GenAI is used for. I did try to think of the positive applications. All that comes to mind for me is its capacity to improve research and streamline data entry. Past those two relatively simple applications I could not think of any of the other ways in which GenAI is used in a positive sense. Perhaps this will help you understand my entries as a whole. Maybe there is some value in that. Maybe there is some value in identifying the native worry that comes with the technology. Hopefully it is useful!13

Text: How am I seeing Gen AI being used: At uni: I'm not. You don't SEE it. No one is like "omg, I totally used Chat GPT to write this paper, lolz". But I see the impacts of other students using it to cheat, which drives me absolutely crazy. Online exams were awesome - my exam notes are 200 pages long, how easy was it to use CTR-F to find what you're looking for rather than spending an entire day printing, highlighting and tabbing a folder full of exam notes, then wasting time in the exam rifling through the bloody thing. And to be able to type! Like we would in the real world - outside of being a duty lawyer (which most never will be) how often am I going to need to be able to pull an answer out of my ass in 5 minutes and build a comprehensive argument around it in the real world? Not often. That students were cheating in online exams to enough of an extent to have them scrapped shits me beyond belief. Besides, law is hard enough, the competition is steep enough - now I have to compete with a robot posing as a student? Give me a break! Although, I do see it being used really badly by experienced lawyers who are overworked or busy or lazy or maybe too stupid to check the output, and winding up before the legal services commission for submitting case lists generated by AI including made up cases. That's a level of stupid I have trouble understanding. But perhaps that's because I haven't been exposed to the real pressures of practice, and I don't know. Maybe they were made promises by the sales rep who sold them the program - a lot of these (a few? I can't say I've heard of a LOT of these cases) solicitors say they trusted the program. For someone being "raised" for want of a better word with access to Wikipedia and the internet, trusting sources you didn't find and read yourself has been just something you didn't do. From day 1. Is it because they've not grown up with "don't trust the internet" being rammed down their throats? And saying that, I'm 37. I did my first degree at a time when they were telling us not to cite Wikipedia; being told not to trust AI just seems a sensible extension of that. In the broader workforce I see GenAI being used most sensibly to do things that no one else is actually going to rely on in any life impacting way. I use it to write copy for the social media posts for my kid's school's P&C group, fundraising flyers, etc. I use it at work (I'm a paralegal at a community legal centre) to change language in my drafting from passive to active voice without me having to spend 15 minutes thinking about it. Like I've already drafted what needs to be said, I just want it to be phrased better. For me at uni, I'm too terrified of having to disclose AI use or academic misconduct during admission proceedings and not being admitted to go near it. Ethics was useful for that! I find ChatGPT better at explaining complicated things than Google, where it gives you many answers but you still need to figure it out. I was reading family law cases this weekend and this judge kept using ridiculously archaic or descriptive words - I would punch the phrase into ChatGPT with a prompt "what is this sentence saying?", and it would give me the answer in plain language, with some examples for context. It's interesting that I trust that - trust but verify right? It's the additional sentences that really help me trust it better than my own analysis of Google results. Hmm. How interesting and contradictory of my own thoughts just minutes ago.. Admin law has a research assignment this semester where we're analysing the issues with automated decision making in executive decisions, and there's a big bias issue where people just say "whelp, the computer said no! Must be the right answer!". It's interesting that I can know that, and know that it's stupid for decision makers to be doing that, or for senior solicitors to be relying on GenAI output without checking, but when I do it just to understand a phrase, I don't think it's stupid? Maybe that says more about my own arrogance than anything to do with GenAI.. I did use it last semester to make my exam notes. I punched in my own work, pages and pages and pages of case notes, with a prompt to reduce it down to a quick reference table, and quick summaries. My fear of academic misconduct was so front of mind though that I had copied and pasted a note into every prompt of "do not use any material outside of the attached documents to create the summaries". How ridiculous. But that's how effective the messaging has been for me! Maybe they should take the research component out of Ethics and move it to first year - if students understood how impactful cheating at uni could be on their futures, they might not even try. But how even are students cheating?? I see Studoco notes every time I google something related to the courses I'm doing - who's paying for that shit?? You have no idea who wrote it and if it's accurate, if your goal is just to pass the courses. If your goal is to actually develop the thought processes and skills to be a lawyer, let alone be a great lawyer, why cheat? I genuinely don't get it. I get the stress. I get the competition. I get that it's hard. But why put yourself in a position to get fired from a job once it becomes painfully obvious that you have absolutely no idea what you're doing? 14

Text: At uni this is the first semester where I have actually been told to use AI in an assignment. Instead of swapping work with a peer to review our draft we can input it to preferably co pilot and ask it questions about how the work could be improved. This is a very interesting request. One that normally I would have steered away from, but being able to use co pilot rather than coordinator with another student makes my life a lot easier. It doesn't matter if I don't finish writing my assignment until the day before its due, because it will only take a couple of minutes for co pilot to give me suggestions. I do find it ironic that I am using AI in a research assignment actually about whether academics should use AI and to what extent. I think their are numerous ethical considerations as well as the usual academic misconduct concerns. If AI gives me a new idea I hadn't thought of and then when its being marked the marker makes particular mention of the excellent idea, should I actually be marked higher for that? It wasn't me that came up with the idea, so why should I be rewarded for it. But then you just question what influence I had ever the AI system, did I adjust the idea, maybe connect it to something else, change it in a way AI couldn't have. For me this is the frustrating part of students using AI in their assignments. If you're using it to check spelling, thats fine, who cares. But as soon as it starts to suggest better ways to write things or new ideas, under the current academic policy there is no way that can be classified as your own work. I don't know if students who get away with using AI do well, but I do also question what benefit using AI has in an assignment. We pay almost $15,000 a year to study, so why wouldn't you want to learn to learn. What is the benefit of having a machine write your assignment if the whole point of uni is to show an employer that you've learnt all these impressive skills that mean you have a unique quality nobody or nothing else can offer. In another unit we have specifically been told we have to save our assignment in inedrive so that we can prove we didn't use AI. A friend at another university is using AI in her assignment this semester. They've been asked to do contrasting paragraphs, one using AI and the other not. Then they have to demonstrate which paragraph is better. I know that cheating using AI is apparently common, but I am yet to know anyone personally who has used it in an assignment. I know people who have talked about it, joked about using it. In the real world I have seen only limited use of AI. At work we don't use it, although I do know staff who have limited skills in writing that use it to write emails etc. I can see it becoming more common place. At my mums work one of the workers there uses chatgpt to write documents because she cant keep up with the work required. With that thinking it doesn't make sense for uni students to use AI if it is an efficiency tool.15

Text: For most of my life, the idea of using artificial intelligence was just a fantasy to me, having a personal assistant with the collective intelligence of the world at the palm of your hands seemed like something that would remain squarely in the realm of science fiction. That was until the start of 2024 with the release and subsequent popularization of GPT-4 brought the idea from the realm of fantasy to a very real reality. Soon what was once simply an idea had now, almost overnight, become something that was brought into the zeitgeist of our time. With tech companies rolling out something akin to the font of all knowledge right at the touch of a button. It was no surprise that it was adopted globally almost immediately. While to my recollection most of the uses for ChatGPT remained in the realm of automating rather mundane tasks for large firms and other fortune 500 companies it became apparently as 2024 marched on that there were more potential uses for the model than those of the corporate world. There is a strong memory for me in August 2024, when the idea of using ChatGPT as a study aid was proposed to me. At the time I was aware that ChatGPT was a large language model, but outside of I was rather clueless. At the time, I felt as if the use of these systems to get ahead of your fellow students and to appear as a better student then one actually was would ultimately undermine the whole point of getting an education. This conservative view is one I still hold to this day, but it is evident as of late that my hardline stance might have been misplaced. While I still hold the opinion that using LLM’s for the purposes of creating essays that you can’t be fucked to write or to create some art that is mediocre at best and ask for admiration is a foolish endeavour. However, considering the constraints of the modern world, using ChatGPT to help you write a professional letter that you would not be able to pen, or to summarise complex concepts in easy-to-understand language, or to organise your day is not foolish but should be encouraged. While I am somewhat hesitant to use AI to the extent that my cohort has, such as summarising whole lectures into study notes or using AI to do a live transcription of a meeting due to my rather conservative views, I can say without a doubt that the insight that AI has provided me in my current day to day life is irreplaceable. It is truly a privilege to be able to hold in my hands something capable of answering my every question, explaining every complex concept, and streamlining menial tasks and I cannot express the amount of gratitude for this gift that has been given to humanity, even when taking into account all of the misuse that comes with its myriad benefits. 16

Text: Reflecting on the prompt, I use ChatGPT a lot and use it in various aspects of my daily life. In terms of how I utilise AI the most is mainly as a study assist tool. Currently, I am a Law and biomedical science student at QUT, and I use AI to produce study notes. Sometimes, I will use another AI tool called TurboScribe, and upload lectures to get a transcript of the lecture, and I combine this with any lecture slides (if there are any), and any other learning resources. I get it to summarise and provide notes that I paste into an app called Notion. Notion does have an AI function, but I don’t pay for premium. The ChatGPT is not 100% first go, I will often go back through and add and finesse the notes, adding in extra information, pictures, or embedding in YouTube videos that assist with my learning. I do not use AI at work as I work in law and there are a lot of laws and regulations that prevent the use of AI in law, for both professional obligation reasons and client privacy reasons.

Text: I see GenAI being used by almost everyone around me. Not just young university students, but even my dad who is in his late fifties. All my friends from uni use ChatGPT (sometimes a different platform, but rarely) in their assessments. They will literally copy and paste the task sheet into ChatGPT and use the response to guide their research and focus. I don’t think I know anyone that copies the GenAI response word for word into their answer because obviously they would get flagged for academic misconduct. However, when I was in high school I know a few students would do that, and they would almost always get found out. But usually those were people who didn’t want to pursue any academics after graduating. I have a lot of friends that use ChatGPT for more personal advice. I use it for that too. When I face conflict with friends or family or anyone else, I will often go to ChatGPT to ask for help drafting a text or for advice on what to say to them in person. It honestly gives great advice. We use CoPilot GenAI in my LLB204 class, which is very interesting. Although I do use ChatGPT for help with uni stuff, I don’t fully trust it. It has, on many occasions, just gone completely off track. For example if I give it a scenario to apply the law to, it will change names and get things mixed up. I go to a Christian Pentecostal church and I used to be a youth leader, and I know some people would use GenAI to help write their messages. I have used it to write a short tithes message. I don’t fully know my thoughts on using GenAI for religious purposes, it seems a little bit disingenuous. When GenAI is used for academic purposes, I do think it is negatively affecting the user. For example, if I use ChatGPT to help with issue identification for a tutorial question, I know I am not developing my issue-identification skills. I think using GenAI for those purposes is lazy and reduces critical thinking skills. Regardless, I still use it. I use it because I don’t have time to prepare for class, I don’t have time to worry about whether I’ve selected the right legal issues, I don’t have time to prepare a speech, or to spend hours drafting a message to a friend. I see GenAI being used to generate images for preaches and for uni assignments. Because who has time to create an actual piece of artwork? GenAI has penetrated every aspect of modern society. And I do think people have benefitted greatly, but the long term effects do scare me. I do think it is making people less creative, less intelligent, less inquisitive, and less unique. But it saves time and energy. And when you live a busy life, you’ll take any help you can get.21

Text: Date: Monday 01 September 2025 Time: 4.25pm It is clear to me that for a lot of people, in day-to-day life, GenAI has simplified many mundane tasks/processes and made them much more efficient. ‘Give me a meal idea using these ingredients in my cupboard’, or for me, who just moved out of home, ‘write me a grocery list for my first home’. For study, it can be great to create a 2-week study plan based on X, Y and Z for an upcoming exam. I’m a schedule and routine person, so this kind of thing appeals to me. It’s ability to analyze large volumes of data more accurately, efficiently, consistently, and less expensively is of particular use to many. But while it is being used for these positive things, I do think that GenAI has quickly become less of a luxury and more of an ‘it’ll always be there’, ‘if all else fails just ask ChatGPT’, etc. My biggest issue with GenAI is the overreliance that people have on it. I work in a school, so while, yes, the students use AI, I am also witnessing the ways in which staff use AI. Things like creating schedules or plans are great, but I don’t understand why people use AI to write an email, or generate a message to use for an Instagram post for a friend’s birthday. It always baffles me hearing people say they’ll ‘just ask Chat GPT’ something. Kind of linked to this is the increase in parasocial relationships with AI. I have seen countless people talk on social media about how Chat GPT is like their friend - they have a nickname for it, they ask it random questions, they talk to it as if they were actually talking to their friend. There’s also the dangerous misuse of GenAI, which is not just a potential consequence, but something that has actually been realized time and time again. In the US Presidential Election, it was used to generate a video (I think, or some other type of media) showing that Taylor Swift endorsed Donald Trump. The dangers of GenAI being able to generate anything one puts their mind to is a disturbing rabbit hole I won’t go down. Circling back to education, I do think it has its pros. It’s clear to me that educational institutions are trying to ‘keep with it’ with AI, knowing that students are going to use it so how can we beat them to it and implement it, but in a way that they are using it in an appropriate manner. And while this approach makes sense, I do struggle sitting in a class that I’ve paid X amount of money for and being told that the first 20 minutes is dedicated to asking AI questions and seeing what it tells us. I really struggled doing an assignment where I have to use AI and get marks for how I used it and evaluating the pros and cons. I know this is a personal view, definitely not a universal one, and probably a minority one. Personally, I don’t really care about AI, in the sense that I don’t think it’s this great amazing thing. I (figuratively) roll my eyes when I get to class and hear a tutor talk about AI. I think it’s a waste of my time, but I do also recognise that it’s a waste of my time because I don’t like and rarely use it, but for a student who perhaps uses AI frequently, it is good to have an opportunity to use it ethically.

Text: The short answer … ‘Extremely rarely’. It's entirely possible that I might have at some point taken the first response that Google has given me but I can't remember when that occurred. If I did, it was only because I was able to craft and extremely accurate or well constructed search query such that the Google search results were exactly what I needed. Even then, I can't think of a time where I solely relied on the first search result. I tend to be much more likely to look at a number of the search results because, as clever as Google is, there's usually a lot more information out there that will help me find the answer to my question than the first result of a Google search. (b) When was the last time you went to page 2 of a Google search? Therefore, the answer to the second part of this query, as to when was the last time that I went to page 2 of a Google search, the answer is, very often. Again, as clever as Google is, even with an extremely well-constructed query, there is usually information out there that is not available on the first page of responses. Either that, or I haven't put in the right information into the search query and as a result, I haven't been able to easily locate the information that I was hoping to find. Given that I google things all the time-all throughout my day given the amount of research that I do in my normal clinical work, but also in my work as an independent expert witness or in my searching for topics or answers as part of my law degree-I will frequently need to go to the second page of the Google search results … and sometimes the third, the fourth, and occasionally the fifth page or beyond. I must admit that once I get beyond the fourth or fifth page of the Google search results, if I can't find the answer I'm looking for, then I assume that I have put in the wrong search query, or there’s no clear and obvious answer about the information that I'm looking for, and at that point I tend to lose interest and either redo the search query, or give up entirely. Given this study is about Gen AI, Google now comes up with an AI answer to my query at the very top of the search results, which I always studiously ignore as I don’t trust any AI, including Google’s, to come up with the answers that I want. Even if it does, there's no references or citations to justify how it came up with the answer, and references and citations are the most important thing to take note of when trying to research something, especially for critical research (especially expert witness reports and/or university assignments). If there’s no way that one is able to determine how accurate the response is because of the lack of the AI providing any form of referencing or citations, then you don't know whether the AI generated answer that Google (or any AI) provides is correct in anyway. And that being the case, what's the fucking point of asking it? Just like a human trying to make an argument, if it can’t provide me with the sources used to craft an answer, then the answer could very well be completely inaccurate, or in the case of Gen AI, hallucinated or confabulated. Irrespective, I can't trust what’s said … at all. The same with other forms of Jen AI, like chat GPT. It's all very well and good to ask ChatGPT to find you an answer on something. Chat GPT has no idea how to read and interpret sources of information especially at high levels of intellectual research. And if there's no way of verifying the answer that ChatGPT provides, then there's no way of telling whether the response is a confabulation or a hallucination, and therefore whether the output is reliable in any way shape or form. So if you can't tell whether an answer is correct or not, then the answer is unreliable until proven otherwise, and therefore why bother asking it in the first place. I am much better off going to sources that I know are accurate and applicable. Usually I don't need either Google or chat GPT to know which sources are reliable and will have the answers I need. I know the answer to that already because they are sources that I know are accurate and have usually paid a subscription fee for or if they are freely available on the Internet, I know how to find those resources without needing to Google or in the alternative ask ChatGPT for an answer. So, whether I'm asking ChatGPT to try and find an answer or I'm going past the second page of a Google search, either way, I need to know how accurate the sources are for the answers that I am provided and that requires education and training which is not something that one can get by using Jen AI. Hence why it is so important for students of any form, whether secondary, tertiary or otherwise, to actually learn the content of whatever they're studying and how to critically analyse the information that they are either provided with, in lectures and tutorials, or the research that they do for an assignment, exam or any other form of assessment.

Text: Before I start my answer proper, I would just like to state that this prompt was quite thought provoking to me and upon reading it incited much reflection within me. It is not often that I have truly thought about how much I take for granted in the pursuit of knowledge. In my personal experience and I assume for most other people, when we are searching google for an answer to our question, we will go with the first answer that pops up and hold onto it as if it is gospel. And while for most questions there is little need to look beyond that point, it has become apparent to me that using this Occam’s razor approach might do more harm than good. While I would not contest its validity if we were looking up something for the point of general knowledge such as if we were looking up Michael Jackson’s birthday or if we were trying to find out which track the next f1 grand prix will be on. It is evident that the quick and easy answers that are provided by most search engines removes a person’s ability to think critically about the information they are being given. I know from my own experience and from the experience of others that while search engines are correct for 99% of the questions that a person would ask, they are not infallible and are can in rare cases provide misinformation. However, while it does concern me deeply as I come to terms with the fact that I have not been doing my due diligence when it comes to ensuring that the information I am given is correct, I do question if the point that I should research the validity of everything might be just outside of the realm of becoming a realistic possibility. As an addition to that point, I question if it is truly possible to fact check everything that one searches for. To use the example of Micheal Jackson’s birthday, without using google the only quick solution would to be ask another person, and while this is a quick and easy method, some would consider this method more fallible as it relies on a person having the knowledge in which you seek. When this is compared to the hundreds of thousands of people that have spent countless man hours doing their due diligence, it is no surprise that most people take the search result at face value. However, I do not hold this view for LLM’s considering that most people treat the outputs of these AI models as gospel does worry me to a certain extent. Considering the fact that AI models can hallucinate or provide plainly wrong answers is a point of concern. While they do work 90% of the time, I do believe there is a reason why most people say AI shouldn’t be relied upon as an infallible resource.

Text: ’ The answer to the first question ultimately depends on what I am searching for. If I’m searching random information (for example, the other night I was having a conversation about disabilities, and didn’t exactly know what cerebral palsy was so I googled it), I almost always read the top answer, or where Google often gives a summary of the information, to get a basic understanding. I often select them based on what they are actually called, as the further I get down the page and the more ‘scholarly’ results come up, they are often very niche so I can pick the relevant ones and flick the irrelevant ones. In this instance, I go through pretty much most pages on Google. I like to use Google Scholar for anything uni-related, and follow pretty much the same process. Text: I don’t know if it is because the fear campaign spread among law classes and the media has won, but I try my hardest to avoid using AI when it comes to studying. Currently, I format my studies by attending lectures, handwriting notes and attending tutorials with dot-points for each question. It would save me a lot of time if I could format my notes in a way that allows me to access them in any location like a podcast could be viewed on a bus or in the car. It also takes out the time it would require to handwrite everything. I know some people who use AI to give a brief overview of the cases we need to read. Text: Well, that’s a difficult question to answer since I don’t have any friends, and if I did, using AI is not usually a topic of conversation. Perhaps the best way I can work this topic is to consider how I use AI, and its potential future in currently unforeseen ways, including in Law. Truth be told, I use AI almost every day, but not in the Gen AI sense. My pre-Law (and unfortunately, still the primary drag on my life thanks to my fucking useless ex-wife) is as a general practitioner in clinical practice. A couple of years ago, a flurry of AI scribes (AI that would listen to the words spoken in the consultation and then transcribe that into clinical notes, instead of the GP, or any specialist, having to manually write clinical notes for the consultation) hit the market. As fate would have it, I came into contact with the developers of one of the AI scribes called ‘Lyrebird’. Lyrebird was written by two IT graduates, almost straight out of uni, in only two weeks in a ‘hack-a-thon’. At the stage when I came into contact with the developers, Lyrebird was still essentially a start-up. The developers were working out of a granny flat out the back of one of their parent’s houses in St Kilda in Melbourne. Seeing the benefit of having an AI scribe taking notes for doctors, especially those doctors who were terrible at making notes of their own which opened them up to all sorts of medicolegal risks, I offered my help in trying to help them refine what I could see was going to become ubiquitous in clinical practice. So, I gave them as much help as I could while they were refining the product, and since then, they’ve gone on in leaps and bounds. I’d like to say it was all because of me, but really, it was because the two of them were hard working and future thinking, and one of them in particular had the greatest leadership skill of all which was to be humble and listen to everyone who had an opinion or advice, and selectively applied that advice to each iteration of Lyrebird. Lyrebird is now one of the most widely used AI scribe software and is growing in its intelligence and functionality. Early on, like most AI, it hallucinated a lot! It also tried to second guess what the clinician may have said, or even perhaps what it thought should have been said, and its grasp of the technical language of clinical medicine was poor. It’s been about 18 months since I first met up with the Lyrebird developers, and the ability of the AI has matured very quickly. It still has its faults, but its grasp of technical terms and when to use them based on the conversation between clinician and patient now borders on that of an experienced clinician. It still picks up a lot of the non-clinical banter between clinician and patient and ascribes some of what the clinician says to the patient (for example, there are a lot of my consultations where the initial output says that the patient is studying law and has x number of assignments due etc), but it’s getting better at that too. The other advantage of Lyrebird which is why most clinicians should be using it is because it doesn’t send any data overseas, but does all of the transcribing locally, on the clinician’s own computer, close to real-time and then deletes it once the file is closed, overcoming the issue of confidentiality and privacy, one of the primary concerns with using AI in a clinical environment. While there are still issues to iron out, the advantages of using an AI scribe is now starting to well and truly outweigh them. The cost isn’t cheap (an annual subscription to Lyrebird, for example, is currently $2400), but the amount of time it saves me every day is massive. Before Lyrebird, I would invariably have to stay back after finishing my clinical work, doing notes for an hour, sometimes more, which was extra time out of my day that was unpaid. With Lyrebird, even as a general practitioner where my average hourly rate is shithouse, saving a minimum of an hour of unpaid work a day at $150 per hour, 5 days a week, 48 weeks a year (which in itself is generous, as I certainly don’t get four weeks holiday a year) is equivalent to $36,000 per annum. As efficiency and productivity goes, that’s a massive difference. While AI in a clinical environment is currently limited to taking notes, the potential is enormous. Imagine an AI that could go through a patient’s pathology results from the beginning of their time in a clinic (we can’t go further back as clinics don’t share clinical notes with other clinics for many reasons, partly technological, partly privacy issues/concerns) and analyse for specific trends which a human wouldn’t have time to do, but could alert the clinician to changes which may identify a disease in its earliest stages. That’s just one potential application. There would be dozens more. Applications of similar technology as Lyrebird to law wouldn’t be difficult to do, though again, the advantages of accuracy and efficiency would be a paradigm shift. The most obvious one to me was apparent when I was participating as a ‘witness’ for an Australian Bar Association intensive for barristers to grow their advocacy skills in a safe place with feedback from senior counsel, KCs and the like. I noticed that while cross examining a witness, the second barrister was typing as fast as possible to keep track of the questions and answers. Imagine an AI similar to Lyrebird that was doing that for them, in real time, with the only job of the second barrister being to correct any possible errors in the transcription and to highlight essential elements of the witness’s testimony. Gen AI is already working its way into day-to-day legal practice, doing a lot of the grunt work that junior solicitors and paralegals do. Not great for the job prospects of paralegals, but huge for junior solicitors who could spend more time learning the craft then doing mundane administrative shit-shovelling. Again, as I discussed in a previous entry, one can’t use Gen AI with confidence in its output unless one has enough skills and experience to pick the inaccurate from the accurate, and that requires actually learning those skills which is why Gen AI should not be used by law students (or any tertiary students for that matter). That said, again, the rapid uptake of Gen AI now is like the uptake of Google 25-odd years ago. The tech will improve as will its effective application, though like Google, Gen AI will only be effective if one already has the skills and knowledge to know how to use it effectively. Gen AI is going to change our society. How society will change because if it, who knows. My crystal ball doesn’t work that well. Only time will tell, but from what I’ve seen already, there’s definitely hope.

Text: Excellent question. I don't really have any to ask. I'm part time in every aspect of my life, except being a mother. I'm full time there. All the time, actually. 24/7 mother. Part time paralegal. Part time student. Part time committee member for clubs. Part time wife, since my husband works away a lot. Friends is a luxury I don't have time for. Moving from the UK to Australia just before a worldwide pandemic didn't do much to help build ties that bind, and starting uni in the middle of that relegated me to a life "other than" everyone else for as long as I can't work full time. I'm not even an on campus student, so even my ability to build networks there has been hampered (if the mother thing didn't fundamentally alter that anyway). So my reflection today isn't likely to be massively useful, unless it triggers some sort of terrifying mental health flag (it shouldn't, please don't follow up. I'm fine.) or connects to some kind of research on online students and the loneliness epidemic. I have heard people turn to AI when lonely, and that concept utterly terrifies me for all of the implications it raises for young people already feeling disconnected from the world. I can't imagine how connecting with a chat bot that's designed to meet your needs and keep you chatting is going to help a person develop the skills they need to connect with other humans. It's in the name right - you might feel like you're connecting with someone, but it's artificial. It's not real. And the reality of the nuance and often contradictory nature of human interaction will be devastating for these people who have turned to AI out of desperate loneliness, then forget how to interact with people. This is my take on the terror of parenting in this generation though. My kids are 10 and 5, and I have the daily humiliation of being shown how to use technology THAT MY GENERATION INVENTED, DAMMIT by a kid who appears to instinctively know how to navigate tech that she isn't allowed to use. Better than me. I use Instagram as a way to destress and find myself sitting on the couch with my eldest some nights looking for funny cat reels and stupid dances - what am I teaching her??? Thank god she won't be allowed to use it herself until she's 16, because underneath that layer of funny cat videos is some insidious bullshit designed to keep me interacting and make me feel connected. And it works. Dammit if it doesn't work. At least I'm mature enough to recognise that, and that the worse I feel about myself and the lonlier I feel in the day, the better I feel about that dopamine hit I get from scrolling. Even with me controlling the screen I get "just one more Mum, let's just find one more". If that doesn't terrify parents worried about tech addiction.. 10 years ago, when I was feeding a baby in the dark of the middle of the night, Instagram existed but it wasn't this easy to get that dopamine hit. The biggest concern was the blue light coming from my screen screwing with my sleep. Look how quickly that changed. What is this going to look like in 10 more years? What kind of world are we building for our kids? I do know I use AI differently to my husband. He's a senior engineering manager with a major international aviation company, and he can't fathom why I'm sitting at my computer for hours scrolling databases and manually reading cases when AI could do it for me. He uses AI whenever it's available - generally in summarising and maths tools, time management, etc. He asks all the time why the uni doesn't give us access to the type of legal language models available in the "real world" to do drafting or legal research for us. Good question actually - clearly lawyers are using these tools to time save in research and drafting. Why aren't we being taught to use them? Why is the uni so afraid? Teach us to use them, and how to use them properly (trust but verify!!!), and maybe students won't cheat? Maybe they will anyway, but hey - those of us who don't will be more useful to our future employers than the graduates walking out at the moment who can't talk to another human being, let alone answer a phone, let alone draft an email, let alone manage a calendar. Let's see how many times over the next few weeks I use the words "trust but verify". That could be the title of my thesis..

Text: This is an interesting question to me as it incites some self-reflection on my part. It leads me to wondering if my initial assumptions about how my friends use AI is correct or if I am off base. While I like to think that my friends use AI purely for productivity purposes, it would be conceited of me to believe that without actually asking them. To the best of my knowledge, I have seen a large variety of uses for AI not only with my friends but with the world at large. In the capacities that I use it, which is sparingly, the majority of my use of it is to answers questions that I might be too afraid to ask under a given circumstance, such as what a certain core concept of a subject means because I didn’t initially understand the material. However, from the discussions I have had with my friends it is evident that my reluctance to use such a powerful tool is inherently a foolish move. And while under certain circumstances I would be inclined to agree, I do believe that using AI to make lecture notes for you, or to summarise entire texts to the essential points while seemingly useful denies you the nuance that you get from doing those things in the traditional way. However, I do believe it is not for me to judge a persons use as if it works for them, then why should they be denied something that allows them to excel. And judging from the testimonies I have been given it is evident that those who learn how to write the correct prompts and how to discern the fact from fiction when it comes to AI outputs truly do excel from its use. In addition, while I am aware that the large majority of people do use LLM’s for this purpose, I would be remise if I did not mention the more niche uses of AI that I have seen in my friends and by extension, the people of my generation. One of the more niche uses that I have bared witness to is for the purpose of entertainment. To elaborate on that point, I have experienced games which relied upon LLM’s as part of the game with players being tasked to try and figure out a way to survive a scenario given by an AI. While this use of AI is little more than a novelty, there is a rather sizeable minority of people that I have seen use AI for more reprehensible methods. I have bared witness to people using LLM’s to help write messages for the purpose of romance. With people using ChatGPT, to help write risqué messages in order to win people over on social media. And while this is often between two people, it would be naïve of me not to discuss the smaller minority people that turn to AI chatbots for a sense of connection and inadvertently end up getting feelings for artificial intelligence. On these points I take a hardline stance, I feel that people use of AI for these purposes would constitute as systematic of a larger issue. In my mind I question if due to the use of these services have caused us as a people to lose our ability to connect and have caused experiences of loneliness to skyrocket.

Text: Since most of my friends are university students, young people in the church, gym-goers, we have similar daily tasks which we might use GenAI to help with. Obviously there is some variation as we study different degrees, have different relational issues, etc. Even just this morning, I had a close friend send 3 different text options that ChatGPT had drafted for her, to send to a guy she has been dating. She wants to have a serious conversation with him in person about how she feels the relationship is going too fast, but because they have been good friends for a while and he is a sensitive, anxious guy, she wants to be careful in how she warns him about this serious conversation. She doesn’t want him to be stressing all day about it. So she asked ChatGPT to draft 3 options, and she sent them to me to ask for my help choosing one. I chose one, and then edited a few words to make it sound better. Although I made some changes, ChatGPT is really helpful in finding the right approach/ the right words in difficult conversations where you want to prevent misunderstandings. When it comes to academic writing, its not always the best. Last night I asked chatgpt to draft me an answer to a uni tutorial question, and to include the word counts after each heading. It provided word counts, but it seemed kind of off, so I pasted the paragraphs into an online word counter and found that ALL of the word counts were inaccurate. Many paragraphs were actually half of the word count provided by ChatGPT. I told it to recount, and it did. The numbers were different but still inaccurate. This is why I struggle to trust ChatGPT when it comes to academic, research and writing purposes. But for help with relational or emotional issues, specifically drafting texts or emails to others or planning conversations, it is really good.

Circling back to the lifestyle conversation, I do think that extreme use of AI and wealth kind of interplay. My friends and I go to uni, go to work, or we are at home studying - there’s not much space in our lives for AI to be useful. AI doesn’t go to work for us. I think if I asked each of them on a scale of 1 - 10 how much value AI adds to your life, everyone’s answers would be around 1 - 4, definitely not above 5 (but of course, maybe they secretly use AI for everything and I don’t know). When I think of the people who are really gunning for AI, I think of extreme wealth and overconsumption. After all, I don’t think anyone asked for a Snapchat AI chat bot, yet it was kind of shoved in everyone’s faces in an attempt to convince us we need it. The Apple iPhone used to have new models released every few years, and now there is a brand-new model every single year, and I can’t help but think to myself, why on earth does anyone need this? Yet Apple justifies it by showing the new technology it has, everything is faster, smarter, better - and does anyone really care? I saw a video a few weeks ago about the latest model of ChatGPT that is being released (or has maybe already been released by now) - ChatGPT 5. As the person in the video listed off the things it could do, I was in shock - it can create a 2D game (like Pacman I suppose) from just one prompt, and open it up so that it’s interactive. From just one prompt, people are building apps with it so that it codes everything. It has better memory, it has better reasoning, better this and better that. That just doesn’t fit anywhere into my life. By contrast, my roommate uses ChatGPT for study in a way that I don’t actually understand and can’t fully describe. But I know he inputs all of his unit content - lectures, notes, readings, etc - into ChatGPT and gets to generate (I think) a kind of revision plan or course summary or exam notes. All I know is that it takes a long time - he will input everything and it might be like 30 minutes he’ll come out and make food or something while he waits for it generate. Again I don’t actually know, but I think I will ask him about it and come back to this point at some time. As I have mentioned previously, at work I know the staff are very fond of Microsoft CoPilot. I work at a BCE school and BCE actually sends out some of their staff every few months or so, and we actually have a 2 hour intensive session on CoPilot, what it can be used for, etc. Granted most of my colleagues are from a generation or two before me, so they are often fascinated by the fact that AI can generate a photo of a hippo wearing roller skates and wearing a tutu skirt (a real activity we did), whereas it doesn’t wow me at all. But other exercises we did saw us asking CoPilot to read all unread emails in our inboxes and provide a summary - which it did. So I guess in summary of these different observations, maybe the use of AI comes down to lifestyle and external factors? AI doesn’t fit into my lifestyle - I don’t use it to read or draft my emails, I don’t use it write my assignments, I don’t use it to even write my exam notes. But I learn by paper and pen, by writing something out multiple times and then by practicing how to apply what I’ve learnt. When I did my Literature External Exam in Year 12, my bedroom walls were covered in different coloured posters - each one for a different theme of Shakespeare’s King Lear, different quotes, analysis, etc. But for someone who absorbs information by listening to it the first time, maybe writing out their exam notes is a waste of their time and it’s more efficient to have AI do it for them. Maybe a teacher who has to plan a term’s worth of lessons for 4 different subjects finds it easier to input the content into CoPilot and get it to generate the unit plan. Maybe people who are ‘numbers people’ (they work in tech, finance, or something of that nature, or they study it) find it useful to use AI for whatever purpose, like analysing large amounts of data, whereas I don’t have a need for that. I think AI use is also influenced by the type of media or information people consume. Most of my social media is very driven by politics, social issues, environmental issues, news, etc. I am very aware of the impact that AI has on the environment, and I think that really solidified for me how cautious I am with using it. I know that not everyone’s media is like that. Not everyone really cares about how AI actually works, they just know that it’s there.

Text: AI Research Study - Entry 3 - 3 September 2025 Hello, let’s talk about AI. Most of my close friends come from school, and cover degrees in all sorts of different subjects, mostly over at UQ. I don’t hear much about how they use AI, but I assume that’s because commonly used AI isn’t at the level where it can do complex mathematics. I know from when I studied math in school it would struggle a lot on carrying values across multiple equations or forget certain constants. While this was on earlier models of ChatGPT I assume this would be a long-term struggle because there’s equations with too many components to consider at once. I do notice this in my own studies sometimes, where the AI struggles to comprehend certain things so it starts guessing and making up stuff. The best example of this is when I asked ChatGPT to tell me what section provided the definition of XYZ in this specific legislation, and it gave me the wrong section. I told the AI to try again and corrected its knowledge, and it promptly responded with something along the lines of "oh sorry my bad, it is not section 46 as I previously stated, it is actually section 47", which was also incorrect. I tested how far the AI was willing to push this, and I got to about section 56 before giving up. I also know people who are adamant against AI and using it. they do hold a valid point on the fact people should write and think for themselves and not be so dependent on AI. I don’t agree to the full extent of this though, because AI is not something that should go to waste, its capabilities and potential are very strong. I still like to figure out things for myself without AI, particularly because I see it as a skill to have the ability to identify problems. AI however as I’ve said previously is still extremely useful in many other respects. My dad is particularly an enthusiast of AI, granted he works in IT. the best quote from him is "this is the worst AI will ever be", which is inherently true. One end being refusal of all AI, and the other being fully reliant to the point you ask AI questions about every small decision in your life. I know my friends at QUT use AI, or at least most of them. they use it in the same way as me to some extent, which is to learn content and revise. Text: Today I paid attention to how often I actually use or even think about AI. I realised it pops into my day more often than I consciously acknowledge. • Morning: I thought about using AI to rephrase an email at work but decided against it, because it was quicker just to draft it myself. That hesitation is typical for me. I don’t like relying on AI for workplace communication unless I’m really stuck. • Midday: At uni, I thought about using it to help me summarise a reading, but I forced myself to push through and do the notes by hand. I think I wanted to prove to myself that I can still process the material without AI scaffolding. • Afternoon: I did actually use it to break down a difficult High Court case into plain English. This is where AI really helps me, it saves time and gives me a clearer picture before I dive into the detailed judgments. • Evening: While reflecting for this diary, I caught myself thinking about how many of my peers probably did use AI today but would never admit it. That thought always circles back when I’m writing these entries. Overall, this feels like a typical amount of interaction for me. I don’t use AI constantly, but it’s always in the back of my mind as an option, like a potential tool I keep reaching for when things get complex or when I want to double-check my understanding. What changes the frequency is context: if I’m on a work task, I hesitate; if I’m studying, I use it more freely. That difference comes down to accountability. At work, my writing represents the office; at uni, AI is more like a personal tutor.
