Text: AI research Study - Entry 4 - 4 September 2025, 1:56pm Today’s entry will be shorter than normal unfortunately as today is very busy. Nonetheless, AI is interesting in the regard of how much I rely on it today. While I do believe I could still perform my daily life normally without AI, having it there to help is something that makes tasks easier. Additionally, I definitely rely on it to an extent with covering content from university, as I have ADHD so focusing and staying on task is a struggle. Having the AI there to help and talk topics through as many times as I ask is incredibly useful. Being able to use the AI to help plan and schedule is also incredibly useful, despite some of its estimates being overly optimistic (like getting 800 words out in less than an hour at 2am). Despite this I find learning with ChatGPT to be a good method with my ADHD as it’s like having someone to talk to and clarify my understanding. Often, I’m typing paragraphs trying to explain a concept as best as I can for my own understanding but also my ability to explain it, and ChatGPT will point out the flaws, errors, where wording can be tighter, etc. In addition to working well with my ADHD, I should also note it pairs extremely well with my learning aptitude. Upon my diagnosis of ADHD in grade 4-5, the report came back with a bunch of other test results about me. This included things like my focus (extraordinarily poor), reading ability, writing, verbal and non-verbal communication, memory and ability to learn. While I was fairly average across the board (apart from focus and attentiveness, which was in the bottom 3rd percentile), the results also showed an extraordinary high score in memory, but also learning aptitude (the speed at how long it takes to learn new things). This result was in the 98th percentile, which I was not told about until around 2023. My memory ability was also extremely high, but not to the extent of my learning aptitude. While a lot of this doesn’t inherently relate to AI, I bring it up because my speed at which I can learn directly affects how I use AI to study. ChatGPT is good because it can adapt to my learning speed and help me make sure I consolidate concepts into my knowledge. It also lets me test it and I can ask it to challenge me about what I’ve learned so far too. The most recent example of this has been the past week, where I have covered the content from weeks 1-6 from my subject equity and trusts. One week ago, I was nearly clueless about any of the content, basically learning things like "what is equity", and "what is the purpose of equity". I managed to do this because of AI. While perhaps I could’ve done it without AI, it may have taken much longer, or I would have greater gaps in my knowledge. AI is a resource that helps me optimize my learning, and its ability to adapt to help me is extremely effective. Despite how challenging it may be to focus on assignments and university sometimes; I make absolute sure of the work I put on my assignments is produced by me. I find it dishonourable to claim work that I didn’t produce. While AI may help me take the steps to learn about the content for the assignment and how to stay on top of my workload, I refuse to let it do the work for me. At the end of the day, I know there is a great importance in being able to produce the work myself. AI probably could do a better job than me, but what really matters is my ability to produce the work myself. Having AI as a means of understanding how to do the work is useful, as that knowledge can be reapplied if I am faced with a similar problem. I wouldn’t have that skill if AI did the work for me. AI’s purpose can extend beyond work and study though, as earlier today I asked ChatGPT about how safe my leftovers were to eat. I know a simple google search can also answer this, but ChatGPT’s answer is tailored to my situation, providing a much more personalized and reasoned answer to my query. This goes beyond what a google search provides, as the AI analyses the facts of my personal scenario. Additionally, with this, it makes me question the accuracy of AI, because from experience I know AI usually likes to stick with its answers, unless compelling evidence states otherwise (in some cases a strong opinion also persuades the AI if it’s a subjective matter). It makes me wonder if different AIs may come to different conclusions on certain questions. I know that classmates have used ChatGPT and CoPilot in tandem to complete tutorial questions, which makes me wonder to what degree that improves their work, if at all. I guess by using CoPilot and ChatGPT to help answer a question you could get different responses, as I believe they are built off separate databases. A lot of the data would be shared though, but to what extent CoPilot may be more knowledgeable than ChatGPT on a topic, or vice versa, I don’t know. It would be interesting to test this out, maybe tomorrow. I take back what I said about making a short response, I got a bit carried away. I apologize if there’s any random jumps between topics or poor spelling/wording/grammar/punctuation.

And I did criminal law, statutory interpretation, Intro to law and tort law. And it was a big step. It was massive jump from, you know, doing other degrees to doing law. Law is such a different degree compared to the rest, so much harder, so much more time and effort that you need to invest in so that was a year ago. But for two years ago, it definitely wasn't. I didn't know what I wanted to do. I was very lost. I had tried many different things. You know, at one point I was even considering dropping out of uni. I just had no idea of what I wanted to do. But two years ago, yeah, just a bit lost, just working a bunch. And I definitely sometimes, you know, being 23 and being at uni for so long now, I definitely get FOMO. Text: I've decided to dictate this particular entry to make it more of a stream of consciousness sort of a thing, in keeping with the ethnographic nature of this study. There's nothing quite like a bit of Freudian free association as part of one’s psychotherapy as part of sharing one’s narrative. The short answer to today's prompt is, ‘no’. When I entered the law degree as an undergraduate in early 2024, my plan was to complete the degree as quickly as possible, studying it full time, and then aiming for the Bar exam to become a Barrister (obviously). Out of course, life is full of surprises and uncertainty, although in reality, I should have known with absolute certainty that my ex-wife would absolutely fuck up my entire plan because she is one of the most incapable, inefficient, joie de vivre parasites … a veritable millstone around my neck … for years, continuing to perniciously bleed my soul into an irreversible existential anaemia, even after our separation. So, halfway through 2024, I had to stop studying law full time so I could go back to my soul-destroying primary job to earn enough money to try and help my useless ex-wife deal with a legal problem that, in fairness, was all Centrelink's fuck-up, yet my millstone … sorry, ex-wife, still found a way to turn what should have been a lay down misère into an absolute clusterfuck that put me into debt, all because she and her equally useless, not to mention insipid, arrogant and dismissive solicitors who were supposed to be specialists in administrative law spend thousands of dollars of my money greasing their barrister buddies and, at the first sign of any resistance, rolled over like the pathetic bitches that they were and just gave up without so much as a whimper, let alone a fight. Text: The answer is very much, no, no, it is not. I have always wanted to be a lawyer. I have always wanted to do law, ever since I saw Tony Abbott eating an onion on national television, and I thought I could do better. Yep. I then found out most politicians did law. I figured out later I didn't want to be a politician, because I just was, like, that sounds awful to be so in the public eye, my very ambitious 10 year old, 12 year old self looked up how much it would be to go to Harvard Law, and then quickly also dropped that dream. Once I realized how much that was, I figured out I liked intellectual property, and I had it in my head at the start of my degree, I also thought maybe public international law. I was very realistic. I didn't think I was going to be like some human rights lawyer. I was like, No, I want a safe, stable career path where I can earn enough money to live comfortably. I was actually really hoping that I would have graduated by the time that AI came about, I was hoping at least generative AI in the sense that we know it now. I was hoping I would have graduated and been working in the field for at least two years, so that I'd be a little bit experienced, so I would be able to help, like write or actually work on the cases of all of all of the really interesting questions that I knew were going to arise because of AI. Obviously that has not happened. I am in my I even if I had stuck to my original career plan, so study plan, and graduated on time, which would have been semester one of this year. I, you know, that's obviously chat GBD was released in 2022 and that forever changed everything. Yeah, everything. I'm not gonna lie. I feel personally, and I know this is petty, but I feel personally a bit resentful of that, that the world has been altered forever. And you know you're not going to put that cap back in its box anymore. Companies are too self involved to desiring of profits for that to ever be the case. So that's a bit of a bummer, won't lie. And yeah, I now have to plan my life around AI and around the concept that AI may eradicate the need for lawyers in five to 10 years, I don't think it will eradicate them at first. I think we've definitely got some time left before that happens. And I think by the time that lawyers are not lawyering as much anymore, I think that everyone is fucked. Excuse my language, because I think eventually it will get to that point of, you know, only the best of the best are going to actually be working, and everyone else will be on probably universal basic income, and hopefully we tax AI bots then and what they generate, which will fund UBI. Fingers crossed, however, between then and now is going to be, there's an awful gap where millions of people are going to suffer. I think, yeah, millions people will suffer as we figure out how this works, what to do the appropriate response. So I count myself lucky that I'm probably in a safe path. I also think there'll be a massive gap between, you know, obviously only the best of the best will do it. But then how do we get the junior people to become the best of the best, if we're not ever paying junior people or giving them the entry level experience, because AI will be doing all of it. So I think that's also going to be an interesting trouble to navigate. So no, my career and everything is not the same as it was one to two years ago, because I'm now having to factor AI into it. Not gonna lie, it's immensely stressful having to factor AI into it. I'm glad that we've got some buffer time. I'm glad that, you know, for a while it'll be just lawyers who don't use AI will be replaced by lawyers who use AI. But honestly, if we could put this entire cat back in its box and pretend it never happened, I would touch that button in an instant. I hate that this is where we are. I hate that it's AI is doing art jobs instead of we're having a robot do dishes like, why couldn't we start with getting AI to do the boring, menial tasks that everyone hates doing. Why is it trying? Why are people trying to use it to take away our creative outlet, which is our one thing that make one of the things that makes us so human? I went on a bit of a tangent there, so I apologize for that. But in essence, no, my career is not plan is not where it was one to two years ago. I've now factored AI into a lot of stuff. And I'm now much more on the intellectual property path, because I think it's going to be safer and more stable. Yay.

Text: My expected career path is not all that different from what it was several years ago. I have held the understanding that I want to go into law for approximately 5 - 6 years now and I am yet to be discouraged in that pursuit. The only difference I would say from what I expected to what I am doing now is that I have specialised somewhat, and honed in on the areas that I am interested in. Other than that I do not see that there has been any significant change. In regards to AI, I am confident that my job will not be replaced, at least not anytime in the near future. As I am writing this I note the recent Federal Circuit and Family Court decision to bar a Victorian solicitor from acting as a principal due to their use of AI. I feel as though I see these articles popping up every week or two at this point, I note that there was a similar recent decision in the Western Australian jurisdiction, but I don’t believe that there was any such punitive response. It is clear from these stories that AI cannot, at least in its current state, do the job of a solicitor. I hope that it will never be able to, and that people stop attempting to give it the ability to. I tend to think about this excerpt that I saw circulating around the internet from an IBM handbook or memo (not sure what exactly to be honest). It read to the effect of that a machine is not a person, and as such cannot be held responsible for a decision and should not be given the authority to make decisions. I think we have strayed too far from that mantra. Even if AI were to achieve the level of competency required in the profession, it would never be able to relate to a client. It would never be able to assist a person in a time of need. It would never be able to be human. I think that element of the profession is vastly overlooked.

Text: I literally have no idea. In the context of AI? I guess? I think ChatGPT may have been still a concept or a toy two years ago. About this time last year I watched as my team in a major government department (Treasury) launched its own AI in order to combat public servants using ChatGPT. As a communications and events officer at the time who suddenly saw how quickly the creative, and largely also the planning, aspects of my role could 100% be done by machine, that was a bit of a wake up call. I quickly found a job as a paralegal and moved into law after that. Side note, but I wonder how that's going in terms of transparency and FOI requests.. From the concept of what I wanted to do as a lawyer then and what I want to do now, all that's happened in that two years is that I've become aware that my ability to practice and be a great lawyer is going to be hampered by my desire to be a good and present mother. I don't have the time to be a junior solicitor working 60 hours a week in a commercial firm, because my husband already does that (not law, sure, but he works more like 70-80 hours a week). Our kids need one of us to be around, and we need to pay the mortgage, so. I guess the being around job falls to me! Luckily I work at a community legal centre, which is ridiculously family friendly and actually pays juniors way better than they could earn in the big firms, and there's no billing (plenty of funding pressure, but no billing). The downside is the work is elementary, it's all initial advice or assisting people to self rep. It's boring. The only time our solicitors set foot in a court room is for DV duty lawyer service (which is NOT boring). And there's a perception of community law drawing in those who couldn't hack it anywhere else, which in the case of my firm.. Harsh, but it's not massively far from the truth.. I'm sitting on first class honours at the moment and have all the things (except enough time) which would may me really attractive to the big firms. I have the potential (and apparently the arrogance) to do really, really well. I want to be a barrister, either in criminal or something to do with social justice (admin law is appealing). We don't even do trial work. I've only seen the type of work that goes into trial prep because one of our family lawyers used to work for a busy ICL, and she preps our parenting clients for final hearings like she's briefing counsel. I'm worried starting out in a community legal centre is going to hold me back. Do I have much of a choice though? This has sweet F all to do with AI. I have seen a lot of ways that community lawyers could benefit from AI. Drafting affidavits and documents for family law (ok, so that's how paralegals could benefit 😆😆), legal research (if we could ever trust the damn things to stop making up cases..), calendar and appointment management - we could even do wonderful things with AI chat bots to expand community legal education and legal information services.. AI could do so much to help bridge the gap between funding and need. But do I want to do it? Not particularly. Not right now anyway.

Text: When I initially read this prompt, I thought that I would be able to answer it without much difficulty, but now as I’m writing this, it has become evident to me that answering that question is much more difficult than I thought. While the general answer I would give to a person on the street is yes, when I stop to truly ask myself about that answer, it becomes complicated. The correct answer is that I still am continuing with the same plan I had since grade 10 of high school, which now is nearly 8 years ago. The career path that I am trying to lay out for myself is to become a mediator, most of this was due to my love for law throughout high school. Legal studies was one of my top subjects and I truly saw myself as capable of being a mediator, and to this day I still hold out hope that the belief will come true. However, when I stop to think about the logistics of achieving this goal, it has become apparent that I haven’t the slightest Idea on how to truly achieve that goal. And while I feel as if I am making progress towards that goal by continuing with my double degree of Law and Psychology, I am starting to question if this is the right path for me, or if the assumptions that I made as a teenager are still valid. While I do believe that I am working towards that goal, I am starting to have doubts if this is the right path for me, while I fought hard to get into this double degree, judging by the difference in performance between my Law subjects and my Psychology subjects, I think it is necessary to question if a job in the legal profession is within the scope of my capabilities. While this may sound rather macabre, I do find some solace in my actions when I remember all of the truly illuminating experiences I have had and I hope I will continue to have on my journey through university. While I worry that my skills may be lacking, I do not for a second regret my choice, I may cast doubt on the choice, as I have said previously, but I do not believe I would have been able to meet the people I know now, get the perspectives I hold now, and learn the skills I know now without the choices I have made. Text: I have been haunted by my contracts exam from last semester and it has made me very anxious going into equity and property law subjects that have 60% exams. I wanted to write about exams today, because I feel their format is really changing as AI develops First of all, I am excellent at assignments. I just love having more time, I can space out my work load and I can really take the time to perfect it. Exams however can be completely ruined if you are sick on the day, some kind of external event happens, or you are just generally stressed by the rush to get on a train at 7am to make your morning exam. Manyyyyyy things like this are NOT qualifiers for a deferral (which are super annoying anyway - imagine deferring an exam in November and having to sit it in February after 3 months of not touching the unit). In contracts last semester, I had been sitting around 45/50 marks pre exam because I had done really well on the assignments. Naturally, I was sick as a dog on exam day and genuinely sat there for 30minutes doing nothing because I feared I would throw up on the floor. I left that exam feeling worse than I ever have before. In the end, I was slapped with a 14/50 grade, my first 4 at uni. These 50% exams carried SO much weight already (= added stress and arguably, is not an effective test of our knowledge because it’s a 3h test on a pre-planned day with no knowledge of the questions in advance. Sounds like a test of memory and not a test of understanding or knowledge.) Mind you, in psychology my exams are closed book too. The problem is, our entire grade falls on this exam, because there is a fear that AI is handling our assignments Skip to this semester when I found our equity and property have 60% exams. I have never been so stressed writing my assignments to make sure they are perfect, because I don’t always handle exams well. Any leverage I had with my strength in research and planned writing is gone. If anything, I’d argue that myself and many of my friends are MORE tempted to use AI to answer questions and confirm our responses because we are so worried of making any kind of mistake on this assignment that could put us in a bad position for the exam. Also, I feel it’s important to mention that yes I understand a 25/40 and a 25/60 means I will pass (for example, if I both the assignment), and a 25/60 could still be achievable (note this is as if I was sick again) however I am speaking as someone who consistently gets 6s. This means I need minimum of 40/60 on that exam. This, is less likely. It is also extremely stressful. I know so many people who are just naturally excellent at assignments, but the stress of preparing and studying for exams is frustrating, at times isolating, and overall is not worth it. In my first year of uni, there was generally 20% worth of quizzes or small tests, 40% assignment and 40% exam (roughly.) This balance meant I was way more confident heading into the exam because I already knew that I was passing or how much I would need on the final exam to get the mark I wanted (and would feel confident when the mark was roughly half the exam score available.) Is this all really worth it? Sometimes it is miserable being at uni because it feels like a constant uphill battle, but this semester I am left feeling like I better get used to 4s and 5s because I’m just shit at exams. Exams are just not realistic representations of what I can do. I am genuinely so disappointed that my academic history will forever show that I got a 4 in contracts when I knowww I am good at it, evident by my assignment mark. I hate that employers will think I’m shit at contracts and I can’t explain it’s because I nearly spewed on my paper. Unfortunately for me, I doubt even that would have been grounds for a deferral. The deferral process alone is so complicated, so don’t even want to get into that. Ideally, exams would not happen / they would be broken up into smaller pieces / they would weigh no more than 40%. Particularly in law - most of my tasks at work span 1-3 weeks. Why can exams be the same? What about take home exams? Overall I just really am disappointed that the only solution I can see as a student that uni has implemented is 60% exams and the cons far outweigh the pros. Long gone are the times I felt confident and almost excited to sit an exam. I constantly feel unprepared and like no matter what I do, a 60% exam will completely derail my mark and undermine what I clearly am capable of as is evident from my assignments

Text: What do I want to do with AI? Ugh, I don't know. It annoys the hell out of me how much I need to think about it to be honest - not in the context of participating in this research, that would be ridiculous. But how much of life is being infiltrated by computer decisions and AI and the prospect of robots.. It's exhausting when you don't trust these things. I guess that's fundamentally it for me. I don't trust AI at all. I see it's potential for good, but I also see the harm it's having, and I don't trust it. Or maybe I don't trust humans to use it properly. That's probably more to the point. In the context of uni, I hate that I've decided to accelerate my degree in no small part because I'm afraid that the overuse of AI is going to taint everyone who graduates within a particular period of time. I don't use it to cheat, I respect the academic integrity declarations I make and I really want to graduate with the skills I'm paying $50k to develop. But I've already been exposed to the impact of other students not sharing my values. In my first semester the exams online, and weren't timed; you were told to complete it in 3 hours, but you were given 24. It took me 5 hours to complete my exam, but due to the academic integrity declaration, I only submitted what I had completed in 3. I didn't finish a question, and didn't do well. I got a 5 for that subject. Everyone else I spoke to got really high marks, and then I find out that they all took about 10-12 hours to finish that exam, and none of them were concerned about the academic integrity violation. I was called the idiot. The following semester was the start of dropping the exam file and the submission link, and then closing the submission link three hours later. The next year a rumour went around that grade release was so delayed because of the level of cheating in one of my subjects, which forced all the exams to be remarked. I started seeing red around then, and made the decision to get out as quickly as possible. Cue return to invigilated exams, which is a massive pain in the ass and not reflective of the reality of practice - when would we ever (outside of being a duty lawyer) not have access to tech and typing in order to construct submissions. It's only a matter of time before the degree isn't trusted or worth as much because of the perception of rife cheating and under qualified graduates. I'm worried I'll put in all this work, but because of the morons using AI to cheat, my degree will be worthless. I guess there are plenty of other ways to cheat. But the saturation of conversation and concern at the moment is all about gen AI. The uni seems to have forgotten that there are plenty of other ways for students to cheat. I pulled out of the legal placement elective this semester because the assessment pieces were designed in order to prevent cheating with gen AI. That made me so mad, that I had to put in all this extra work in a way that wasn't logical or reflective of the way I approach assessment or run my life because other students have used AI to cheat too much in the past. That took me a lot of time to set up my placement and get the approvals (my boss could do with using AI to help manage her time, tbh..).. But it was the principle for me. Don't trust me? Fine, I'm not doing the work at all. We also see judges losing their minds over lawyers and self-repped litigants submitting documents prepped by AI laced with made up cases - but how do you avoid that? Particularly for self repped litigants, they don't know that the cases are made up, and they have no way to check. The general population trusts AI - it's going to get a lot worse before it gets better. The solicitors should already know better, I'm so glad that principal was stripped of his principal practicing certificate - he shouldn't be supervising if he's not sensible enough to realise AI isn't trustworthy. What do I want to do with AI? Nothing except edit my own work. This seems like a good time actually to reflect on my work from Wednesday. I spent hours working on a letter of advice for Family Law and whittled it down as far as I could, but I was still 500 words over word count. That’s what I used AI for. My work was all my own work - the piece was fully referenced and ready to submit if the word count had been higher (I’m just noting here that I’m not trying to protect myself; I get that this could appear like I’m trying to present myself in the best light. I’m not. Actually reading back over my reflections for the past week, I think I come across pretty arrogant. And not very nice. It appears I think that literally the rest of the world is dumb. K=So that’s kind of horrifying. Not loving that for me… Something to work on…). What was I saying? Oh yeah, family law. I fed sentences from my work into ChatGPT with prompts like: make this better, does this make sense, make this shorter and snappier. And it worked really well. I never copied and pasted out of the browser into my document - it became pretty apparent when I was going through all the rules for the legal placement assessment that they can pick up on things like that - and I never used exactly what the tool gave me. I did take it’s suggestions and put them into my own voice. Sometimes ChatGPT would ask me if I wanted to make it shorter but keep the formality for legal writing; so without me giving it any clue as to what I was doing, it figured out the context of what I was doing just from the words. That’s brilliant. But not great for a student who is actually giving it an assignment question and telling it to write the letter. That’s so dangerously stupid. I don’t consider what I was doing to be cheating. Studiosity does the same thing, albeit not to the same extent. So I guess in my dream world, this is what I would use gen AI for at uni. Just to make my work better. Not to do it for me. I guess it kind of is cheating a bit when writing skills are in the CRA… Meh, I used to get paid to write, my career proves I know how to write. I don’t need law school to teach me that. And to that end, I also have a suite of 7’s from the law school that I’ve achieved without gen AI suggesting improvements (hilariously, I write so well that I got a high 6 for my constitutional law research assignment only because I researched and wrote it well. My application of law to the facts score was bloody awful.). I know what I’m doing, I’m just time poor. But that’s scary too. Not everyone who uses gen AI will know what they’re doing, and they will use it not just to improve their work, but to do their work. They’ll trust it, and it will harm people. Who wants a doctor who graduated medical school care of ChatGPT? No thanks. AI is dumbing down the world. I can't see it ending well. You ever see that movie Idiocracy?? That's where this is going.

Text: Today I am working on two assignments which are both due tomorrow. I used ChatGPT to help me find different ways to phrase clauses and to get me thinking. But I find it funny when people, usually older people, say that students can use GenAI to write their assignments. Due to academic misconduct rules, I think it’s almost impossible to get away with something like that. And most students, particularly in law, are not willing to take such a stupid risk. GenAI only really became more known and popular when I was in grade 12 in 2023, but I rarely used it then. I thought that people who used it were dumb, if I’m being honest. As in, the only people that would resort to that are people that aren’t smart or dedicated enough to just do the work and thinking themselves. And since I was young I have had pride in my intelligence, so I didn’t think I needed to resort to it. But since high school my mentality has kind of shifted. I think working harder doesn’t always mean you are working smarter. I think there are just some activities or jobs that you don’t need to waste brain power on. I.e. it would be a wiser choice to spend time on work that is not easily produced by AI. Yes it might be a shortcut, but what’s the harm in taking shortcuts if they end in the same result, or better. So now, when people tell me they use AI, I no longer assume that they’re lazy or unintelligent. In fact, when my 22 year old sister told me she never uses GenAI for anything uni related, I honestly questioned her intelligence. I was so taken aback. Text: Date: Saturday 06 September 2025 Time: 11.04pm But I guess I would like to write about how my sister, in Year 11, uses AI to study for her exams and why I think it’s so detrimental. This is a conversation I had in the car with my mum yesterday and I think it would be useful to put in here. I studied Literature in year 11 and 12, and my sister is now in year 11 also studying Literature. I did get 100/100 in year 12 (in a humble way) and I find lots of enjoyment from helping my sister study. Unfortunately, she has never loved school like I did - she doesn’t enjoy learning and she hates studying. This year she has failed 2 exams already, and so we’ve been on her about studying for exams this time around (before she starts year 12 content). However I feel like her use of AI is actually a detrimental reliance on AI. We told her to make some flash cards for biology, which she did… kind of. She got some AI website and input all of her content and then got it to create flashcards for her. Which I guess might have been okay if she had already studied the content and this was a last little bit of revision, but that wasn’t the case here. She uses AI to study, and I just can’t help but feel like she’s not actually retaining any information (I guess we will see when she gets her exam results back). I learned all about memory in psychology, and how the more associations you have with information, the better you will remember it. This is why for my exams, I had coloured posters hanging on my wall, I wrote out flash cards, I wrote out skeleton responses for over 20 potential essay questions, etc. Because you aren’t just reading the information, you are now physically writing it, and you’ve associated it with the colour. Not to mention, you take an exam at a desk and it’s handwritten, not on a computer, so if you study by writing, there’s that kind of atmospheric or environmental association as well. I feel like her use of AI is pretty much stripping every method of memorization because all she is doing is reading the information.

Text: Today I was noticing how normal AI feels in my routine. It is almost like it is just sitting in the background, even when I am not using it. When I study, I know I could ask it to break down a tough reading or explain a concept. At work, even if I do not actually use it for drafting, the thought is always there that I could. What has been standing out to me is how it changes my confidence. In some ways it is reassuring, like a safety net if I am unsure about something. But sometimes I do wonder if I rely on it too much. With law especially, I know skills like judgement and precision are things I need to practice myself, not outsource. That is why I try to keep AI as a support, not the whole solution. Something else I have been thinking about is how hidden AI use feels around me. People do not really admit to using it, even though I am sure most of them do. It feels like there is a bit of silence or stigma there. In the legal profession, that sort of secrecy would not work. Policies and ethics will have to shift because AI is not going away. Text: There are a lot of ideas about Gen AI fairness and justice swirling around my brain and it’s hard to try and connect them, though I guess the best way I can summarise what I’ve been thinking about is: ‘Universities risk falling behind the very environments they are preparing students to enter, unless they develop nuanced, transparent, and pedagogically sound frameworks for what AI use is acceptable and where.’ At the moment, the easiest and (dare I say it when referring to institutions of higher learning) the most intellectually lazy solution is to just blanket-ban Gen AI. Yet AI, and yes, even Gen AI, is becoming normalised in day-to-day work in the wider corporate world. Simply banning it without finding a way to balance the nuanced considerations of learning first principles of law and legal thinking to understand how to efficiently use AI is like training surgeons in surgical techniques but banning scalpels from exams. Or perhaps a better analogy would be in training architects to design using CAD software, but then require them to draw blueprints by hand in assessment. In some ways, I get why the Law Practitioners Admission Board wants hand-written, in-person, on-campus invigilated exams for Priestly 11 subjects, but the similarities of the analogy of training architects to design using CAD software, but then require them to do an in-person, on-campus invigilated exam requiring them to draw blueprints by hand to prevent the use of Gen AI begins to show the subtle deficiencies of the Law Practitioners Admission Board’s anti-Gen AI policies. A corollary to this that Gen AI, and AI generally, is almost ubiquitous and will inevitably become embedded in almost everything we do. At the moment, it’s sometimes visible and known, though even now, AI, and Gen AI to a point, are camouflaged, but there will come a tipping point in the insidious, invariable spread of AI, even Gen AI, where it is so pervasive that it becomes invisible. Even where it’s known to be there, people will be so used to it that it will hide in plain sight where people won’t see the AI wood because of all the trees. How then can universities have meaningful policies which prohibit the use of AI and Gen AI when it is everywhere? And, further to my discussion in my first essay, it’s not only hypocritical for universities to have policies that punish students for using technology out of desperation due to the failure of universities to have policies, or to enforce those policies, about the quality, consistency and transparency of their teaching and marking. What’s also hypocritical, and deliciously ironic, that AI, and early Gen AI, is not only embedded into ‘acceptable’ tools like Grammarly, Word, Google Docs, Adobe etc. Machine learning algorithms and AI are already embedded in software that universities rely on like Turnitin. So, the very software which is used to try and detect AI use in submissions is, ironically, reliant on AI to do so. Thus, even if a student was doing the right thing and refrained from getting ChatGPT to write their assessments for them, the same students are unknowingly using AI and simple GenAI (using spelling and grammar checking, and predictive text tools) to help form sentences or rephrase ideas. Meanwhile, universities are banning Gen AI while relying on it themselves. Universities develop official policies treat ‘unauthorised’ use of AI as if there's a clean, binary on/off switch, without recognising just how much they rely on it themselves. All this begs the question-as AI becomes so embedded in learning tools that it’s use is implicit and unconscious, how can academic integrity policies meaningfully distinguish between 'assisted' and 'unassisted' work? And further, is it even fair to punish students for the university’s own educational and assessment failures while hypocritically relying on AI themselves? Universities need to first understand how Gen AI is used in the modern legal workplace and tailor their curriculums to match. Then, and only then, can they come up with meaningful policies about the use of Gen AI by students, and how to fairly enforce those policies without being a bunch of sanctimonious hypocrites.

Text: While I would like to think that the current curriculum taught to us throughout our journey in the law school will be enough to survive in the modern world, it is evident that that assumption is based in naiveite. To extend on that point, while it is evident that the law school does prepare us for the most part, with the teaching of essential skills such as statutory interpretation or the different facets of law such as contracts. For a lawyer to be both efficient and productive in this modern environment it is evident that they will need to be able to use every tool at their disposal. Therefore, while AI is a rather recent development, there can be no dispute as to the power it provides someone in the legal sector. However, while learning institutions are quick to denounce and demonise the use of these tools, which is understandable considering their position as educators, it is evident that taking a hardline approach to it’s use will only end up being a fruitless endeavour. Therefore, if the use of AI is going to happen regardless it begs the question of if students should be taught the correct way to use these systems in order to maximise the benefits provided by AI while avoiding the detriments that are attached with its use. While I have previously stated that I hold rather conservative views on AI, if I had a chance to be taught how to use these systems to the fullest, I would be the first person to raise my hand for it. Text: ’ I think that the most important skill a person in the law profession needs with respect to Gen AI is knowing: (a) when it’s helpful and when to NOT use it; (b) having the discipline to check accuracy every time you use it, and not letting it slide because you’re too tired to check and go over it; (c) being able to recognise patterns or common mistakes that it makes so you know you definitely need to check that information (even though AI is advancing and is probably making less of these mistakes). These were my key takeaways (aside from not using it at all) from the case where the lawyer used Gen AI in their submissions and in fact submitted a large number of cases that did not exist, and that ChatGPT (or whatever GenAI they used) made up. I think that the responsibility for learning these skills is imposed on both the person and our educational institutes. I think it is a huge part of ethics, and probably a whole new realm of ethics which has developed since the creation and take-off of GenAI. But, as often talked about, lawyers are to be honest, display integrity and be of good character, and I think that someone who consciously makes an effort to display those traits will have self-discipline in their use of GenAI, and not take the easy route even when no one is watching.

Text: When I think about what AI skills, I’ll actually need as a lawyer, the main one is just being able to tell when the tool is wrong. That news story about the lawyer caught filing fake cases using ChatGPT is a perfect example, the problem wasn’t the tech itself, it was the lawyer not checking the output. So, I think the real skill is fact-checking, cross-referencing, and having the discipline to slow down, even if you’re under pressure. At the same time, I can see how tempting it would be to lean on AI when you’re drowning in work. That’s why I think it’s not only about technical skills (like good prompting) but also about judgment, knowing when AI is useful, and when it’s way too risky. Who’s responsible for teaching us that? Honestly, it’s a mix. Uni should definitely give us more than just "don’t use AI or you’ll get done for misconduct." The profession also needs to step up with clear guidelines, so new lawyers aren’t guessing what’s acceptable. But in the end, it’s on me. If I put something in front of a judge one day, it’s my name and reputation, not ChatGPT’s. So yeah, the AI skills I need are less about fancy tricks and more about being careful, skeptical, and willing to do the boring part of double-checking everything. It’s not glamorous, but it’s better than being in a Guardian article for all the wrong reasons.

Text: Personally, I think that in the legal industry, AI can replace/help humans in more ways than we thought. One typical thing is that AI can store client/case information accurately and in large quantities, which would take humans more time to find. If programmed carefully, I think AI will be a useful tool in storing and synthesizing case law for use by lawyers. One skill that I see some countries/legal institutions applying is using AI for authoritative drafting. Using AI to draft documents in a certain format, to synthesize information and to check style/clarity are not new. I have always thought about how AI should be taught more in general education and in the legal industry in particular to maximize its capabilities. Instead of letting students use AI in a vague and sneaky way, schools should teach and companies should train students how to apply AI to legal work. Schools can guide students on how to find and apply AI, for example, brief analysis, case summary, "explain this term", because the law industry has a lot of confusing and new terms. Instead of waiting for the professor to explain via email after 3-5 days, students can talk to AI, which will always patiently answer the question immediately after how long. Instead of warning students that AI may give wrong information, why don't universities program the right information for AI? In the current era of rapid AI development, if basic training does not include AI, the market will produce "two layers of lawyers": those who understand and know how to take advantage of the tools and those who are left behind by the tools. I believe that law schools should teach the basic methods and ethics, which go hand in hand with AI tools.

Text: AI Research study Entry 7 - 8 September 2025 - 9:10pm I missed yesterday's entry log however I learned something interesting about AI. My manager mentioned to me how he uses math GPT, an AI specifically designed for engineers and physics students. It made me curious as to whether a Law-GPT existed. After searching, this AI does exist, albeit requiring a subscription to use. It's made me consider where we are headed with this technology where there's a contradiction in what student today are being taught, compared to how the workplace is changing because of AI. On one hand there is a strongly importance in not using AI for everything. Having the skill to analyze evaluate and apply knowledge that is being learned is something every generation has had to do in some regard. This skill remains important as its helps define as people what decisions we make and how we adapt to our circumstances. This is referring to a professional or academic context but extends to many other faculties in life. On the other hand AI is something that will not slow down as a developing technology. It was only earlier this year when AI could start producing lifelike videos which anyone could access. Comparing AI models from 2023 to what is available now is an incredible leap in capability. From 2023 chatGPT was only able to provide certain responses and had very limited knowledge. Today chatGPT is able to have persistent memories, send reminders to my phone and set up personal goals to achieve. It can even generate a visualized road map of where I am in my uni degree if I wanted. Nonetheless I find there is an importance in understanding both these skills, because AI is something that cannot be ignored in the workplace. In my opinion, finding the cut balance between utilizing AI for productivity and engaging critical thinking skills when producing work is a new skill that needs to be nurtured into education carefully, knowing where AI can help but still being able to produce quality work without it.

Text: Today is seventh of September, 2025 It feels like you're reading my mind, because this is exactly what I talked about at the panel discussion that I was on, which is really, really cool. Okay, so Gen AI and the legal profession is obviously changing the legal profession. And as I've said a lot, it comes down to critical thinking. There's a real fear. It's not actually just not even talking about law. There's a real fear around AI, and the immediate response is to ban it, which we see time and time again in history, is not the right solution. So what is unfortunate to see in education is this ban. We're never, I would say, only this year have I seen university assessments where we're encouraged to do it, and actually they both come from teachers of the law, tech, innovation, minor. So it's still not widespread, still within small sect of law and tech educators that are pushing it. But yeah, right now law students strictly those who just do their law degree are not-universities are not teaching them generic [generative] skills. Now what Gen AI skills will be needed in law? Well, prompting is massive. I hate the word the job title, prompt engineer, or skill prompt engineer, because it feels like it's just degrading the engineering profession, because anyone can be a damn prompt engineer. But in seriousness, like that's what this lawyer's loss [lawyers/law] or career in law needs-someone who knows how to prompt AI and how to use it critically. And I also want to note that law firms, basically every big law firm, has their own internal AI now, which is shocking and like how it's such a disconnect that universities are blocking, banning it from assessments, yet it's super desirable in industry and like, every paralegal and grad lawyer I've spoken to have just kind of just basically said, Oh yeah, you know, I use the AI every day. I'm like, what? Which is quite serious. Now, when it comes to who is responsible for teaching it, it's a very complex thing, as I've kind of said. So yeah, in terms of responsibility, I definitely think it should be universities, and I think it actually starts at the bottom. When we think about tech skills like coding and even, let's get even more granular, like language learning, that all starts at a very young age, building up very simple skills and ultimately bringing you to today's date where you're an expert at it. Safe to play is what I want to emphasize-that, you know, there's fear mongering. There's fear mongering of Gen AI. Text: Sam would be right, and Maria is not only being very, very naughty, but also self-defeating. Maria might get away with what she’s doing with Gen AI, but she’s losing the opportunity to develop the essential skills of research, analysis, critical thinking, learning to apply logic/avoid the traps of cognitive and logical biases, and formal academic writing. All of these things are absolutely crucial to being a good lawyer (assuming that she is indeed studying law), though in fairness, those skills are crucial to any tertiary academic discipline, from a bachelor’s degree in fine arts (qualifying graduates to rely on Centrelink payments or if they can get a job, it’s asking, ‘Would you like fries with that?’), to STEM subjects, law, engineering or medicine (qualifying graduates to actually get a job). Indeed, those skills are crucial to preventing living one’s life with nothing better to do than circulating moronic social media memes. Once upon a time, universities were not just sausage factories pumping out graduate white-collar professionals that are only able to regurgitate the socialist rhetoric fed to them by the equally socialist academic elite ‘teaching’ them, who themselves were shielded from reality by the impenetrable silo they all occupied. Universities used to be a hot-bed of freedom-of thought, of expression, of passion, of politics, of rebellion, of individualism-and shit-tons of cannabis and mind-altering drugs. There was no political ‘correctness’, there was political debate. Students were encouraged to explore ideas, push cultural norms and challenge their own opinions. Now, if a university student lets slip that they voted ‘no’ in the Voice Referendum, they’re not genuinely asked why they came to that intellectual, political position … they’re dismissed as anti-intellectual racist bigots by everyone else on campus, from the Dean to the janitor who are all ‘enlightened’, though couldn’t construct an alternative argument to their social media feed if their life depended on it. Anyway, I digress. Maria needs to learn to think for herself. That requires skills. Skills in research, critical analysis, logical construction of arguments with awareness of cognitive biases and logical fallacies. ChatGPT is clever, and is getting smarter with each iteration. I got an e-mail advertising ChatGPT version 5 today, so I gave it a challenge. I asked it to write an academic analysis of a relatively obscure case decided in the NSW District Court in 2023 which centred on a judicial interpretation of ss 5B, 5O of the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW), with a particular emphasis on the judicial tension of interpreting s 5O from a generalised cf a specific, granular analysis of professional performance over hundreds of individual consultations in a GP setting over an extended period of time (Curran v Yaramati [2023] NSWDC 546 if you’re interested). I was safe to use this as a test of ChatGPT’s new powers as the case has nothing to do with any of my current law subjects, and I knew the case well anyway being present in the Court for much of the trial (though I can’t really say more than that without risking my anonymity in this study). ChatGPT’s academic review of the case was exceptionally detail-specific, yet nuanced in its analysis. I think ChatGPT is getting to the point where it’s going to overtake the intelligence of a lot of junior graduates. And I guess that’s the point with Maria. Graduates will have to be able to at least match, or better to outdo, Gen AI upon graduation. Thus, any student using Gen AI to do all of the thinking for them at university is, in effect, making themselves redundant when they eventually graduate and have to outperform Gen AI in the workplace. They’ll invariably wind up with the Arts graduates lining up at Centrelink or manning the Maccas drive-thru. In my opinion, it's better to fail and learn from that failure than it is to take short-cuts-whether that be using recycled work published on some random internet service or Gen AI- and ‘succeed’. Maria might graduate, but she’s failed in the workplace before she’s even started, devoid of critical thinking skills and a pay cheque … an intellectual, occupational and experiential waste.

Text: It's interesting because by no push of my own I had a conversation with a fellow QUT law student friend about this sort of scenario today. We had discussed how Gen AI isn't accurate for law assignments. That it will give you dodgy answers that do not follow the law. That it'll make cases up and spin a bizarre tale on different cases. That its unreliable. But then she said that she has used ChatGPT on her assignments to help with structure. She said that once she's done all of the research she'll get ChatGPT to give her a rough draft which she then edits thoroughly before moving onto the next paragraph. She justified it by saying that really the work and ideas are all her own, ChatGPT just does the first step of setting everything out. I had never considered using ChatGPT in this way. Like her I agreed that you couldn't use it for actual information, it is unreliable. But ChatGPT does give a very good summary and structure of things. Its not that we don't know how to write an assignment and structure an argument. It is simply a slightly more efficient and easier way to right an assignment. When you're pushed for time and under pressure, having a tool that gives you a start. Often its really difficult to start writing, for me it's rhe biggest hurdle. I'll have all the research and information, but then knowing what to say first and whether an argument is actually two sub arguments and should be separated. Theres a lot that makes completing uni assignments difficult that has nothing to do with the actual assignment. So if there was a tool that gave you that start, perhaps a headstart, why wouldn't you use it? I think there is still a massive concern about genuine learning. If we continue to rely on ChatGPT to write our first draft, will we lose the skill of drafting? Will we get lazy and not fact check the output. At this stage, given the limits ot ChatGPT or CoPilot it seems vital that everything produced by it is thoroughly checked so that there are no made up cases cited or incorrect law. But imagine if we didn't have that initial stress. In a way we are still learning, especially if you're redrafting everything into your own words. It's simply a tool to assist in writing. While previously I may have been totally opposed to using Gen AI, now I'm starting to question whether it is the way to go. This questioning I think comes from wanting to get ahead, wanting to achieve a 6 or 7.

Text: Before I provide an answer to this prompt, I would like to acknowledge that while this prompt is by its very nature contentious, it is a question worth asking considering the predominant uses of AI especially in the educational sphere. In my view, while I would like to both agree and disagree, that would not answer the question. Therefore, a more realistic answer, and one that in my opinion is more appropriate is that this cannot be considered learning. While there are some who would contest my answer on the ground that it would in some capacity teach how to properly structure an argument, if the AI is presenting both the structure and the arguments, then it becomes necessary to question at what point the critical thinking required to come to those conclusions actually takes place. In my view, if a person uses AI in this way, then it cannot be considered as genuine learning as none of the experiences that occur during one’s regular process of learning occurs. To elucidate what I mean by this point, it is no stretch of the imagination that in the process of trying to learn something, a person will hopefully read up about a subject of interest, and once learning about some of the principles of this interest they will start to ask questions that extend their knowledge beyond this initial point. Hopefully as this cycle continues the person is able to comprehend the guiding principles for what they are trying to learn and then start to think critically about the knowledge they have been given and create a system that allows for them to understand and interpret what they have seen and answer the questions they may have. While that thought may not be easy to follow it is essentially a water downed version of the work of Jean Piaget and his constructivism theory. However, it would be hasty of me to not consider the other side of the argument where this use of AI could be considered as genuine learning. If I disregard my view on the matter, there is an argument that can be made that while Maria blatantly ripping off the AI is not learning, the structure and arguments that the AI output provides might allow for Maria to have access to information that did not occur to her at the time, or that might not have ever been conceived without the AI output. In those situations, I would make an argument for that being genuine learning with the AI providing a learning opportunity that would not have been present with Maria’s current knowledge alone. However, the crux of that argument, at least to me, is that it relies on Maria being cognisant of what the AI has presented to her, and what that prompt has made possible, and without being acutely aware of the points that have been presented and what points you have not considered, then it is essentially a game of copy and pasting the output while trying to make it look like you actually did the work you were supposed to do.

Text: Personally, I do not agree with this way of learning. I believe that each assignment is designed to exploit and test students' knowledge. Therefore, building structures and arguments from the beginning is a must, to test students' knowledge. If AI sets the framework, Maria's edits will be purely formal and empty of knowledge. Especially if students never experience the "brainstorming moment" of building a foundation, the first steps when starting to do an assignment. However, I also find that using AI to build structures for an assignment is very "addictive". When AI can provide perspectives that we have not thought of, when AI can talk about our ideas in a more polished, logical voice, we will not be able to stop thinking about them when starting to do another assignment. Text: AI Research study Entry 8 - 8 September 2025 - 10:07pm Today I saw a classmate using ChatGPT and tabbing constantly between it and a word document. Using AI for structure and arguments in your assignments is well within this blurred line. It really depends to what extent the AI is applied. Using AI for structure and arguments can scale between having it produce simple headings and generally dot pointing what concepts should be addressed, or can involve a full scale layout with arguments prewritten. In my belief academic misconduct should be judged on the level of input from the person. AI should be allowed to a limited extent in my opinion. I do understand that a 0 tolerance policy works effectively to prevent any unauthorised AI use, but I feel like there can be a level of leniency where it could help point students in the right direction, rather than letting them write a completely incorrect response. This is because I find having a system of feedback can be extremely beneficial to learning, reinforcing better responses and ideas, and discouraging bad writing behaviours.

Text: Yeah, sure. There are some tasks or roles that don’t require much mental effort. Whether we should farm them out to AI is actually a very nuanced, philosophical discussion given the flow-on effects, now and into the future. The cynical part of me loves a quote from the January page of my despair.com calendar I got this year. (see image on side) It’s funny, because like all of the best parodies, they’re actually scarily accurate mirrors of reality. There are going to be a lot of tasks or roles that don’t require much mental effort that someone is currently employed, though may not be for too much longer as AI takes over. How do you make your job AI proof? According to Geoffrey Hinton, the ‘Godfather of AI’, become a plumber (https://youtu.be/giT0ytynSqg?si=PbU995GbB2jQVU5A). Of course, that’s assuming that AI hasn’t become so much smarter than us that it’s sentient, and every dystopian sci-fi movie ever made will become reality. Assuming that AI doesn’t become sentient and takes over the world, whether it’s a good idea to farm out simple tasks to Gen AI, it depends on whether that task is required for learning. When I was a medical intern, fresh out of med school, my job was to do all the menial tasks from writing medication charts and discharge summaries through to formally confirming that a dead person was actually, you know, dead. Most of those tasks-sans figuring out that dead people really are dead-were the building blocks of learning good communication, early clinical reasoning, familiarity with medications, and working in a busy hospital, learning to work effectively with lots of other people to form a cohesive team. Looking back at those tasks, there would now be an AI that would do most of them way more effectively and efficiently than a first-year doctor trying to learn how to apply all the theoretical stuff from med school in a real-world environment where there’s actually (albeit, limited) responsibility. Even now, there are entire health professions that could easily be taken over by a clever AI and some basic robotics, like every pharmacist in the world. Despite their delusions of grandeur that they can be just like doctors without the additional ten years of training that actual doctors have, the primary role of pharmacists is simply to take prescriptions issued by real doctors, take the box of pills off a shelf and put a sticker on the box … and then try and upsell some useless herbal preparation to unwitting, vulnerable people to increase their profits. Well, an AI can do exactly the same thing, only better. All it needs is the right technology connecting prescriptions from real doctors to a cloud-based server that patients could forward to any AI-based dispensing machine. The AI could check the medications against the health information of the patient on the cloud, and either robotically retrieve the box of pills, put a label on the box and get it to the patient (at the point of sale, or via some form of delivery service, like Uber for prescriptions), or if there’s a possible problem, send a message back to the prescribing doctor for their clarification. It’s a win-win, well, for the patients anyway … not for pharmacists (though personally, I wouldn’t miss them. Perhaps they can all become plumbers). If the intern scenario is applied to junior solicitors fresh out of law school, then the same issues apply. The work of a junior solicitor is (I would imagine, not having been one) mostly menial grunt work doing forms, writing affidavits, preparing court documents etc, all of which could be done way more effectively by some form of Gen AI, except that would deprive the junior solicitor of the early real-world training they need to become senior solicitors or barristers or magistrates or High Court judges … So, if today’s prompt refers to tasks or roles like writing personal emails or having something to talk to for IT geeks on the autism spectrum with no social skills or ability to interact with society, or to replace all pharmacists, then great. Gen AI all the way. Though if you’re talking about using Gen AI to do the work of junior doctors or junior solicitors who need those menial tasks to build the foundation of the rest of their career, then that’s not so good. If you want to have GPs or surgeons, or solicitors or barristers, in the future and not a swathe of plumbers, then we need to be very selective about how Gen AI is integrated into workplaces, at least until Gen AI becomes sentient and we’re all plugged into the Matrix.

Text: This is a very interesting hypothetical. Considering both sides of the argument it is clear that a person could be convinced that either view is correct. However, in my opinion I would lean more towards the side of not taking the shortcuts even for menial tasks. While I cannot contest that using AI to automate grunt work is a hard argument to invalidate, there are several points that at least to me should be considered instead of mentioning efficiency and calling it a day. It is clear to me that the reason why I would not take this short cut is because I might be biased towards a task having a human element, there is a certain level of merit that is held when a person is able to perform these tasks, and it shows in people having a general sense of trust in the quality of the work when it is completed. But, upon giving this thought more consideration there lies the argument that an AI is not subject to problems such as human error and there is a statistically higher chance that the AI’s output is both more time efficient and correct. However, while many would be quick to join the camp of people that say AI should replace menial labour, I do believe that there is some benefit to be gained by people performing these tasks. Yes they can be mind numbing, and yes they can be done quicker, but a broader problem that I see in adopting AI in this fashion is that it would deny humans certain job opportunities. While, this thought may sound stupid, if we truly believe that everyone has a place in society then is it really ethical to deny people a chance to do these jobs, even if by most metrics it would be considered beneath them. Would implementing AI deprive people of the ability to learn these skills, and what would happen if a company that had swapped to using AI to do such work suddenly had an outage. In that scenario it is evident that it would be quite detrimental as there would be a large set of people who would be incapable of completing the day-to-day functions of a business. However, I can understand if a person were to interpret my ramblings as a fringe case that is tantamount to clutching at straws. But, in my view while there is certainly a place for AI to replace people doing menial and repetitive tasks day in and day out and allowing these people to have more enjoyment in their lives, I do question if the implementation of these systems would lead to massive amounts of people becoming redundant and to extend on that point, where the line is drawn in terms of menial work. If we look to popular media, there is a large sense that once AI is unleashed in these capacities, it might lead to a world where mass unemployment becomes the norm, and a world where animosity towards AI may be more common.

Text: ’ I spoke to my partner about this, reading out the prompt and asking him what he thought. What I feel like has been evident throughout a lot of my entries is that I view AI very strongly from a morality / ethical standpoint, so I was keen to hear some other perspectives on this. His perspective was based on time management - allowing time to focus on more important things, allowing for efficiency. Especially if the tasks are not onerous or meaningful, and if AI performs them to the same, if not higher, standard. And while I do agree that it would help with efficiency, especially in a world that seems to be moving so fast and people don’t really have time anymore, I told him that I always see it from a moral/ethical standpoint. While having AI read and summarise all of your emails, and getting it to respond to them, is helpful, I feel like using AI to write a few emails is a waste of resources and environmental harm for something can easily be done by humans. Which brings into question kind of a spectrum or continuum of how much AI is too much? How do we balance the use of AI and the aspiration to improve efficacy in our lives? After all, writing emails can take a really long time when you have a build up of many. But maybe we need to consider that we actually ‘need’ AI for - meaning, what can AI actually do better than the average human? I don’t feel like writing emails is something that AI is crazily beneficial for (and I do feel like the time it takes to give AI a prompt to respond to the email, you could have just written one yourself). But something that requires analysing large amounts of data, then yes AI would seem to be extremely useful, less expensive and more time effective. We both then agreed that if AI took over ‘simple roles’, like in the context of administrative work, it might impact the availability, opportunities or meaningfulness of entry roles for graduates or others trying to break into an industry, especially in a law context. For SO many students, getting an entry level role, admin role, or something similar is the aim while you’re in law school so you can finally crack into the industry and get your foot in the door. It’s also important for experience - especially for those who have no prior connection to the law - and slowly being exposed to a new environment, starting with basic work and then increasing to harder work as your skills and experience improve. If we all went from law school straight into being a solicitor, many people might have quite the culture shock. But working in a firm or a similar environment allows exposure without huge responsibilities, showing you the ropes and giving you a feel for things before what you do REALLY matters. As an aside, I am currently doing an assignment researching automated decision making and its impact on establishing legal error in administrative law. I think it’s easily forgotten or overlooked just how much of our lives and processes are automated now - and how this is not going to slow down in the future.

Text: Some things really do not need my full brainpower, and in those cases I am happy to let AI help. For example, if I need to quickly reword an email or summarise a long document just to get the gist, I do not feel guilty about using a shortcut. It frees up time and energy for the work that actually matters, like analysing cases or writing arguments in my own words. At the same time, I am careful not to let AI do the thinking for me on the parts that actually build my skills. If I used AI to write my entire assessment structure or come up with all my arguments, I might get a neat answer, but I would not have gone through the process of learning how to do it myself.
