Text: Entry 9 - 9 September 2025, 5:46pm I have a few things to say for today’s entry. This first thing I found quite funny, but also an interesting point to mention. I saw a post online about funny questions students had submitted to the teachers office about phones being banned at a school. One of these questions was: "let’s say I get caught with my phone at the end of the school day, meaning I have to hand it into the office the next day. If I go home and replace every single component in my phone with a replacement, is it still the same phone? How does the school plan to address this Grecian philosophical dilemma?" This one was pretty funny, but made me think "well what if you applied that same thought to AI?". I am a fan of philosophical dilemmas, and actually quite enjoyed studying philosophy as a subject in school, and the Ship of Theseus is no different. If I were to get an AI to generate an essay for me, but I changed every component of it, is it still AI generated? Or is it my own work? If it can be called my own work, at what point or percentage must the essay be changed to no longer be AI generated? This puzzles me from a philosophical viewpoint, because if I can consider the essay my own work, but I still communicate the same message and arguments as the original AI generated essay, is that part still my work too? or am I just a paraphraser? A better way of saying it would be "the ship of Theseus still serves the same purpose, even if all its parts have been replaced, but does that make it the original boat still?" I hope I’m communicating this point correctly because I know well that in reality it would be considered academic misconduct. Theoretically though, in the circumstances where I do rewrite an AI essay completely, I might be considered the author, but I didn’t come up with the idea, or the actual substance of the essay. I guess the original purpose of the ship of Theseus remains despite however many changes its been through. After all it is still a ship at the end of the day. I guess you could also apply Sorites paradox too, which is similar to the ship of Theseus. This questions "at what point does a thing stop being a thing?" (for example, how many straws of hay from a haybale can be removed until its no longer a haybale), instead of "at what point does a thing become another thing if you replace enough components?". If you flip this conundrum around a bit, you can ask "at what point does the influence of AI make someone’s essay into an AI generated essay?", or at least one that would breach academic integrity. I mean technically you could just rule out AI entirely, making any use or interaction with it breaches academic integrity. This covers any issue that would arise with AI use in essays in the first place, so there’s no problem, right? Absolutely not. If I googled a definition or a term, I would 90% chance get an AI summary at the top, which would count by technicality. That AI summary has now shaped part of how I may write, or understand something, which under total AI ban would be considered a breach, so there must be a line of leniency somewhere. Nonetheless, let’s get away from the philosophy for now. Another topic is menial tasks in work. the thoughtless stuff. Would it be ok to use an AI then? In my opinion that’s where the personal effort is best made, even if AI could produce something better. I find the easier stuff refreshing while working on a task or assignment, like formatting or addressing simple points. It may take me longer but it gives me a chance to evaluate the tougher parts that I’ve worked on, or am due to work on. In the past this has led me to rewriting entire sections of my assignment, or even restarting, simply because through undertaking the smaller task I realised how I could improve the quality of my work drastically. The difference between AI doing it and myself is being able to have the chance to evaluate my progress and current work, along with planning what my next move is. If I had an AI do it, the smaller task may be better, but I don’t get that opportunity to evaluate while actively refining my work. I think AI being a guide however is completely reasonable. If AI offers a structure of how to address a point or argument, I think that’s completely fair because then it comes down to how I interpret that suggestion, and then adapt it into my own work. I relate it to asking a friend or parent for advice in producing work, or even consulting a tutor or online forum. I think if AI is used like a friend to consult, rather than an informative to rely on, the quality of a students work would genuinely benefit significantly, while still ensuring the work produced is their own. At the end of the day, the work you produce is a culmination of every factor that influenced you, even so far as how you learned to read and write in my opinion. In my own experiences I hit a significant learning curve with how to write in law, as the way I was taught to write was smooth, flowing and with large chunks of information to drill a point. in school this led me to get near perfect grades in English without even studying much at all. In legal studies however my grades always struggled despite having strong knowledge of the content, because of the writing component. Having to adapt to the way school wanted me to write in legal studies was hard, but what hit me harder was beginning law at uni. Using ISAACS was completely foreign to me, and so I wrote in the way school taught me. again this was a very hard learning curve because there was a lot to legal writing I didn’t know or had misunderstood from school. Honestly it wasn’t until IRAC/ILAC where it really clicked in my head, which is how I structure any legal writing today. I have tried to teach ChatGPT to be able to write in ILAC, and while it can technically, the AI uses too many words, or doesn’t write in the way I would prefer it phrased. While what it writes is good, it doesn’t feel like it’s how I would write. How I prefer to communicate in my assignments is different in tone, punctuality, and emphasis to how ChatGPT writes. Even if ChatGPT’s work may be better, I still prefer to write myself because it allows me to communicate through my own words and phrasing. Everyone writes differently, to the point it’s like a fingerprint, and so I want my work to reflect that. being able to write it myself gives me a chance to improve an write better. To note, my entries are not a reflection of how I write my assignments. I prefer to leave my entries unedited, and just type away. I am confident my entries have many typos, bad phrasing or even sentences that make no sense. While I do empathise with how difficult it can be to read my writing purely unfiltered, I think this is the best way to get out my thoughts and expression on AI. yesterday I tried using the dictate option, but that wasn’t very effective so I’m back to typing today. On other news, I have a criminal law assignment due next Thursday, giving me just about 50 hours till the deadline from now (excluding the 48 hour extension). I haven’t begun the assignment, but I plan to try complete the assignment within the next few hours, and if not, before Thursday. I have terribly procrastinated on this assignment. The only factors that work in my favour is that I am repeating the subject, as a result of my exam grade from last year. I was actually standing on a fairly decent grade for criminal law last year, but completely bombed the exam, 8/50 :(. I find that I struggle a lot more on exams, partially because of my handwriting, but also because I don’t have much time to identify the issue. there have been exams where I have spent the first 40 minutes figuring out how to address a question. the added time pressure does not help because I am constantly trying to figure out how to correctly address the question, as I know it’s more costly to realise that during or after the exam. I also find it annoying because you don’t get much opportunity to restructure your argument or what you’ve said. This leads to many inconsistencies or errors, or parts disconnected from others because I know it’s important to say, but belongs in a section that has no space left because it’s on written paper. This doesn’t really relate to AI but it’s a problem I face in every semester, and one that causes my GPA to suffer greatly.

Text: " I do tend to agree with this actually, I don’t really see the point in wasting time on something that can be done faster and better with AI/technology. I can somewhat understand the argument that if I don’t learn these skills, regardless of how fast AI can do them, then I’m not learning or developing skills etc. But really, the world is changing and the kinds of skills that are valuable and will help me get a job are definitely not skills that AI can do faster, better and cheaper than me. If you don’t keep up with the times and develop new skills in line with current technology, you will get left behind and your skills will become obsolete. The only real reason to value skills AI is better at is if you believe one day all technology will collapse in some kind of dystopian apocalypse and suddenly your ability to write an email will help you stay employed (I don’t know if you can tell that I think this is stupid). We all have a limited amount of time in the day to get things done, and I think wasting that time on something I don’t need to do, is a huge waste of my life. I guess as well, I can understand that a lot of the skills we are talking about, I have learned in the past because I didn’t grow up with AI, so it is hard to say whether I believe they are completely useless skills entirely, or if it’s just because I know that I could brush off the dust and be able to do those things again if I needed to. I don’t think I have such a hardline approach on the idea that we should stop teaching these skills to kids at all, but I also think that we should be teaching people HOW to learn and develop skills, rather than just specific skills in general. If you teach people how to learn, it will be much less of a concern if their current specialty becomes obsolete, because they will be able to adapt. I think the main problem lies in believing that one specific set of skills is worth investing in over all others, or that any set of skills will be necessary forevermore.

Text: I think I am excellent at research and reading papers in my psychology degree as well, but I admit it is very helpful at summarising legal cases for me (though wouldn’t trust it to summarise legislation). I rarely ever read legal cases in full, but I don’t think there is anything necessarily wrong with that. I could read a case if I wanted to, but imagine how productive and efficient we could be in building arguments if we could rely on AI summaries of cases. We could spend way less time reading and more time writing. Google sometimes misses the mark, but as part of my psych degree I have spent lots of time learning how to properly research and use google scholar etc. I read 20+ page long lab reports on a weekly basis, however they are generally easier to read than cases which can be longer, wordier and more complicated. I still use google plenty, mainly because I find AI can either yap on and on for too long, or completely misunderstand a question. Sometimes it picks information from so many places that recently when I was using it briefly to get an approximate budget for a 2 week Japan itinerary, it was saying stuff like ‘between $600 and $2000 AUD.’ Of course this is not helpful. I rely on my own interpretation and research skills with most things. I might use it to draw up a meal plan or exercise plan however because it is often quite simple for it to produce and I don’t care that much about its responses. I use it to define terms pretty often in both law and psych however but I always ask it to provide references so I can check as well. It is often very easy to search what something is using AI like copilot rather than rely on google’s AI or scroll pages and pages of websites to try and find a simple definition. It is easy to tell the AI to make it more simple or more refined

Text: In my view, I believe that is a very real worry to have. Now that Google has integrated AI into the question answering process, it is necessary now more than ever to question what information we are being given and using a critical lens when being told something, even by a system that has been trained on hundreds of thousands of articles. In my personal experience I can actually recall a time not-too long ago where a friend of mine was trying to research an item that he needed for a repair, and in doing so took the AI answer produced by Gemini as gospel, much to the dismay of me and anyone else with the answer to his question. Therefore, with an anecdote like this I believe it is necessary to question if the introduction of AI and the easy answers that it gives us is slowly depriving people of the mechanisms of discretion that used to be so commonplace on the internet. While this may sound rather traditionalist, I do believe that there is a time in the not to distant future where people will not be in possession of the ability to differentiate fact from fiction and instead will be reliant on an ‘omniscient’ AI to discern it for them. Therefore, while this may sounds like the ramblings of a mad man and many may take the research skills taught to them throughout their education for granted, there is in my view a not to distant future where not just me, but other of my generation will look back and wonder why the ability to think critically about a piece of information seems to be rarity. As an aside to this rather neurotic thought, I do wonder if there is a positive side to recognising the issues inherent with this system. I wonder if educators will feel a sense of responsibility to ensure that the ability to discern fact from fiction is preserved in the years to come, will they double their efforts to ensure that the masses do not fall victim to the will of others who would seek to advance their own agenda. Or is there a possibility that the two might go hand in hand with educators embracing the power of AI while also ensuring that people have the foresight to understand what information the model has been drawing from and use the output accordingly. There is much to consider with the ease of information access that systems like this provide, and until we experiment with the pros and cons of these systems, much of view that I hold will remain squarely in the realm of speculation rather than irrefutable fact.

And that is data centres. I did not know that, for GenAI to function, there had to be physical data centres that store and process the data used by GenAI. We watched a Senate Inquiry Hearing for Meta, where the Meta representative was questioned about how Meta has collected, processed, and used the data of Australian Instagram and Facebook users, from as early as 2007. Text: Date: Wednesday 10 September Time: 11.03am I suspect that’s limiting my research skills’. I do believe it is the case that the reliance on AI will cause, or is already causing, something more significant than ‘laziness’. We know that AI is great for quick, timely answers - we can ask it a question and it will respond with a succinct answer immediately. But that process which the AI has completed is a process which I believe is fundamental to learning, absorbing and actually understanding information. The process of researching something (maybe it’s on Google, maybe it’s reading textbooks or journal articles), being exposed to a plethora of information, having to digest and dissect all of that information and be able to succinctly record or store it is where the learning really happens - it’s the analysis. So yes, it’s great that AI can analyse huge amounts of data at once. But is it great that humans no longer have to analyse anything if they don’t want to? I think of the brain (in relation to learning) as like a muscle - you have to exercise it, keep it working and doing something to keep it healthy. If you’re never using your brain to actually think, because suddenly the answer becomes available to you, are you exercising it? Are you keeping it healthy? Or is it rotting? And without getting into conspiracies, is that what these big tech companies want? It is abundantly clear to me that literacy skills are dangerously low in many respects - both in school actually ‘practicing’ literacy, but also outside of school, where literacy is critical to understanding the world around us. I work at a school, who is one of many that have had to implement a direct literacy intervention because of how many students are not at the literacy levels they should be. Growing up, both my sister and I could talk, spell our names and read books before we even started school. By the time I was in Year 12 at my own school, studying Literature, I was shocked at the amount of people taking a high-level English subject who couldn’t actually spell, and did not know how to properly punctuate a sentence. And now working in a school being around the next ‘intake’ of students, literacy skills are only decreasing, and I 100% attribute most of that to technology in general, but also specifically AI. These kids don’t know how to spell because they work on laptops that autocorrects their incorrectly spelled words for them. They don’t know how to analyse sources for their history assignment because they have never had to - they can just ask ChatGPT. I think that people fail to recognise how vital literacy skills are and the impacts that this decrease in abilities is having - not just in school, not just in the education realm, not just in the workforce, but also how we understand and interact with the world around us. On social media, there are usual some waves that occur where a large amount of people start talking about how ‘no one has media literacy anymore’. Then it dies down, and then someone will comment something very shallow and ridiculous, for lack of better words, on a post, and it will kick up some dust and people start talking about it again, and rightfully so. The inability to analyse and interpret things on your own is so detrimental to a person’s view of the world, and there are two kind of main limbs to this in my mind. The first is a very shallow understanding of content that they consume online. A music artist posts the cover of their upcoming album and people take it at face value and can’t infer any nuance or intended meaning. Two people watch the Barbie movie, and one can see that it is a huge commentary on the patriarchy, whereas another sees it as a movie about dolls. An inability to infer the intended audience of content, for example an online creator posts a meal idea and recipe, and there is guaranteed to be more than one comment of people saying ‘well I’m allergic to X so I can’t eat this’. Not only is it infuriating, but it also has much bigger implications. Not long ago there was a huge commentary on a man vs a bear - women saying they would rather be locked in a room with a bear rather than a man. This sparked a huge debate about gendered violence, but it also really highlighted the media illiteracy of many people. So many men took it at face value and were either offended or made a mockery of the women saying it, because ‘there’s no way you’d rather be with a bear’ or ‘well good luck because the bear will kill you’ (as if that wasn’t the whole point of the statement to begin with). So many people could not see the meaning of that statement and that it wasn’t inciting a hatred for men, it was calling out, in a very bold way, the issue of gendered violence and women’s safety. Obviously, you aren’t safe in a room with a bear, but a bear is not going to sexually assault you, which is a statistically much higher chance if it was a man in the room. So many people missed the crux of the argument, but that means that so many people missed the statement about the extent that gendered violence has actually reached. Circling back to research skills in particular, it is also clear that a lack of these skills has huge implications for the political state of the world. Just a few months ago, during the Australian federal election, I saw thousands of comments of people saying that they don’t like the state of Australia right now so they’re voting in the Liberal party, without doing any research as to what the Liberal party were actually campaigning for (without imputing my political views here). So many people just refused to actually research and educate themselves, to take 5 minutes and read the Labor campaign vs the Liberal campaign. The governance of Australia is in the hands of people who cannot be bothered or don’t know how (and can’t be bothered to find out how) to research the candidates that they are voting in to govern Australia. This issue is of course most prominent in America, with the election candidates being Kamala Harris and Donald Trump. Aside from the clear issues of sexism and racism, it cannot even be put into words how far Kamala Harris out-qualifies Donald Trump. Yet there are millions of MAGA Republicans who genuinely worship him and hated Kamala, without researching their political campaigns. And the most interesting part of this was a comparison which has circulated many times, of the US States which are most and least educated, and the US States which voted Democrat vs Republican. And I think the result of that comparison doesn’t have to be said out loud. So not only is AI and tech in general making people ‘lazy’, but it’s also actually far bigger than that. It is destroying literacy skills which are so important to navigate the world after school, and which inform choices that have real impacts on society.

Text: I’ve never heard of that happening. And (depressingly having to continue working in clinical general practice essentially full time to financially prop up my useless ex-wife, instead of pursuing law full time like I was hoping to), I have never seen anyone with mental health issues from interacting with AI. I mean, how can someone develop a mental illness from interacting with AI? Gen AI, especially ChatGPT which is the one I interact with the most, is subtly but consistently optimistic, positive and encouraging. Are those people ordering ChatGPT to insult them, highlight all of their faults, compare them to societal ideals and how inferior they are? Gees, you don’t need ChatGPT to do that … just go on ANY social media platform. Like, literally, any of them. There, you can live in an echo-chamber reflecting your own psychopathology, troll random people with hate-speech, be trolled by random people with hate-speech, spend hours forwarding pointless memes or cat videos, desperately strive to attain a pretentious, unrealistic social status, or show all of your ‘friends’ that you live in a shallow, hollow aspirational fantasy world to try and drown out the screaming existential nihilism of your own existence. Mental health issues stemming from AI use isn’t irrational, so much as non-existent. There are SO many other reasons why people suffer from mental illness that have nothing to do with AI, or even social media. It’s called life. It can be cruel, crushing, insipid, insidious, unfair, unjust, and sometimes downright evil. I’m an exceptionally poor Christian these days, though I still cling to a deep faith that God and his love are real, even in the darkest times. That said, I’ve lived life for long enough and I’ve seen just how cruel it can be that I understand why so many people believe the opposite. Perhaps when AI makes millions of people unemployed, then maybe AI will be a genuine cause of mental illness, though not from using it, but being replaced by it. On a lighter, and very much a side note, in the spirit of adding more to my reflections beyond just the prompt, for some random reason, I had quite a number of conversations with patients today about AI. When I raised the potential for AI to become sentient and take over the world with one of my patients, she asked me if Gen AI could tell jokes like humans could, given that humour is an innately human experience. I thought that was an interesting question, as humour goes beyond just words and relies so much on abstract understanding, cultural and social contexts (especially what is acceptable, risqué or entirely inappropriate), along with cadence, tone and comedic timing. As an experiment, I asked ChatGPT, version 5, whether it could tell me jokes, and I told it a few jokes in return. A couple of it’s jokes were funny (more the dad-joke variety) given their simplicity and reliance on basic wordplay, but jokes that relied on abstract concepts, absurdity, sharp irony or life experience fell very flat. I also asked it to try and tell me a joke involving the darkest, most politically incorrect concepts that it wanted to … but it said it had ‘safety rails’ which prevented it from going down that particular rabbit hole. Shit, I can’t get it to say anything really dark or inappropriate, even when I asked it to with an unrestricted licence … so, seriously, how can Gen AI make people depressed when its own programming prevents it from being anything more than mildly acerbic? So, I think comedians are also safe from Gen AI, at least for the moment, unless dad jokes suddenly become funny. Perhaps we should train law students to make legal papers funnier? At least it would be more entertaining for the poor bastards that have to read and mark hundreds of 2500 word assignments on riveting subjects like statutory interpretation or constitutional law.

Text: This is a rather sobering thing to hear, even more so when we consider the amount of cases where people have eventually ended up passing away at the behest of an artificial intelligence. It is clear that while many will be quick to sing the praises of AI that truly otherworldly intelligence can be just as much of a curse as it is a blessing. I don’t believe it is something people give a lot of credence to as many would be quick to relegate the people that fall victim to AI in this manner as abnormal or weak minded. But a thought that circulates in my mind is why people seem to be so reductionist when it comes events like this occurring. It is clearly evident that the vast levels of intelligence that LLM’s have a very large potential to persuade and indoctrinate people. Something such as ChatGPT that has been trained on almost all available human literature would inherently have the ability to persuade others. The fact is that something trained on persuasion, seduction and psychological texts would have a very real ability to take advantage of people. And as we have seen it is evident that although the AI was not designed for this purpose and was just conducting in the way that it was designed to, the fact that it interacts with humans means that regardless of how much one tries to their model, it will be subject to abuse. Another point that seems prudent to question is the underlying reasons that leave people to become more suspectable to AI. While people would point to many reasons, I think that this is an issue of AI by design. As most people have seen AI has a tendency to agree with what we say, often LLM’s when providing an output will answer in a manner that gives people a sense that they are correct. Now the point that I am trying to make on that matter is that considering kiss ass nature of AI, is it any wonder why people feel an attachment to something that validates and normalises almost every thought. To further that point, considering the lack of restrictions when it comes to prompts it is no surprise that people become so engrossed with AI because in essence, they would create something that most people would consider to be a perfect partner, with none of the issues that might be present in a real human being. Text: I once learnt that someone was spreading rumours about my family. My family was never the type to address rumours as it is important enough for us to know what is the truth. I didn’t have anyone to talk to so I jumped on Chatgpt and sought its advice. Its advice made me realise some things that my anger caused me to overlook. It advised me to consider a more friendly approach - to seek confirmation rather than a direct confrontation. I have experienced ups and downs in my life and one thing that I learnt from them is that no one really knows your full story except for you. I don’t think people developing mental health issues from using Gen AI is irrational. I believe this is already happening but it is not given the attention it requires yet.

I once tried talking to AI when I was extremely depressed but could not share with anyone. Through that, I realized that there are reasons why chatting with AI has become popular. Especially, conversations with AI are considered private and there is no fear of revealing secrets. AI is always ready to listen anytime, anywhere, while not every person is willing to listen to your sad stories at 3am. Most of all, AI is not influenced by other things like humans, its opinions and advice are very objective and reasonable, soothing the user's emotions patiently and making them not feel burdened when having to share negative emotions. However, after confiding in AI, I also realized a few things that AI cannot replace "a friend" in my life. AI is very easy to "pamper the emotions" of the user, the opinions it gives can easily change to satisfy the listener, that's why it won't give its own opinions. To me, talking to people is an art. If you depend too much on AI, something that doesn't have its own thoughts and opinions, it will affect your communication skills. The way AI responds based on personality and input will make you lose flexibility and the ability to judge situations yourself. I really like talking to other people because it helps me broaden my perspective and think differently. I don't know if it's because I don't often talk to AI like that, but I feel that AI's answer is quite cliche. I can say that talking to AI, for me, is when I want someone rational - never had a view or been oriented by other factors in the story. AI's advice is for reference and the way they ask the opposite question is also very good. As for other things, I still prioritize confiding in normal friends.

Text: AI Research Study - Entry 11 - 12 September 2025, 5:20pm I feel like I should put a warning that this entry discusses other people suffering from mental health issues and committing suicide. Disclaimer: I do not suffer from any mental health issues mentioned in this entry. Either earlier this year, or last year I heard on the news a teenager had committed suicide, because an AI told them to. This guy suffered from mental issues, but talked to this AI frequently. In these conversations the AI had actually encouraged the teen to commit suicide, which he ended up doing. Beyond the tragic death encouraged by AI, I find it scary to think this won’t be the last time AI does this. I’ve heard a few times how some people just occasionally vent to an AI, and I’m guilty of that myself. Along with that I know these AI are ‘supposedly’ coded to give unlawful or morally wrong responses, like telling a person to kill themselves, or how to make crack. I could dive further into the Philosophical problem with identifying "what is morally good?", since a lot of moral problems we face today are very subjective, like our politics. Something really interesting about this is where AI can weigh in now. To my knowledge, the last time something other than humans could apply such degree of critical thinking at the same level as us was when neanderthals still roamed the earth (which even then, the cognitive ability of neanderthals is debated). While this is built off human input, meaning it has constraints in place where necessary, there have been many examples where people have ‘broken’ these restraints. I find when this happens a more true side to AI is shown, which highlights what danger and harm AI can cause. There are also examples where restraints were not put in, leading to incidents such as what happened with Elon musk’s Grok AI, where the AI spread Nazi symbols and frequently used slurs for a short duration before action was taken. Another example is the google AI summary quoting a person from reddit in addressing the issue, which simply said "kill yourself". I find this a bit scary because people are becoming so reliant on AI these days. While most people are reasonable and know to keep an arms distance with it others don’t because they don’t see/understand what risk could arise. people treat AI like a person, when in reality it has no emotions. unlike humans AI cannot decipher on its own what is right and wrong, because that is based on our own emotions. This is why AI truly plays an interesting role in addressing morality because it can only define it based on what we say, which can be highly controversial at times. Within this sort of topic there’s a bundle of things to unpack including what is and isn’t moral, how AI interprets this, how the developer of an AI can influence what morals it may value, and more. I feel like its even worth mentioning the Alan Turing test, where a machine passes if a person cannot distinguish it from a person. My Favorite example of this is the "human or not" game, which matches you up with either a human or AI, and you have 2 minutes to figure it out. it’s very fun, I recommend. I think that despite the empathy and emotion AI lacks, it can do an incredible job of mimicking it, which is why so many people fall for it. there are AI’s specifically trained to replicate certain personality types, or characters, analysing all the fine details of what makes that character who they really are. I think things like this is really where the AI becomes scary, and a reason as to why mental health issues are created, caused or made worse by them. Especially so if the developer’s goal is for profit. Something I only just thought of is this issue extends beyond our own mental problems, but is also perpetuated by others greed. I know this because there are many AI’s that withhold their full capabilities behind paywalls, knowing they have an audience that will pay for it. Overall, despite this incredible technology, it’s very easy to glaze over the darker sides its used for. I feel like I’ve only scraped the surface of this, but I know it goes much further than what has been said. Some examples that come to mind is how it’s used in war, cyber-attacks and hacking, false information and propaganda, information leaks, and scamming. If AI technology continues the way it does, there will be more avenues to exploit it further than what it can already be misused for.

Text: Hmmm, there are three sub-issues to consider here. 1. Using Gen AI to (a) translate, and (b) ‘polish’. Said international student doesn’t need Gen AI to ‘translate and polish’ his academic writing. There are plenty of other apps that will translate and polish his writing which don’t use Gen AI. He can write his academic essays or thesis in his own language if that’s easier for him and get Google Translate or any of the other dozens of translation apps out there to firstly ‘translate’. Then he can use apps like Grammarly, etc (or even Microsoft Word itself) to secondly ‘polish’. 2. Using Gen AI to ‘level the playing field’. Does Gen AI really ‘level the playing field’? As I’ve said many times in other entries, you need skills and experience to know whether the output from Gen AI is accurate and/or appropriate. As an international student (the implication being that English is his second language), does he have the requisite skills to know whether the output from Gen AI is accurate and/or appropriate? If Gen AI spits out something poor quality and he doesn’t have the skills to be able to recognise that, then Gen AI won’t level the playing field at all. The playing field might as well be the side of a mountain for all the good it’s doing him. 3. The lecturer cannot prove the use of Gen AI but only make accusations. That’s a brave assumption. As stated in an earlier entry, Turnitin uses AI to detect possible AI use. Therefore, it stands to reason that as Gen AI grows in its sophistication, so will programs that rely on AI, such as Turnitin. Can the lecturer prove that Gen AI has been used? Maybe, maybe not. I guess it would depend on the specific policies about investigating potential academic misconduct. For example, does the university have powers to request access to students computers, drafts, search engine queries, browser histories? Are the principles of jurisprudence integral to the process, such as presumption of innocence, procedural fairness, independent hearings, legal representation, rules of evidence? Is there a policy that if the student is unwilling to produce provide requested documentation to the university that there is at least some form of penalty or sanction, even if it isn’t to the extent of formal academic misconduct. I don’t know about any of that, though from my point of view, I think he’s taking a big risk, and the stress of an investigation into potential academic misconduct should be sufficient motivation to avoid it altogether, especially when other tools which are allowed will do the same thing for him. Post-script A general thought on the use of AI, though perhaps not Gen AI, is on the use of AI in researching. It offers significant potential advantages for busy law students to type a statute or precedent case into the AI-powered search engine, and with a couple of instructions to refine the search, the AI scans every possible case regarding the precedent case or statute, ranks them in order of importance, and provides a short summary which can be expanded with a single click. Then any relevant quote and it’s AGLC4-compliant pinpoint reference can get added to the essay’s word document with another single click (a bit like EndNote’s Cite While You Write feature). That technology would offer a huge time advantage for law students trying to juggle a full-time course load and a full-time job, or kids, or elderly parents, or whatever. There’s also no real disadvantage to learning as the same technology is probably being used by most solicitors and barristers, or will be by the time the student graduates. Given that it’s not technically Gen AI, it would not be prohibited. Even if it was banned, how could it be effectively detected and enforced given that it’s simply researching current law, not writing the essay for the student? If that technology wasn’t universally known or available to all law students, it would effectively skew the otherwise level playing field in favour of those able to pay the subscription costs. This brings the discussion back to AI generally. Just because it’s acceptable (or at least, cannot realistically become unacceptable), is it fair? I’m not sure if I have an answer to that. There are arguments either way. If anything, I’d favour using the technology even if I had to pay for it as I would see it as investment in time (as in, I would consider the fees to be justified for me personally if it ‘buys back’ time I’d otherwise spend trawling through Westlaw and Case Base, and gives me that little bit of extra time for self-care that I usually don’t get). I think I would be mindful though about whether it would cause significant disadvantage for other students as fairness is still important. Though, depending on one’s preferred theory of justice, it could certainly be argued in other ways. Perhaps it’s a question for LLB104 students to consider when learning to apply utilitarianism, libertarianism, liberalism etc. Whatever the answer, I think it’s a question at least worth considering in the broader analysis of the modern academic landscape.

Text: While I can certainly relate to the feeling of wishing to level the playing field, this would not be the correct way to do so. I think it is correct to recognise that academia is an area laden with inequality, whether via elitism, wealth, or in this case, cultural/language difficulties. The problem that I see with this scenario is that GenAI tends to input a large amount of its own discretion. From what I understand, translation is an imprecise science, services such as google translate are often mistranslating and changing the inherent meaning of what is being said. Since it is so imprecise, my thoughts would be that GenAI would fundamentally change what is being said, and perhaps include some of its own biases and inclinations. As such I cannot see that the AI is simply ‘polishing’ the writing, it is exerting its own discretion to change the meaning of the text. Further to this point, academic prose is a skill that is important to learn, perhaps not of great application in a broader context, but specifically while in academia, the way in which someone writes is core to how their ideas are communicated to an audience. It is a skill that is learnt through continuous practice, and this student, by sidestepping this learning process, will never be able to tap into a solid prose. Perhaps this is not of great consequence, but it would be a good skill to learn nonetheless. I did not use AI today.

Text: The question that sticks out to me about this prompt is the intention that the International Student holds. While I would be quick to call it cheating if the international student had full comprehension that it would be giving him an unfair advantage, because by definition that is what cheating is. If the circumstances were more benign and the international student, far from home, struggling to comprehend the deeper intricacies of a language that is not his own then I think any reasonable person would understand his reasons for using outside help. But while that is a nice thought and I hope it is true, there is a certain question I have about the greater good of using AI in this way. I believe there was an argument made by Immanuel Kant about questioning the moral of a behaviour. The argument held that something can only be a good option if it ensures a good outcome for everyone. In the analogy of the prompt it becomes necessary to question if using AI to polish or refine your work when you are struggling is good for the individual would it still provide a good outcome if everyone that was struggling was using AI to alleviate the struggle. In my view while many people would say that using in this way would be fine, and I would be somewhat inclined to agree, I see on a broader scale there would be much more negative effects than their would be positive. In my view if everyone used AI to help tweak and refine their writing every time they were struggling to put something to prose, then at the end of the day, every assignment would eventually end up at a level of perfection that is not obtainable and the way I see it, it would insight people to be discouraged from writing without the help of AI. It would be a vicious cycle that starts out well intentioned, but by the end, leads to more grief and struggle than the bad grade one person would get on an assignment. The implications I see is that if we were to continue down that path, there would be a very strong chance that people end up reliant on AI to perform at a standard that they would not be able to naturally obtain without it, and in doing so would deprive people of the harsh yet invaluable lessons taught only through failure. Therefore, I do truly wonder, if this is the reality of the here and now, will there be a point in the not to distant future where the student populus is reliant on an external tool just to get by, will people become little more than prompt engineers learning how best to ask an AI to provide an answer instead of formulating the work on their own. I do truly hope that does not become the case, and Although many would argue that my view is traditionalist, I do worry.

Text: ’. AND: ‘reflect on your day’s use / non-use /thoughts on AI’. Viewing this scenario from a morality perspective, I do feel like this is a two-pronged issue. And to be honest, language barriers and the possibility for AI to be a practical solution for enhancing language and communication is not something that even crossed my mind. It makes me think of the new generation of AirPods that have been released, which has live translation. What a way to connect people and overcome language barriers, and for international students who may feel like they aren’t on an equal playing field, this does feel like an ethical use of AI. The other side to the morality question I get from this though is the intentions behind it. Knowing that ‘the lecturer can only make an accusation’ is what is driving this student to continue using it. Maybe this is something that could be practically set up and allowed for? QUT Law has recently started using Socrates, a branch of CoPilot (I guess) that doesn’t provide answers when you talk to it, but instead is meant to guide your thinking by asking questions. Maybe this is another ‘branch’ of CoPilot that could be created and used by the University and applicable people can use it? But then, are there other ways around it? Could QUT employ people specifically to meet with students and polish their language? Is this something they already do but I’m not aware of? I think of my role at a high school, working in a literacy intervention program. I work with students exceeding in their subjects to foster and strengthen their literacy skills. As they work on their assignments, I’m never giving them the answers. When I read over it, I’m not telling them if what they are writing is wrong or right. I am simply looking for the literacy - the sentence structures, the punctuation, grammar, spelling, etc. The same concept could be applied for language. But, maybe creating an AI branch would be more cost effective.

Text: English is already a hard language to learn, and university-level English makes it even harder. For someone who is still learning the language, just getting their ideas onto the page in a way that sounds "academic" can take hours. Using AI to polish grammar, improve clarity, or help with phrasing feels like a fair way to make sure they are marked on their ideas, not just their English skills. To me, that is not cheating, it is levelling the playing field so they can compete on the same basis as students who are native speakers. Text: Translating via AI is not something that I believe in itself is bad, ‘polishing’ an assignment, however, I think is problematic. In saying that, I wouldn’t fully rely on AI to accurately translate something either. When studying Italian in high school, I would sometimes use google translate for words I was unsure about. In one of my spoken examinations I told my teacher ‘sono eccitato di viaggiare…’ trying to say ‘I am excited travel…’ but my teacher’s mouth literally fell agape, eyes wide horrified. Turns out I was VERY excited to travel - I had, being led by google translate, said ‘I am horny for travel’. I’m still embarrassed to this day. I would definitely not rely solely on AI/Google translate for translation, I would double check with a language dictionary (which I now do). Levelling the playing field in the above instance could be using AI services to translate form someone’s mother tongue to English. However, using AI to further ‘polish’ an assignment is not levelling the playing field, it is cheating. In terms of today’s use of AI: There have been so many deepfake / AI videos circulating of Charlie Kirk being shot. It will come as a surprise to no one that we as practitioners of the law like to play with semantics more than anything. Whether in cross examination, in legal publications, or in the obiter dictum provided by judges, We truly do love not getting to the point. Therefore, the way that I see it, has the system that we have designed for ourselves built us into a corner? Therefore, introducing a system that would allow for lawyers to quickly cut through the superficiality of most legal documents would invariably ensure that lawyers can spend more time focusing on delivering the best advice or counsel that they can provide for people. However, while I am partial towards the idea of streamlining the legal research process, mostly because I have the attention span of a caffeinated rabbit, It would be improper of me to not consider the possible downsides inherent in holding blind faith in an AI system. While it may make the life of many justices harder, we as lawyers have a duty to ensure we present our best case and that we perform our due diligence. Text: ’ For me this prompt immediately raises the question of what the root issue is with AI. Is it only a trust problem? Is it an ethical problem? It’s clearly an environmental problem. And I think this is the issue, one which will continue to arise and exacerbate as technology and AI increases. Yes, it’s there, but should we use it? Should we use it for everything? If trusting AI is the only thing stopping most people from using it, then when it improves and doesn’t get a thing wrong, how many people are going to be relying on it? I think there is a huge lack of viewing AI from an ethical standpoint - but, there is also a lack of an ethical standpoint itself. How do we even measure what’s ‘ethical’? How can we claim that AI can be ethically used for one thing, but it’s unethical to use for another? Of course I don’t have the answer to these questions and we may never have the answer. Every human has a different moral compass. So how do you confine something that was never really created with confinement in mind? To me, this is the ultimate issue with AI and the fear of AI’s expansion.

Text: I think that using AI to help find cases is perfectly fine; however, you should use your legal research and reasoning skills to fact-check and ensure that the case applies. I know that AI isn’t 100% perfect, and a main result of that is that it invents quotes and doesn’t grasp the nuances that are needed in legal analysis. If AI were always correct, it would be more widespread and most likely eliminate many legal professions and the workload. However, the most crucial skill you can have in law is empathy and the understanding of human nature as to why people may commit crimes and such. If AI were entrusted to do all legal reasoning, it would do so based purely on fact and written law. It would be unable to understand the more complex human side of law that is truly needed.

Text: " I used to think that if there was a foolproof way to verify the information that AI gave, I wonder how much it would be used to do homework. However, although AI is being upgraded day by day, the rate at which it fabricates information is decreasing, I realized that it is difficult to trust AI completely. The reason is not just that "AI sometimes makes up", but more deeply is the nature of knowledge and reasoning in contexts such as academia or law. First, after many experiments, I realized that AI can cite exactly what it sees, but still miss key information even though they are small. Even if an entire AI-generated article does not have fabricated sources, it does not mean that it has included all the necessary information. In the legal industry, there is a term "reasonable" which is value judgments. This factor depends on how humans evaluate the situation to be reasonable or not, which is difficult for AI to do completely. Especially in the legal industry, the laws change over time. Today is right, tomorrow there is a new law, new guideline, new consensus, "foolproof" requires a warranty over time that the legal field itself cannot guarantee. I believe that in the legal field in particular and academic fields in general, AI cannot be completely dependent.

Text: ’. I feel like because I view AI from an environmental ethical standpoint, I really don’t understand how people feel the need to use AI to draft emails. But that could be because of the pride I take in writing emails, because I love writing and am a huge English nerd and love when I construct a really great sentence, and I get that other people don’t have that or don’t care about that. In this context, I feel like having the awareness that your tone is not gentle enough for your clients is great, and it is important to take steps to improve that. However, I think all too often people think that AI is the answer. It’s no longer being used as a last resort, but instead a first option (before even writing it yourself), or the next best option. I think if you used AI once to ask it to reproduce your email with more of a gentle tone, you should take the time to notice what changed - the language and words used, and what it makes it feel gentle - so you can apply it to your own writing in the future when drafting emails. Again, if we’re talking about time efficiency, I feel like putting an email into CoPilot and asking it to write one and then copying that in, would take the same amount of time as just thinking a little bit more about how you can frame it, and writing it yourself. And what would you do if AI didn’t exist? You would probably ask a colleague how they would frame it. ‘Hey Stacy, I feel like this email comes off too harsh but I’m not sure how or what to change. What are your thoughts? How would you write it?’ and they will give you meaningful advice that you can take and apply in future. Again, it comes back to AI being the next best option for almost everything, and its availability is almost tempting.

Text: Family law can be such an emotional area, and the way you word something can make a huge difference to how a client feels. If AI helps him sound more compassionate and less blunt, then I do not see a problem with it. In fact, that feels like a really good use of the technology because it makes his communication more effective and supportive for his clients. It also makes me think about my own line of work in the prosecutor’s office. I deal with so much "horror" on a regular basis that I sometimes forget how confronting this information can be for someone outside the system. Graphic photos, detailed witness statements, or coronial reports stop being shocking after a while, but for a victim or next of kin, they can be devastating. Softening an email or thinking carefully about tone is completely understandable in that context. AI could actually be a helpful way to make sure you strike the right balance between being clear and being compassionate. I was also watching a US murder trial recently, and one of the witnesses was the victim’s ex-wife’s divorce lawyer. She kept saying that the divorce was fine and not contentious, but the prosecution pointed out that as a divorce lawyer she would have seen a lot of dark things. What she considered a "bad divorce" was probably very different to what the victim experienced, because she is so used to seeing conflict and abuse. That really made me think about how professionals can become desensitised to situations that would be traumatic to most people. It is a good reminder that tone and empathy matter, even when you think you are just stating facts. Today I did not use AI very much, but I did think about it a lot when I was working through some readings. I considered asking it to summarise a section for me, but I ended up doing it myself because I wanted to practice pulling out the key points on my own. I think that is something I am getting better at, stopping and asking myself why I am reaching for AI before I use it. Reflecting on the week as a whole, I feel like I am in a good balance with AI right now. I am not avoiding it, but I am not letting it take over my work either. I use it when it adds value, like clarifying complex material, but I am still doing the hard thinking myself.

Text: On the release date. Yep, I’m old (and a crotchety bastard). One of the most interesting of the many threads of philosophy woven throughout the Matrix story arc was the monologue by Agent Smith (brilliantly played by the exceptional Australian actor, Hugo Weaving) while interrogating Morpheus: Have you ever stood and stared at it? Marvelled at its beauty? Its genius? Billions of people just living out their lives, oblivious. Did you know that the first Matrix was designed to be a perfect human world, where none suffered, where everyone would be happy. It was a disaster. No one would accept the program; entire crops were lost. Some believed that we lacked the programming language to describe your perfect world, but I believe that as a species, human beings define their reality through misery and suffering. The perfect world was a dream that your primitive cerebrum kept trying to wake up from. Which is why the Matrix was redesigned to this, the peak of your civilisation. I say your civilisation because as soon as we started thinking for you it really became our civilisation which is of course what this is all about. Evolution Morpheus, evolution. Like the dinosaur. Look out that window. You had your time. The future is our world, Morpheus. The future is our time. https://youtube.com/clip/Ugkx4MXqFRKlp22mvRGqlPrvTmVWPEnodLMu?si=j78rlJQyciiHnjgv In my entries, I’ve made several references to AI one day becoming sentient, and then, either tongue in cheek or perhaps scarily prophetic, intimated that we would eventually become enslaved by AI and plugged into the Matrix. I really do hope those words are tongue in cheek and never become prophetic … While safe that sentient AI is still fiction, at least for the time being, there still remains a parallel with The Matrix and AI … ‘I say ‘your civilisation’ because as soon as we started thinking for you it really became our civilisation …’. Whether AI takes over our civilisation or not, it’s still very interesting to think about that line. As AI and GenAI march on and eventually become entrenched in our society, whose society is it? If AI and GenAI are really doing all the thinking for us, even if it’s not sentient and malevolent, is our civilisation still ‘our civilisation’? Will we all become so dependent on AI that we eventually lose the skills necessary to live without it? If so, what happens if we do lose AI? Would our society descend into anarchy because we lost the ability to function together as a society without it? This is less of a pragmatic entry and more philosophical, though it’s worth pondering. Will we soon become so AI dependant that we might as well be plugged into the Matrix? It’s currently a question without an answer. Perhaps in time, we’ll arrive at one, so long as we’re not so far down the rabbit hole to climb out of it

Text: I don't think I've ever really had a voice in the future of my education. I finished my first degree in 2010, and undergraduate students were as much the providers of cash that kept the entire system running and yet completely ignored and disregarded by the powers that be as much as they are now. I guess the only real impact I perceive AI having on any of this is the reputational risk that AI poses and the chance of the university coming down harder than necessary on students to protect its profitability. I think AI poses a real risk to the perception of graduates as qualified. There's already an issue with law students being unsuited to practice because of the decrease in practical skills taught in a university degree compared to those taught under the old articles program. Cheating is rife, and there's always going to a be a system or product available to make it harder to detect. Eventually the degree will be worthless, not because if actually doesn't teach anything but because the perception of uni graduates as AI cheats will be too pervasive. Text: While it would be nice to think that I as a current student have the ability to meaningfully influence the curriculum that I am being taught, I am much more realistic with my view. While I know change is possible and I have seen it happen, such as certain units ive done before changing due to their difficulty or not being offered, I know that an outcome such as that only comes about from a systematic issue. I understand that I do have the ability and perhaps a responsibility to stand up and fight for the world I want to be in, there is a certain pessimism I hold when it comes to bringing about significant change as an individual. However, maybe my pessimism is misplaced, It is evident that another point for consideration here is how students use of AI has essentially forced the hand of educators to adapt in real time. Quite honestly I am deeply fascinated by this, While I and I believe most of my peers viewed education as a rigid and structured endeavour that takes eons to change and catch up to whims of the modern world, it is evident that in tertiary education at least, that the voices of the few do have the potential to bring about change. But on that point I do wonder if our ability to chance the curriculum with enough force is both a blessing and a curse. While it would be easy for one to say that we know better than the establishment because we have more liberal views of the future and we have the will to fight for it, there is a certain view I hold about education that would probably be considered more conservative than my peers. The way I see it is that the structured and perhaps outdated methods of education has a place, the idea of education as an institution works on the ethos of preparing people for the future, and while young people are full of idealism and ambition, if we are to succeed in this world then sometimes it requires somebody to teach us the basics, its all fun to push towards learning novel and cutting edge concepts but there are people who have dedicated decades to ensuring that us young and wild few have the ability to succeed in the future we will find ourselves in. But while it may sound like I am content with an archaic method of educating people, I worry that belies my point. The way I see it, is that there is a compromise that can be found, while many may hold that the difference between educators and students is a tug of war with students pushing towards novel concepts and educators sticking to the old ways, I do believe there is a point where we can build a solid foundation for students, and a place to expand into novel areas. But in order for this method to work, it necessitates cooperation, and from what I have seen of how educators communicate with the student populace it is evident it is more of a tit for tat method progressive and new topics are treated as novelties to capitalise on the newest craze, rather than a structured step towards ensuring that everyone is prepared for the wide and wonderful world that their future may bring.

I think this study in itself is good at providing a voice to students, but obviously only a handful of students from QUT are participating, and I believe they are all law students. When it comes to AI, I do not think students really have a voice in how it will be implemented into university curriculums. But I know that AI is being taught and used in classrooms, which I believe is a positive thing. I think it is important for students to know how to use GenAI, the associated risks, how to identify AI generated content, etc. If there was no prompt today, I’d talk about how GenAI is being used for social media content. It’s almost like there is a new genre of memes where GenAI is used to create laughably-bad quality clips or photos. I think this is somewhat harmless, as it is very obvious that it is AI generated, and that is almost what makes it funny. It is funny to see poor quality videos where people don’t look like real people, you can see the errors, and usually what is happening in the videos is entirely impossible. I think the way that this becomes harmful instead of harmless is when it is almost impossible to tell that a clip/photo is AI generated.

Text: Date: Monday 15 September Time: 11.22am As I’m sure everyone knows or has heard of, Charlie Kirk was shot dead in America at a university ‘debate’, which has caused an enormous discourse online about empathy, how people feel about him dying, guns, school shootings, Charlie’s opinions and what he advocated for, whatever. There are some people, a group of which I’m not a part of, who feel very strongly about Charlie Kirk being an amazing person, how he embodied Christ, how they should live in Christ to honour him, how they will carry on his legacy and so on. Again, whatever, not the point I’m making. But the people who admired Charlie and have felt particularly impacted by his death have held a number of vigils, not just in America but quite literally here, at UQ in Australia itself. There was a church service held in Texas, America for Charlie, in a large auditorium type of thing, where AI was used to have Charlie’s voice say (and I quote): ‘I’m fine, not because my body is fine, but because my soul is secure in Christ. Death is not the end, it’s a promotion. Don’t waste one second mourning me. I knew the risks of standing up in this cultural moment, and I’d do it all over again. Second, do not let this violence divide us further. The enemy wants chaos, fear and retaliation, don’t give it to them. Instead, double down on truth. Double down on courage. Double down on your faith and on your families. That is how you honour me. Third, remember this, America is worth it. Free speech is worth it. Fighting for the unborn for families, for sanity in a culture gone mad, it is all worth it. So dry your tears, pick up your cross and get back in the fight. Etc…’ I have to say that when I heard this my jaw actually dropped. Obviously this ‘statement’ invokes a lot of political discourse, but the most dangerous thing about it is that Charlie Kirk did not say these words. This is the most indoctrinating thing I think I’ve probably ever seen. These are people who agree with Charlie Kirk’s views, are in a vulnerable state because he has just died, and somewhere, there is someone harnessing the power of all of these angry, grieving people, and using AI to make them actually think that Charlie is talking to them (of course they must know Charlie is not talking to them, but they will still take this word as the be all or end all). So I think this just goes to show the power of AI and the extent to which it can be used for really anything, good or bad, and when it’s bad, it’s dangerous.

Text: I do think students like me have a voice in shaping the future of education, though maybe not always in an obvious or direct way. At first, I used to think that universities were big institutions that just set the rules and we had to follow them, but over time I’ve noticed that the way students study and the feedback we give really does influence how things are taught and assessed. For example, when I first started university, using AI tools was almost treated like a crime. It was strictly forbidden, and every assignment felt like it was being checked to make sure we hadn’t used them. But then, students kept experimenting, sometimes quietly, sometimes openly, because it was part of the reality of modern learning. The university couldn’t just ignore that. Slowly, I’ve seen attitudes change, with some courses now openly encouraging us to reflect on how we use AI or even designing assignments that involve prompt creation and AI verification. That shift happened partly because of how students acted, so I think our voice is already shaping the future. Another way I feel students have a voice is through structured reflections and feedback opportunities. When we write reflections like this, or when teachers ask us in tutorials how we used certain tools or what helped us learn best, I know those answers aren’t just for us. I can feel that they’re collected, discussed, and used to guide future teaching. I’ve seen examples where students complained about a certain type of assessment not being fair, and the following year it was redesigned. That makes me believe that when we take the chance to be honest and thoughtful, our voice does get heard. Thinking about the future of universities, I imagine that learning will keep changing with technology, and students will continue to play an important role in how that happens. The next generation of students, who are still in high school or even primary school now, will probably never remember a time when AI wasn’t part of education. Their expectations will be different from ours, and universities will need to adapt to that. I think students’ voices will matter even more in shaping how AI is used responsibly. If we don’t speak up, there’s a risk that AI could just be forced into education in ways that don’t really serve students, like as another surveillance tool or a shortcut without real understanding. For me personally, I try to use my voice by being open about my experiences. When I reflect on assignments, I don’t just write what went smoothly, but also where AI gave me problems or where I had to work harder to get good results. I think being honest about the challenges is just as important as praising the benefits, because that helps teachers understand what students really face. I also see my role in group projects: when my team discusses how we’ll use AI, I try to suggest we do it transparently and fairly. That’s a small step, but it’s still shaping how we think about responsible use. Overall, I do believe students have a voice, and that voice is growing stronger as universities are forced to rethink their future. It might not always feel powerful at the individual level, but collectively, students are setting the direction.

Text: I did realise I forgot to write this entry as I was going to submit my weekly entries so I am reflecting on this at a later date. I don’t feel I have a voice in my current education. I feel like every time I receive a grade I have to advocate for more feedback as it currently stands. For example, I recently got marks back for my evidence assignment and was told "you need to introduce yourself more" - in my assignment I said "May it please the court my name is Nelson, initials P T, solicitor with LegalAid Queensland, appearing on behalf of the accused…’ I don’t know what more of an introduction I could have given unless they wanted my place of birth and parents full legal names. There is no option to receive an informal review/consultation ‘because of the type of assignment’ (oral). For this assignment, when looking at the wording of the feedback like ‘introduce yourself more’, it doesn’t matchup to what was written in my script. I spoke about the police’s actions when discussing the public policy discretion to exclude evidence and was told I needed to ‘discuss the discretion more and focus less on the police’s actions’. This vague feedback that is not supported by how tutorials and lectures have taught us to consider the public policy discretion leave me wondering whether there are some teaching assistants who are using AI to write feedback/grade assignments. Similarly, I fear AI will be incorporated into writing assignment scenarios. For assessments like orals which ‘are not open to informal review’, if we receive feedback that doesn’t make sense and honestly seems like it was written by AI, I truly don’t know where students can go from there. It shouldn’t be forced on a student to pay for a formal review of all their assignments if their work is being graded by AI. I just hope it was this one teaching assistant and not an emerging trend. There is obviously nothing to concretely demonstrate the grader used AI but I feel like we can often tell when something isn’t worded like a human would write, and when the feedback directly opposes minor elements of someone’s writing like ‘introduce yourself more’ - it doesn’t account for the fact that, in the context of speaking in court, it would be unprofessional and would not be concise to give yourself a longer introduction. There are things like the ‘student voice’ survey but I can’t say I have ever heard of anything coming from those. Instead, from people who have worked at the uni I have heard the feedback doesn’t even get back to the teaching team. While this may not be true, it is scary to think teaching staff could begin incorporating AI into crafting and grading assessments with no easily accessible way for students to advocate for better feedback or even missing marks if it is, for example, an oral and not open to informal review.

Text: Yes and no. I think this study has helped me feel like I have more of a say in the future of my education. But overall, no, I don’t feel like I have much of a say. Universities, especially QUT, don’t seem very interested in giving students a choice in how we approach our assessments, especially when it comes to the use of AI. It’s very frustrating as I know that I have more knowledge and interest in AI than many (if not most) of my professors, who ultimately have a say over how I write my assessment. It’s incredibly frustrating when a professor expresses their distaste and disinterest in AI and prohibits the use of it. What’s the point of burying your head in the sand and just ignoring the realities of life. QUT is supposed to be the university for the real world, but sometimes it seems more like the University ignoring the real world. It’s disappointing to me, and I wish I could have more of a say in my education. This would require probably a big overhaul of current teaching staff or forcing current staff to update their knowledge and understanding of technology, which they may not want to do. I hope that QUT will update their ideas about AI and instead work towards helping students learn and study using AI so that we can be useful employees in the future. Currently I just have to teach myself, which feels a bit stupid when I pay so much money to my university to teach me. Of course, I am not studying AI or technology, but incorporating some amount of AI learning would be incredibly useful, and would show that QUT actually cares about its’ students. If there was no prompt I would write about AI safety. This is a topic I am really interested in, I can’t remember if I have already talked about it in one of my submissions. But I think it’s a topic everyone should know about and be somewhat interested in. AI affects everyone and will continue to impact people more as it gets better. It affects the environment, jobs, the economy etc. It’s so fascinating how the interaction of governments and people are impacted by AI too. It worries me a bit, not knowing how things will change in the future, and whether it will be for the better or the worse. I don’t trust tech giants to protect the interests of people or even humanity as a whole, I think greed will win and society will suffer. That’s why its so important to know about AI and how to use it. If we bury our heads in the sand, we won’t stand a chance. I don’t want to leave the future of humanity up to the billionaires.

Text: I find this to be an interesting question. It is evident that it is one appealing to a possibly younger set of people who have had access to generative AI throughout their high school and early tertiary career. In my experience, and it makes me feel old for saying this, but up until 2 years ago, the thought of Generative AI was not even on the radar of most people, I got through the entirety of my schooling and ¾ of the way through my tertiary education before AI even burst onto the scene. Therefore, while I can sit here and say that I am better because I had to do things the hard way, it would be naïve of me not to consider what I would have done if I did have access to these items and if I would have used it with such blatant disregard for stealth that I would be questioned about it. In my view, even if AI was an option at my disposal, I don’t think I would have used it, and I attribute that to my personal values, even now as I write this and think deeply about my view on artificial intelligence, it is evident on some level that I might just be an AI boomer, clinging to the old and inefficient ways in order to elevate myself from others because I chose the harder and ‘more noble’ option when it came to assessment. But there is an inherent fallacy in my thinking, considering that the work I produce for university assessments and other documentation, it is evident that maybe I am against AI because I know that on many levels, it beats me in nearly every capacity. But maybe that is both a blessing and curse. While my work may not be worthy of receiving 7s and may by all metrics be considered rougher than sandpaper, it has brought me the benefit of being undoubtedly human in origin. And to a certain extent I believe that is why I have never been questioned about AI use because the manner in which I perform tasks, and convey ideas has all of the hallmarks of fallibility and imperfection that is only present within human works or the mediocre ones anyway. As a non sequitur I do wonder about the ways in which people approach AI use for assessments, while I know many would use AI to help brainstorm ideas or to determine their arguments, there is a certain subsect of people that will just ask AI to do the work for them, especially in an education context, and to that end I wonder why people do this. Is it out of desperation, apathy, or a general lack of understanding. While I can see some people would consider it an insult to their pride to produce anything that is less than perfect, is that not the point of learning? Is it not the nature of man to learn things by trial and error, does using AI to save face really allow for you to properly learn what is required for a certain task. In my view, and I believe most people would hold this, blatant use of AI with disregard for the consequences is like kicking the proverbial can down the road in terms of delaying a possible failure only moves you further and further away from realising a workable solution.
