Text: Date: Tuesday 16 September Time: 8.09am In the first semester of this year, I learnt about AI in Legal Research and what it means for the future of the legal profession. This semester, I’ve learnt about the effects of AI in Law, Governance and Sustainability, and across all subjects in general AI and what it means for lawyers is discussed. However, what I have seen in general is a rise in university students (and I would assume school students as well) being accused of AI because of their writing. I am an avid em-dash user, but I have seen SO many students get flagged for AI because they used an em-dash, because apparently that is a dead giveaway that someone has used AI. Well no, actually it is a piece of punctuation that is used in writing. AI has learned to write. Humans are not using ChatGPT just because we used an em-dash. So many students now have a sense of fear that they will be accused of AI because of their writing style - their vocabulary and the type of punctuation they use. I feel like if academics want to catch AI, they need to try and seriously identify the factors that give away that it is AI - which are becoming increasingly harder to detect. When AI is continuing to advance, you cannot use the same simple methods to detect it. An em-dash is not a giveaway that someone has used AI - it shows that someone knows how to punctuate a sentence. The ‘giveaway’ might be the fact that AI writes so shallow, and has a way of cleverly dancing around the question and giving a wordy response that isn’t actually an answer to the question. But even still, that might just be the genuine response of a student who doesn’t know the answer but knows how to write and tries to write their way around it so they can get something on the paper. I know that was me in school - if I didn’t know the answer, I just wrote as much as I could, even if it was shallow or stupid or dodged the question. So is there really a ‘giveaway’ of AI? I would argue no - not unless there is an actual tool like Turn It In, that can accurately say that AI was used to write a response. Especially for law students, an AI accusation is huge in university, and students are being negatively impacted and prejudiced for using AI when they haven’t, without any regard for how serious the accusation is and how damaging it can be if it is wrong.

Text: and (b) Reflect further on AI - if there was no prompt today, what would you write about? Part (a): Hmmm … next gen … honestly, I’m so far beyond secondary education, let alone primary education, that I don’t know if I could provide any insight into this question. I graduated high school in 1991. That was 34 years ago. My kids went through secondary education much more recently, though being the primary breadwinner (scratch that … ONLY breadwinner given my dysfunctional ex-wife’s inability to do anything productive with her life), and the fact that I separated from my ex when my youngest son was in year 6, I didn’t get the opportunity to be a significant part of their education. The upshot is that, when it comes to education below the tertiary level, I have no idea. Though from what I’ve heard from teachers I know, I don’t think the issue with modern education has anything to do with GenAI. The future learning environment of the next generation is pretty fucked, because the authority teachers used to have has been insidiously eroded away so that the little shits can get away with anything they want and there are no consequences. What a great way to prepare for either a tertiary education or a career, both of which require self-discipline and a respect for authority. Here’s to future Centrelink queues growing exponentially. Of course, it doesn’t help that teachers aren’t taught about learning. Like most modern university courses, teaching students are fed a steady diet of socialist propaganda and politically correct bullshit. Ask any modern graduating teacher about the neuroscience of learning and watch them look quizzically at you, never knowing there was even such a thing. Honestly, I don’t think AI will have much to do with it. People think that GenAI is going to encourage cheating. Maybe so, but every generation of students, irrespective of whether they were primary, secondary or tertiary, has had the ability to cheat. The only difference between the generations is the technology used to cheat. If someone wants to cheat, they’ll find a way. The students who will go on to become criminal masterminds will get away with it. The dumb fucks will get caught, but they really weren’t criminal masterminds to start with, so getting caught cheating wasn’t going to have any significant effect on their educational trajectory. Part (b): Reflect further on AI. This is getting trickier by the day. Text: I am extremely concerned about the next generation of students. I don’t see that AI would greatly impact their education, but it would almost certainly make it worse. We see the problem enough now, students using AI to submit work and teachers using AI to mark work. I see more of that into the future, more laziness. I think at its heart AI is a tool that preys on human laziness. I mean sure there are people that are adopters because it can be helpful for them, and there is a fine line between tools that make things more ‘efficient’ and tools that make people lazy, but I certainly see AI in the latter class. The issue with AI that I have is that it replaces mental faculty. If it continues to see widespread use it will continue to infiltrate the classroom and it will continue to decrease the amount of thought people put into things, on both the side of the student and the teacher. I think people will lose their foundational skills, particularly within writing. I think that as a result of this education will become more elitist. There was a time, I mean there really still is a time right now, where most information in the world was easily accessible by the masses. It still is and I suppose it will continue to be. I think that went a long way in reducing the elitism and classism in education. But with the advent of AI, and its continued use, I think we will go backward and become a post-literate society. Knowledge used to be confined to the elites because that was the only group of society that had the means to access knowledge, I believe in the future the elites will be the only group that can access knowledge because they are the only ones who understand it. Public schools will cut corners, because they have to, and rely on AI, and their students will not gain an actual knowledge of anything. Prestigious schools, with the resources to work intensely with students, will be able to teach students from the ground up. But again, that is a very cynical way to look at it I suppose.

Text: This is a thought that I have given a lot of personal credence to as when I reflect on my own experience of schooling and university. It is clear that while I went through schooling at a time before the introduction of generative AI, I cannot stand here and argue that if I was in the position of students today, that I wouldn’t be using AI as well. While I could say that I am more well equipped for the modern world since I had to learn to educate myself when the materials were incapable of doing so, it is evident that with the nature of AI, students of now may be able to have a more intuitive understanding of concepts as they may have one of the most patient and well read teachers that man could create through AI. Therefore, whilst I have previously discussed my concern regarding blatantly accepting the output of AI as gospel, there is a certain level of consideration that should be given to using AI as a learning companion. It is entirely possible that one in the current day could survive on old fashioned methods of information gathering in order to learn, the ability to tailor an explanation of a concept to a manner that you are able to understand is invaluable and will provide more effective learning than any spaced repetition cycle can provide for a person. Thus if we are to consider the learning environment of future students, it would be impractical to try and force these students to learn in the same way someone like me did, students now have access to what is essentially the holy grail of education at the touch of their fingertips, so while I would like to know that the fundamental skills of learning and information gathering are still taught, if students are forced to rely on old and archaic methods in order to ensure that they can survive without AI, then it could be seen as rather absurd. And I do not believe I am alone in this as there has been news articles that have demonstrated educators creating AI tools in order to assist students in their learning journey. While some may seem it as a step backwards, the way I see it, it is a step towards the future. It would be no stretch of the imagination to hold that AI will not be fading into obscurity within our lifetime, but instead will become a generational marker, separating people into a pre and post AI era. Text: ’. I think that the next wave of education reform will be an acceptance of AI / the safest assumption that educators can make is that work done at home is co-created with AI in some way. I think that educational institutes are taking the view that schools are here to prepare their students for the future, which is undoubtedly underscored by, and will increasingly be predicated on, these new emerging technologies such as GenAI. In this way, there is no point in ignoring AI or trying to prevent its use. It may be monitored in the classroom, but it has to be assumed that it is being used in some capacity at some stage of a student’s learning. So, the future of education may be entirely reformed so as to flip the learning and guide and assess learning in another way. The focus may be less on ‘content’ and more on the critical thinking, e.g., students will do the research at home and then in class critical discussions and analysis will take place. As an aside, with this I think about the people that AI/technology driven learning is leaving behind. People who don’t have computers or internet at home, struggling to access all of their work which is contained within OneNote, and complete their tasks which is done online, and researching using ChatGPT. In my own opinion, I think that schools need to hybridise learning so that there is some computer but just as much, if not more, pen and paper (of course university is different, but in terms of primary and secondary school). As a university student who uses technology, I am able to do so safely, responsibly and with knowledge of risks, because I grew up writing with pen and paper and learning the fundamental skills of problem solving, critical thinking, application of knowledge, studying and memorising content. I think that there is a major difference between people who have acquired those foundational skills and can now operate in a tech-heavy complex, compared to students who have only ever used computers and now have the overwhelming presence of AI. Those critical, foundational skills are missing. When they get to university and are studying for exams, they aren’t going to know how because they’ve always used ChatGPT. Typing on a laptop does not have the same effect on learning as writing things out. Typing something mindlessly on a laptop is very different to creating those synaptic connections from reading what you’re writing, and physically writing it out, and associating it with the colour pen you’re using or where it is on the page. I think that as schools continue to adapt to AI and shift how they approach learning, they need to remember that they don’t need to change the entire operation of schools so that it fits within a technology-hungry agenda that is being *strongly* encouraged by society and these big tech companies. Don’t be so quick to restructure the entire architecture of schools and learning. Not all things have to be faster, easier, more efficient - because the most important skills that adolescents need are the ones they acquire while figuring stuff out. Sure ChatGPT can give you all the research you need in one prompt. But you actually learn how to analyse and dissect information when you research yourself. Yes, it’s easier to have all the content there on OneNote and have students type in their answers. But there are SO many students in the school I work at whose handwriting is appalling - they literally don’t know how to physically handwrite. And they don’t know how to spell because laptops autocorrect, and they don’t know how to punctuate because laptops have the suggestion pop up. The point I’m making is that not everything needs to be revolutionised by AI and technology in general.

I think AI has already had a big impact on what schooling looks like for the next generation. It does worry me a bit, as I talked about in one of the previous prompts, I feel secure in that I have been well educated in the kinds of skills AI does well. This means that if AI suddenly disappeared, I would be okay because I could still do those things. However, the younger generation may not be able to do that and may struggle. I find that the more I use AI for uni, the more I want to rely on it and avoid using my own brain. Kind of like a muscle, if you don’t use your brain, it will be harder and harder to do. This does worry me a bit, as I could foresee myself being more and more reliant on AI until I suddenly can’t make myself do the work anymore. Of course this is a pretty intense example, but it could happen, especially as AI technology progresses and becomes more useful for even more tasks. If there was no prompt today I would write about how I have been using AI for one of my assignments. I feel like using GenAI for essays can be extremely helpful and has been a lifesaver for me this semester. Partly because the subject is extremely boring and not something I wanted to do (but had to). It helped me to create a structure for the assignment using my own ideas, the criteria sheet and the assignment task. It helped me to flesh out the initial structure of the assignment and weave important concepts through my essay, which I may not have done as well myself. It then helped me to write sections I needed more help on, or provide me with some more ideas to research. If you learn how to prompt well, you can get the AI to give you some really good suggestions that are helpful for assessment. I really don’t understand why universities don’t want us using these tools to help make our writing better. I go through everything the AI gives me critically, take some and leave other bits, and research every point it provides. I feel like I have a much better understanding of the overall topic after this strategy. I’m not just researching one section and then running out of time, the AI helps me to see from different angles the same way it’s helpful to talk to another person about your ideas. This is especially helpful if the university doesn’t want us colluding with other students, because the AI can gives helpful advice, point us in a different direction, without compromising another students work. This seems like an ideal situation. Of course not everyone is using AI to help better their understanding of a topic, but just to write the essay for them, and that’s not what I would consider ‘ethical’ use of AI. This is why I think it’s so important to teach people how to use AI properly, rather than to just ban it. Research has shown that banning things is extremely unhelpful. Text: AND "Reflect further on AI - if there was no prompt today, what would you write about?" I have already discussed using AI in assessments in previous prompts, but I have two due today and I have used CoPilot several times to help cut words. I definitely know people who have used ChatGPT to write entire business assignments however and it’s so easy to just give AI the criteria and problem scenario, and then submit it on its way. One of my best friends recently got 27/30 on a business assignment that she said was entirely written by AI, because she was not granted a necessary extension. Why should we feel bad for using it (in any capacity, but predominantly these editing type scenarios) when there are people out here getting such high scores for using it? Even on these assignments I’m submitting today, the task sheet says AI can be used to refine and edit work so long as I have ‘attempted to write it first.’ Ok… so how is that tracked? How is this proven? Personally I DO attempt to write it myself, but I did have a giggle when I read this because I then look at my law assignments and in big bold words it says AI is prohibited. I think there should be more consistency across uni’s approach because it’s doing my head in. Can’t say I’m that mad about it though because it feels like psych is allowing me to use AI in exactly the way I already use it, in the way I think it should be used. I also feel that I am subconsciously learning how to write better from reading the stuff it spits out. Every time it refines or rewords a sentence for me, I go, oh yeah I see what you did there. I would say though, as someone who works 3 days a week (don’t get me started on the ‘you are a full time student, study full time BS’ - uni doesn’t know what any individual person is going through and why they need to work or why they need money and it shits me) I really struggle to find time to juggle tutorials, lectures, readings, and work (plus obviously a general social life and a relationship - I need my coffee dates). Using AI to edit and refine my work saves me so much time and I don’t think that’s a crime, let me live! It’s not uni’s fault students get so busy, but I am so tired of tutors or lecturers having digs and jabs at students who can’t make it to tutorials later in the semester or who don’t do the readings. I think it’s time to recognise that times are changing and there are more things young people have to worry about and we need more tools to assist us if the workload is not changing. Yesterday a new admin girl was hired at my work for a 5-day fortnight. One of the solicitors I get along with actually gasped when I told her this and she said ‘what is it with no one working full time and studying full time anymore?’ It felt so tone deaf and I was so offended (I am a law clerk, not admin, but am part time obviously). Work was looking for non uni students for the role because they don’t tend to stay longer than a year in the role. I told this solicitor that while I understand it’s important to have full time admin staff, of course uni students want the part time admin role because they need it to get their foot in the door (especially women). Where was this anger coming from with her? I just told her I didn’t think that was very fair and immediately she doubled down and said back when she was studying, she didn’t give a damn about her grades, so full time work was fine. I just wonder about the ways we can be more efficient with producing assessment / even in the workforce so we can get more done in a shorter time

Text: and (b) Reflect further on AI - if there was no prompt today, what would you write about? Part (a): Reflect on my assessments this semester … well, they were … ah, so much fun … *ahem* … Did I use, or would I have used, GenAI? No. As I’ve said in previous posts, I want to learn law. Getting GenAI to write stuff for me defeats that purpose. But also, it only takes getting caught once, and the ‘fit and proper person’ test goes out the window. As an aside, I think the ‘fit and proper person’ test is bullshit. It’s a throwback to the musty paternalism of yesteryear, when a panel of ‘esteemed legal professionals’ (who were sanctimonious, or hypocrites, or most likely both) got to sit in a place of judgemental faux-authority and decide on a law graduate’s character based on what the graduate has ever done wrong, the ‘guilty unless you can prove yourself innocent’ approach. It’s not only contemptable but also antithetical to every fundamental principle of jurisprudence. The very idea of this test is viscerally offensive, and the fact that it’s still a thing is reprehensible, repugnant. Anyway, now that I have that off my chest and returning to the prompt … I might not get to practice law given how fucked up my life has become, but I’m also not going to jeopardise the slim chance I have, risking it on academic misconduct that’s not only self-defeating, but really stupid. Part (b): Reflect further on AI. This is an anecdote, pure and simple. There’s no particular commentary on GenAI. It’s just a story. A few months ago, I was with a friend who has an emotionally manipulative sociopath of a mother who, during my friend’s childhood, was psychologically abusive to her (and, very possibly, physically abused her in a Munchausens sort of way). While at my friend’s house, her mother was sending her texts which were subtlety narcissistic and antagonising. My friend didn’t want to emotionally engage with her mother as she was cognitively and emotionally wrecked, so instead of coming up with replies to her mother’s texts, she put her mother’s texts into ChatGPT and asked it to come up with replies which met fire with fire. ChatGPT excelled itself. The comments it came up with were pure gold, and in fact, my friend had to water some of ChatGPT’s replies down as they were too acerbic. So, ChatGPT took what could have been a frustrating, emotionally draining conversation, and made it into a conversation which allowed my friend to one-up the subtly provocative comments of her sociopathic mother, minus the emotional drain on her already taxed emotions. GenAI to the rescue. And that’s the end of my story.

Text: I have not used AI in any of my assessment items this semester. I don't believe that there was a single item in which I would have benefitted from its use. One of my assignments spoke specifically to AI actually, so that was an interesting one. That assignment was a research assignment in an essay style into the challenges that automated decision making presents when attempting to challenge an administrative decision via judicial review. While automated decision making casts a wider net than just AI, I ended up talking about AI in specific for large parts of the assignment. I believe the assignment was likely written to capture AI issues, given the rise of its use in everyday life as well as government services. The thing that piqued my interest about the topic was just how much accountability could be dodged when decision making is handed to a machine. In many ways it breaks or makes opaque the judicial review process. I do have to wonder if there is some vague sinister intention with the inclusion of AI in government decision making. Perhaps it is implements so when a decision is received poorly, those who should be accountable can simply point to the technology and not to themselves. I think this goal is greatly strengthened by the fact that the general public seems to hold this notion that AI and alike technologies are in some way purely reasonable, that they may make better decisions because they are not lead by human emotion. But this is simply not true - any tendencies, any bias that people have is replicated by AI. But I don't think most people understand that, which is what concerns me. If anything, AI is lead more by bias and in a more detrimental way, because AI cannot be 'reasoned' with in a traditional sense, it cannot be interrogated to provide a rationale for what it has produced because it simply cannot, and the people implementing its use cannot determinate this either. What concerns me are the little biases that aren't statistically relevant. Those that may skew an AI's outcome ever so slightly. Because those may never be identified, they go untouched, and the AI continues to push out tainted decisions to a public that believes it to be an entirely logical machine. This obfuscation is my concern.

Text: I've reflected on my own AI use in assignments pretty frequently throughout this project. I have used it to check understanding of terms or words in judgments, because AI gives better quick hit context than Google can. It takes less effort to get the understanding I need. I've also used AI to rephrase my own words to reduce word count or to make my writing more active. Through this reflection process I've acknowledged that this is probably considered "cheating" by the uni's standards as I am being assessed on my ability to do these things myself, but I kind of figure that I'd be using these tools in the workplace for this exact purpose, so, meh. I'm not using it to construct the work, the research and the arguments are all my own. As is the initial draft and the redraft. It's just the finessing that I'm using it for, and even then it's only for suggestions. I'm not trying to convince the readers that I'm not cheating, or myself, just to explain. I'm also using ChatGPT extensively this semester to summarise my notes, summarise legislation, build quick reference tables, etc, in preparation for exams. I don't super trust it, but it's faster for me to get ChatGPT to do it and me to check it than it is for me to do it from scratch myself. I think it would be really good to be able to trust AI to maybe turn my notes into practice questions, facts etc. This is the first semester that I'm actually up to date and on top of my course work, including having prepped and attended all tutorials. It's great, but I don't really feel like I'm at any better advantage than in past semesters where I have attended tutorials but haven't prepped. Usually I use tutorial questions as practice exam questions to revise once I've prepped my exam notes, and I'm kind of at a loss this semester as to what to do to revise now. Maybe I could feed my course notes into AI and ask it to come up with questions to test my knowledge. It would be amazing if it could develop test scenarios, and give me the answers so I could practice, but I don't know that I'd trust it? Also there's sort of a feedback loop of incorrect information possible there, if I get something wrong in my notes and then feed that into a system that then tests me on my errors, entrenching the wrong knowledge. Kind of like one of the major concerns with AI systems used in executive decision making - wow I did learn something from that assignment, yew!

Text: While I would like to answer this prompt in the manner that it was asked, I ended up taking a Hiatus for writing entries during this period because of the intense nature and limited time to turn in 3 back-to-back assessments. But in the spirit of the exercise, I may be able to reflect on my feelings now. While I the thought of using AI did cross my mind during the assessment period and I did use AI to help me confirm the ideas I already had, in terms of meaningfully using AI to help me with my assessment I cannot say I did use it to that extent. 90% of my AI use during this period was for the point of confirming ideas I had already had and fleshing them out with the level of depth required for the assessment. While I would like to reflect on why I used AI in this fashion, the only thing that truly comes to mind is the fact that I needed some candour from a person that understood the subject, and who talking to about the assignment wouldn’t count as collusion. While I cannot deny that AI did provide me a sense of comfort in ensuring that the ideas I had was valid, and I was happy to test out AI more than just superficially. It is evident in my view that my relationship with AI at least for the time being is transactional and rare rather than friendly and consistent, which I may change at some point but for the purposes of ensuring my academic integrity I feel as if it is better for me if I keep the use of AI to a minimum. However, there is an anecdote I would like to provide as it was rather novel to me. For one of my psychology assignments (PYB306 Psychopathology) generative AI wasn’t outright banned and was instead allowed for certain purposes. This was incredible to me as up until this point the only mention of AI, I had ever seen on assignments was for the point of outlining that it cannot be used. Thus, seeing that we could us AI to help with brainstorming and prognosis was truly a culture shock to me, and makes me think about the previous prompt about how the learning landscape is changing as we speak. Evidently the hardline policies that were initially adopted by educators to crack down on the use of AI have now softened with more understanding and research pertaining to the benefits and drawbacks of AI usage. Thus, maybe the future of assessment may involve the use of AI, to a limited degree I would hope but this does show promise that a world in which AI is integrated into learning can exist.

I find that I use Gen AI for assessments mostly in the earlier stages - when I am trying to wrap my head around what is required and how I can best respond. And then as I continue with my assignment, I will refer back to what GenAI (ChatGPT) said at the start to make sure it fits within the big picture. Text: " Looking back at my recent assessments, some of them actually asked me to show how I created prompts for AI and explain the process. At first I thought that would be easy, but I realised pretty quickly that writing a good prompt is not simple at all. It wasn’t as easy as just typing a question and getting a perfect answer. Writing a prompt that gives you useful, clear, and accurate information takes a lot of trial and error. Sometimes the AI misunderstood what I meant, or gave a very generic answer that didn’t fit my assignment. I had to rephrase, test different approaches, and think carefully about what exactly I wanted from it. I didn’t know how to create a good prompt at first, what words to add to make it effiect. From that experience I started to see AI as more like a tool that depends a lot on the person using it, rather than something that just gives you the answer. If I could add one reflection, it would be that I wish the university offered more guidance or even small workshops on how to design prompts and use AI effectively. I didn’t address too much about my use of AI with assignments; I think a bit because I’m nervous that talking about it could get me in trouble (even though I know that this is all secure). I find it a bit hard to think of anything else to say aside from the prompts themselves. I’m not sure why this is, maybe because I feel like I talked a lot about the things I thought were important at that start and kinda ran out of things I really wanted to say. But I think its also because I don’t want to keep repeating myself. I have reviewed all of my past submissions, but especially those from the last week as I have had a lot of assessment due recently. I think I would add more about how I used AI for my assignments and be more specific about how I have used AI for different subjects. There were some days where I used AI almost all day for an assignment, but then days where I didn’t use it at all. This almost entirely depended on what kind of assignment I was doing (law or business) rather than the structure of the assignment. I would say I rely on AI much more for the business subjects and not at all for law. I used genAI quite a lot for one of my business subjects, mostly because I just ran out of time and had so many other assessments to work on, and I wasn’t really interested in the subject or the topic I was working on. I find AI is really useful for times like this, when you aren’t particularly interested in the topic of you have a lot of other things you need to do. I think it would be really beneficial if QUT allowed us to use AI and taught us how to use it ethically and responsibly. I think this would only serve to improve our work and our efficiency, rather than just forcing us to try to hide our use of AI (well or not). It seems like a pointless waste of time, when we could just be teaching people how to use these tools we now have access to. We teach student show to use Google, Google Scholar, Zotero etc. Why not ChatGPT? It would save the university time trying to figure out if students have used AI in the first place and focus on the quality of our work. Or we could change the way we examine students in the first place, transition to more exams etc. I don’t pretend that I know the best way or the best answer, but I do know that what we are doing right now isn’t working and is actively harmful in some ways. It’s far too easy to accidentally accuse someone of using AI when they haven’t, and how are they supposed to prove they haven’t? AI is getting too good and we have to keep up, or at least try to, otherwise educational institutions are going to become less useful to society. I don’t want to seem like a doomer, or to suggest that AI is awesome and excellent, it definitely has issues, and I think I have outlined my thoughts on that in previous submissions, but I just don’t think the current approach is any good. I don’t think students shouldn’t be learning and using AI to bypass any actual work/study, but I think it is a tool and should be used as one.

Text: To be honest I do not believe that I would change anything in my previous entries. I think being tasked with reflecting regularly on AI has made me more cynical. I think I have always had a particularly strong stance on AI, and every piece of further information or analysis that comes out surrounding AI has only further strengthened this stance. I think at this point, more than simply disliking AI I have come to wish that it was gone. Personally, I do not see any benefit from AI. Despite this, its allure to the finance and C suite types has made it practically an invasive species in the online world. Social media, misinformation dreamt up by AI and bot personalities constructed to spew division. Adobe, offering me a summary for a 2 page PDF. I mean, even when I was getting furniture delivered the other week, I had to negotiate with an AI chatbot to provide me an expected delivery time which felt as though it was defending that information with its life, all because this solution was cheaper than having an actual phone line. In society, I do not see any benefit arising from AI, not in the present tense, and certainly not in the future. I think AI will continue to be a tool to seed division, to weaken our education systems and ultimately our people. I do not believe that I would have written much differently, but I know that I would likely have spoken with more certainty. As I said, my opinion has become less nuanced if anything. My present stance would be that AI should not exist, it should never have existed. Perhaps I would have made that more clear.

Text: Date: Friday 19 September Time: 7.24am In reflecting on how my friends and the people around me are using AI, I wanted to add another use and my thoughts on it here. My partner and his friend are looking at starting a business, and have been floating ideas around, building the picture, etc. While we were all sitting around the table (them working on their business, me doing uni but actually tuning in to what they were doing), we bounced off of each other and narrowed the idea down, and then began to brainstorm events. When we had come up with three or four event ideas, they asked ChatGPT for some other ideas of events/fundraisers they could run. Whatever response it gave is not the focus of this entry. It made me think back to when at work we were holding a musical and had to run fundraisers to raise money. After I had thought of a few, I asked CoPilot for other fundraiser ideas. So, in seeing this paralleled, I had two thoughts - first, why did we ask AI for more ideas? And two, how is AI useful for things like event management or fundraiser ideas or business startups, which is a perspective that I haven’t previously considered in my entries. In why we asked AI for ideas, I guess my reason is simple - there’s really only so much you can do at a school, and after a slushie stall and free dress day, I really was just lost for ideas. Being at work and wanting to come up with ideas quickly, CoPilot was truly just the simplest way to get a plethora of ideas presented to me for me to choose between. For them, I guess it was quite the opposite - their scope is so broad and they have so many possibilities for things they could do that they didn’t really know how to narrow that down. I then thought about how beneficial AI can be for things like starting up a business. Having started my own small business years ago, I didn’t use AI for it (but it is a creative based business, so there wasn’t too much room for the help of AI). But for people like these two friends, who have a massive idea of what they want to achieve, but need to step it out into smaller, bite-sized pieces, AI would of course be helpful. In this sense, could you say it’s being used ethically? If they are creating a business with the goal to be a sort of organisation fundraising for places overseas in need, the use of AI is helping them achieve this goal. But if someone was using AI to create an organisation or a group of people that come together for a very different purpose (maybe it’s a major ‘political-based’ group, who have strong feelings about a minority and are empowered to spread hate speech), then we would look at that and say how AI is detrimental because it helped these people create this. So then is ethical/morality problem really about AI? Or is AI just reflecting the moral compass in each individual who uses it? And then how do we regulate that?

Text: Date/Time: 19 September 2025 After reviewing all of my previous entries, another note that I would like to reflect on, is that universities appear to inadequately prepare students in the best way to write assessments, in the current AI climate. There appears to be a greater gap in education around the tools available to students, to ‘prove’ they have undertaken their work by themselves. Universities should educate students via library sessions called "Writing Assignments in the AI Landscape", alongside "in-unit" modules and tutorials. Text: Wow, what an absolutely delicious statement. There are a lot of ways to unpack this, though I’ll focus on one element, otherwise we’ll be here all day. I agree with the statement in almost every way, except for the final part regarding the ‘relevance’ of universities. In that regard, I don’t think universities will become redundant or irrelevant, GenAI or no. Whether universities are relevant in our society’s future comes down to how each university chooses to define itself. If a university chooses to remain a sausage factory for white collar graduates who simply regurgitate the socialist rhetoric they’ve been fed for three or more years and have never learnt to think independently, then I think that university will rapidly become irrelevant and redundant. GenAI, and AI generally, will soon subsume many of the roles/occupations that such graduates are being trained in, like pharmacists in one of my previous entries, or journalists, paralegals, or the generic corporate drones that write anything-from guidelines, to policies, to research and analysis reports-because various AI’s can already do most of that, and they’re still rapidly evolving. On the other hand, if a university is willing to break the mould and stop indoctrinating students, and instead, not just teach critical reasoning but actively encourage it in an open intellectual space, free from judgement, political correctness and socialist group-think, then those universities will offer something different … different from almost every university in the world at the moment, and different from what AI can churn out. As it’s been said of AI, This sort of content is so valuable because it’s the pinnacle of human achievement. These models are very good at copying what they find, but they're not so good at creating what they find. And so if you want high quality content, you go to human authored content. Similarly, [What are we at risk of losing?] The individuality of the human spirit. AI doesn't have personal experiences. They’ve never suffered a loss. They’re not gonna know what it means to really laugh at a funny joke. They’re not gonna know what it means to be intimate with someone. I guess my problem is if we wanna use AI for things that are intrinsically human, then what’s left for us to do? What’s our reason to get out of bed every morning? AI technology will change the world in so many ways, ways we think we know but are yet to come to fruition, though probably more realistically, are simply beyond our ability to even predict. If universities want to remain relevant, they need to start teaching students to think critically in ways that AI cannot … not just experience life, but to explore it for themselves, to immerse themselves in it-to truly be original versions of themselves and to really know what it’s like to be human-something which an AI will (hopefully) never be able to imitate, no matter how good their language models are. It’s been said that ‘change is inevitable, growth is optional’. Social disruption from AI is coming (assuming that it’s not already here). This change is inevitable. Whether universities will actually grow, not by just adjusting to the change, but to go beyond it and actually shape the future, is ‘optional’, though if we’re going to be honest, it’s not merely optional, but essential! At the moment, from what I can see, QUT remains trapped in the traditional academic echo chamber. It’s still forcing students to engage in irrelevant socialist rhetoric, like LLB108, ‘Law, Governance and Sustainability’ … forcing a ‘core unit’ consisting entirely of left-wing, politically correct, aspirational propaganda-essentially a socialist academic’s wet dream-onto intellectually naïve and impressionable 18-year-olds. Does QUT really think that ‘sustainability’ (whatever that means) is going to make any tangible difference as AI changes everything about the future? Oh, and teaching ‘critical thinking skills … about public international law as a global system of rules to address transnational sustainability issues’? Really? Somehow, I doubt that. Be that as it may, unless ‘transnational sustainability issues’ include the global social disruption of AI and the resulting seismic shifts in the global economy, employment, health care, welfare, social and racial inequality etc etc, and on promoting real-world tangible solutions (which are already out there, if people bothered to look), and not more theoretical bullshit about climate change or whining about the Voice Referendum, then QUT will ‘change’ (i.e.: delude itself that it’s innovating) but not ‘grow’, and will, unfortunately, become another relict of the white-collar sausage factory that AI will soon replace. Text: There is a large amount of weight to this prompt, and in my view, I believe that my answer should also provide a proportionate amount of gravitas. In my view the answer is yes, there is no doubt that the pandoras box has been opened in terms of AI, and regardless of whether people learn to accept the change or not, the march of progress waits for no man. As an extension to that point, I do wonder if the actions that we as students have taken in relation to AI has led us down a path that we might not be able to come back from. While it would be easy to assume that this path will lead to the benefit of everyone, I do wonder if the path that we have chosen may lead to problems that we are yet to see. While students are able to reap the benefits of AI with almost total impunity, there is a worry in the back of my mind that our blatant disregard for AI’s use may lead to educators taking a more hardline and intrusive approach that ensures that the use of AI for an assessment becomes exceedingly difficult, if not impossible. However, while one would be quick to argue that it would be a fever dream or that the view would be misguided, I see a very real possibility that people who do not respect the power of the tool they have been given abuse it to the point where enough is enough and as a result, educators have to restrict the use of it in order to minimize its abuse. However, I will also concede that there is a more realistic possibility that due to the pervasive nature of AI and its ubiquitous use, educators would have half a mind to just bite the bullet determine a way to weather the storm whether by integrating AI into the learning process or by creating better AI detection methods that are kept proprietary in order to deny students the ability to adapt to the countermeasures. And to extend this point I hold that the same view would apply in general, there are two paths for AI, either we restrict it’s use in order to assure that it is not abused by those who would seek to do so or we learn to accept that our control over the resource is limited and learn to accept the reality that it ai will be as much part of life as electricity or running water. While it is divisive in my view I feel like with the way we are seeing AI being used now it is just a matter of time before it becomes part of the status quo, rather than a quirky novelty that only a select few will truly be able to grasp the complexity of. As an aside, on the point of my role in the future and AI, it is my view that I as an individual would most likely have little to no effect especially due to my sparse use of it, however, we currently stand at a point in time when both our actions and inactions will lead to a significant result regardless. So while I may believe that I might not change much, maybe my apathy and the collective apathy of others similar to me may give way to a future that we might not have expected.

People in the comments were arguing about how this use of AI might benefit or negatively impact researchers. Text: Universities are watching how students interact with AI and building their policies based on what they see us doing. If most students secretly use AI, it pushes universities to either make rules stricter or redesign assessments so that AI use is openly allowed and guided. That means every time I choose to use AI, or not use it, I am part of that bigger shift even if it feels small at the time. For the future of learning, I think this means universities will need to focus less on memorisation and more on skills that AI cannot do for you. Critical thinking, ethics, oral advocacy, teamwork, and judgment will probably become more important. Research might become more about checking and improving AI output rather than starting from scratch. Students now could end up being the last group to write completely AI-free essays, which feels like a strange but exciting shift. My role in this feels both personal and connected to something bigger. I have tried to be careful with how I use AI. I do not let it do the thinking for me, but I do use it to plan, check my understanding, and make my work clearer. If more students used AI this way, I think the conversation around it would be less negative. I want to be part of the group that shows AI can be used responsibly without losing the value of education. Reflecting on the past few weeks, I can see how much my thinking has changed. At first, I was cautious and a bit defensive about using AI. Now I feel like I have a healthy balance with it. I am not afraid to use it, but I also do not trust it blindly. The biggest shift is that I stop and ask myself why I am using it before I open it, and that pause has made my use much more intentional. These reflections have also made me think about AI’s bigger impacts, including mental health, ethics, and empathy. I have thought about how tone matters when talking to victims, how vulnerable people could be harmed by chatbots, and how trust is the biggest issue holding back AI in law. I do not think I would have considered those issues if I had not been reflecting on AI every day. Text: I agree with this idea. Every student’s choice about whether to use Generative AI or not is already shaping how universities adapt. If a lot of us use AI to draft essays, summarize readings, or debug code, then assessments will have to change. They’ll be less about just the final answer and more about showing the process: how we got there, what tools we used, and how we checked the results. AI speed up scanning articles or generating ideas, but the real value is still in designing experiments, checking data carefully, and explaining why a result matters. On the other hand, universities need to give guidance and provide fair access. Today, most students are already using AI for drafting, debugging, and simulating, so courses that ignore AI will start to struggle to deliver. I believe that departments should move into the curriculum, and have academic integrity policies that are aware of the use of AI because that is what we need for effective and ethical learning. If students hide their use, universities will respond with bans and controls. If we present transparent, high-quality work powered by AI, they will respond with better guidance and grading. This also works the other way around. Instead of just submitting a final PDF, evidence of process (version history, reminder logs, validation steps) will be required. The curriculum will add an "AI layer". Not a single AI course, but AI across multiple subjects. Policies will evolve from "don’t use AI" to "state how you used it, demonstrate your testing, and take responsibility for errors." Universities can provide basic access and training to avoid unfairness. I’m on the side of proving that AI can raise standards, not lower them.

Text: Yes I’d agree with that quote. Whether we use AI or not, it’s already changing how unis think about teaching and even what their role is. If students lean on AI, it forces unis to rethink assessments, plagiarism rules and the actual skills they want us to graduate with. Instead of just memorising stuff or cranking out essays, it’s more about critical thinking, creativity, and how to use tools responsibly. Research is shifting too. AI can crunch data, summarise papers or even suggest new ideas but it also raises big questions about originality and ethics. For me personally, I think my role is to figure out how to use AI in a way that actually helps me learn, not just get work done quicker. If I’m transparent and use it as a brainstorming or learning tool I’m showing how it can be useful without replacing the human side of uni. things like judgment, problem solving, and collaboration. Basically, the way we use it NOW shapes what unis will look like in the future, so I try to see AI as a partner rather than a shortcut. I think AI forces us to rethink what it means to know something. To learn effectively, contributing to human knowledge. I think it is hard for unis to be able to assess students properly. With AI, we can say for now that students have theoretical knowledge, but if we assess them it may as well become a real project. But if we are assessing them on things they need to know, but AI already helps with that, how are we supposed to assess the students? I guess it makes sense to say no AI allowed and closed exams, although I think closed exams are a very old age way of examination. It does help with counteracting AI but we also DO HAVE AI. There is a lot to it, but the main thing is, I would like to think of it like a new invention that helps humans. Like computers, calculators, all have benefited us, and we will find new ways and systems to integrate into our lives.

Thank you to the coordinators of the project, and I hope that my insights, musings, anecdotes and outpourings of pent-up frustrations, have been helpful, enlightening and, with any luck, mildly entertaining. I know that the entries are supposed to be raw, unadulterated personal narratives. Except, I know I can be expressive in my writing, my inner thespian finding voice in literary form. So while I didn’t set out to write in a more humorous, blog-like style, I couldn’t help myself, and if I’ve been able to make the dissection of hundreds of ethnographs that little bit less mundane, then that’s an added bonus. Ok, to the topic at hand. Considering my week 1 entries, would I have written anything differently on reflection? Well, I did something similar for entry 19 and I had to go back the next day and filter my response to remove the frequent use of expletives that would melt the paint off walls from 30 metres away. So yes, some of the topics were triggering in the sense that I still have immense frustration, bordering on pure and unadulterated hatred, of the way I’ve been treated by some of the ignorant, arrogant academic elite who were unable to see the log in their own eye while looking for the speck in mine. Having learnt from that experience, I’m not going to go back there. Though would I change anything that I wrote in week 1? I don’t think so. My final thought about AI and law comes from a 60 Minutes story I referred to yesterday (I think). One part of the story I didn’t discuss, though is definitely worth a discussion, was of Law Connect. This is the relevant transcript: Journalist (J): No one is harnessing that opportunity more than Christian Beck. The multi-millionaire owner of Superyacht Law Connect is a master of embracing new technology and winning. He's taken line honours in the Sydney to Hobart for the past two years. His super maxi is named after his company, a world first AI assistant website that's revolutionised the way people get legal help. So this is Law Connect, how does it work? Christian Beck (B): Well, basically if you've got any legal problem anywhere in the world, you can go to Law Connect and it'll give you free information about it and then it'll connect you to lawyers that are experienced and willing to take on that type of legal matter. J: All AI generated? B: Yes, all the answers are AI generated, yes. J: So you pop your scenario in, what's the best sort of example? B: Well, let's say you've got a violent ex-husband or something like that and you just want to sort of find out how to deal with that. I could say, I have a violent husband. You don't even have to spell it properly, it'll kind of figure it out. And it'll basically then ask you a range of questions to work out how to help you. J: The AI system is impressive and accurate. It's been trained by years of legal data and case law. But it's just one example of how Law Connect is investing billions of dollars in the technology. Christian and his team are also programming robotic dogs trained and operated by AI to confront intruders and protect victims of domestic violence. So this is a very unusual thing to be bringing into the legal system. How does it work? B: Well, the main thing it's doing is it's running a camera with face rec talking to the cloud. So if it identifies a person that it is looking for and it identifies a match for something like an AVO, it can call police. It can explain to the person that they're being recorded and they may police potentially on the way. It can have a conversation with them. It can stand between them and the victim. It can do a lot of things that a static camera just can't do. J: Christian insists far from putting jobs at risk and replacing lawyers. In legal practice, AI will have the opposite effect. Do you think there'll be lawyers out of work? B: I don't think so. Like if you turn up to the family court, you might have eight cases being mentioned on one day. Two of them typically will be people acting for themselves. And the family court is the worst place in the world to act for yourself. You can ruin your life doing that, right? So I think that success would be that everyone can get access to justice and get help from lawyers, combination of lawyers and AI to solve their issues. https://youtu.be/b75zSsXII_c?si=7GG-OQKJbW1Ibx7X Ok, so first of all, ANYONE who is building robot dogs that may one day have the ability to become sentient, highly efficient killing machines needs to watch, and rewatch, and re-rewatch ‘Metalhead’ - Season 4, Episode 5 of the brilliant, though eerily realistic and absolutely horrifying Netflix series ‘Black Mirror’. As exceptional as Black Mirror was, I had to stop watching it after that episode because the boundaries of science fiction and potential reality were irretrievably, irrevocably blurred and I wanted the nightmares to stop. That said, and more to the point of this study, it’s interesting how AI has already reshaped the perennial quandaries of the theories of justice and jurisprudence by democratising accessibility to law. If this keeps going, LLB104 will have nothing to talk about … John Rawls, John Stuart Mill and Jeremy Bentham replaced by Christian Beck and AI gurus. Though the question remains … given what AI is already doing to law, will AI eventually replace lawyers or enhance them? Beck is confident. No one else is. And honestly, who knows? This is a technological revolution that we’ve not seen the likes of before … who knows how far it will go, what change it will force on our social fabric? And perhaps, whether there are enough people in work not replaced by AI that will be able to actually engage a lawyer after their interaction with AI in a perpetual state of evolution. What will the law look like by the time I graduate? God only knows. Will the feeble attempts by universities to regulate GenAI use, when no one has managed to yet, really stop students from using it as it continues its iterative develop on a seemingly daily basis? Again, who knows. I think one thing’s for sure. The moment this study is able to publish its findings, they’ll likely already be outdated as AI and it’s ever-growing influence, for good or for evil, continues its relentless exponential growth. To the researchers brave enough to take on this challenge, God-speed.

Text: As on the 19th, there is not much that I would particularly change about my entries in week one. If anything, I have only become more against AI as I have continued to reflect upon it in these entries. In terms of this research, I don’t pretend to know how you will interpret these entries. I suppose that you could slot me pretty easily into the category of ‘Against GenAI’. But I hope through these entries that you can see that my position is slightly more considered than that. It is a position based in principle, but we already, I think, see the dangerous effects that GenAI has on our society. I have covered a lot in my entries, but there are plenty more that I haven’t talked about, things that are materialising right here and now. The inane amount of energy and water that AI uses, and for such vain and frivolous pursuits. The deep-fakes and misinformation that exist currently, the many people who have had their likeness put onto bodies performing acts that they would never do nor put to camera. I think I have not spoken on these as much as I cannot relate to them as personally as I can the other issues. I have seen the damage that other advances in technology such as social media and short form content have done to the young generation - I would identify myself as a ‘victim’ (for lack of a better word) of the damage. I view AI in a similar vain, producing the like problems of misinformation, reducing our ability to think for our-selves, reducing our attention spans, etc. I believe these are the issues that I focus on when reflecting on AI because I see firsthand what the like problems of social media have done. I think, ultimately, that the issues with AI go to the very heart of the issues that we have with our broader societies and economies at large. Growth for growth’s sake is unsustainable. It feels, at this moment in time, that we are at a technological standstill. The grand sweeping advances of past 20-30 years have altered the fabric of our society, arguably, more than anything in the one or two centuries before it. Never before have people been so connected, and this growth led itself to more growth. The more connected, the more could be communicated, the more could be learnt and improved - it was exponential. But we ran out of things to invent and improve. Think of the technological advances of the last ~5-10 years. What is fundamentally different? After the smart phone, after the world wide web, can you think of one advent that was as impactful? I mean sure, we have cars that can half drive themselves, everyone thought we would be living and working within the ‘metaverse’ 2-3 years ago and parallel to that a decent portion of the population believed that cryptocurrencies would become the primary form of currency and remove centralised currency altogether. To me, none of these things feel like innovation, and the most recent breakthrough - GenAI, feels to me to be the least bit innovative. It feels as though we are turning backwards. And that’s what AI does, right? Scrapes the efforts of all the painters, poets, technicians and educators to give a half skilled imitation of the best minds that history has to offer. All without permission. You need only look to the US government, ‘ghibli-fying’ images of a lady sobbing as she is deported to see how disgusting and truly rotten this technology is. It is art without soul. Literature without meaning. And sure, all of this could be ‘besides the point’. AI isn’t pushed as hard as it is because it can create awful art for free. It is being pushed because it has the capability to perform procedural tasks to a certain degree of success. And again, this is great, for the C suite and the stakeholders who can cull a majority of their entry-level roles and reward themselves with hefty bonuses, effectively blood money in exchange for the lives uprooted and the damage that a lack of entry-level roles does to any professional industry. I see AI, at its best, as just another tool to shift capital upwards and pull the ladder out as it goes. At its worst, it’s the deliberate removal of humanity from our pursuits. Growth for the sake of growth is unsustainable, and eventually, the snake begins to eat itself. I hope and I dream that the AI ‘bubble’ pops. That the technology is deemed financially unviable and investment is pulled. That it can stop being implemented on every single application and in every single business structure. I fear if not, that we won’t have anything left, any creatives, any academics, and that the next generation will grow up in a truly post-literate society. So, as I have said, I think it is pretty clear that I can be thrown in the basket of those against AI. And don’t get me wrong, I have grown up knowing nothing but modern technology. I am accustomed to change and to innovation. But I have never been as fearful as I am about any other innovation. I have never been afraid of the future that is being promised to us.

Text: I don't have any changes. But I did want to reflect on using AI and the way it makes you feel. I was asking ChatGPT questions today about my parenting style, how to manage particular issues I'm having with my kids, and it's just so comforting. Google can't do that, trawling through pages of resources to find information that answers your question is great from a critical analysis perspective but you still have that niggling doubt; what if I missed something? Google only gives you what you search for, what if you got your search terms wrong? It always leaves me feeling like maybe I've missed some crucial piece of information. But suprisingly for someone as cynical and distrustful of AI, using ChatGPT has this undertone if like, talking to a therapist. It can pull out the nuance in your question and answer what you have been too afraid to ask, like, here's what's going on developmentally with that dinner battle you're having with your kid, and also you're not a bad parent or doing something wrong. Here's why your 5 year old can't empathise yet, and also she's not a psychopath and you haven't failed as a mother. I kidnof hate how good that feels to read, particularly when I a) know it's machine designed to get me to keep interacting with it and b) am creeped out that it managed to identify other questions that I did actually need answers to but was too scared to ask. I see why people use it. It feels safer than Google. Academically, I was using ChatGPT over the weekend to build and summarise notes for family law. It's an elective, so the lectures are a lot of "this is important, go read these very long sections but we're not going over it in the lecture". I'm comfortable enough with the legal framework because of my job to be able to check that the summaries are correct, but it saved me literal hours being able to punch in the entire division I wanted summarised and have it come out in a table a few seconds later. I was also surprised though that when I hit enter on a prompt before giving it the piece of legislation, it was still able to give me a pretty accurate summary from its own search. I usually include in my prompts that it can only use the information I give it, but now I'm not sure if that's actually working or if it's still pulling from its training data. The contrast of distrust between those two scenarios is interesting. Text: Date: Sunday 21 September Time: 5.02pm Reflecting on my first entry back in week 1, I talked about how my observation of AI are largely seeing it be used in areas I don’t think it needs to be use for. And I do feel like this attitude is consistent with that of many others. When seeing discourse about AI online, most perspectives can be grouped into two distinct groups - somewhere in the space of either for it or against it. It’s hard to determine what makes peoples’ views differ - why do some people think it’s great and others think it’s terrible? Why do some use it for every assignment and others won’t go near it? Some are excited about its constant improvements and developments and others are scared? I When I reflect on the kinds of people that have these opinions, I can’t really put it down to one or two variables, aka the stereotypical trope of the older generation not liking it but the younger ‘techy’ generation likes it. My generation is very divided on the topic - on one hand, there are people who literally cannot function without ChatGPT - not just in the educational realm but life in general. Their source of information IS ChatGPT. They talk to ChatGPT like it’s a friend (much like we used to do with Siri). Then there are others who don’t like or use AI, which is the group I fall into. Then I guess there are people who don’t completely rely on it but do use it and find their life easier for it. I guess determining the use of AI is difficult. There has obviously been a clear uptake in it and people have found it is great at many things. I think this group far outpaces the amount of people that don’t like/use AI. So in terms of educational institutions operating, workplace processes etc, the safest approach is that AI is here, it’s being used, so let’s not try to ignore that. It’s like trying to take a phone off a kid - if they want to play a phone, they will find a way. If someone wants to use AI, of course they’re going to use it. SO the introduction of ‘Socrates’ in my law degree at least is, I feel, a very over-optimistic approach of managing AI use. People don’t use AI because they want to think about it, they use AI for conveniency - because AI will give you the information. If someone has CoPilot or Socrates available, it can’t realistically be said that the person will use Socrates - maybe they will, but probably not. And in terms of the students who don’t use AI - I know I haven’t touched Socrates since it was introduced to us because I don’t really care about it, now there’s a wasted resource. At the end of the day, I think as long as AI keeps advancing, people will keep adopting its advancements and institutions will have to work around that. I do think that working with AI, like in Legal Research, to actually physically demonstrate that it doesn’t give you the answer you need (or the depth you need), is a practical, beneficial way of combatting AI use. Showing students that it is actually disadvantaging you to use it to write your work. But to include in assignment outlines that GenAI is not to be used under any circumstance is difficult, because the same student might say of course they’re not going to use ChatGPT to write their assignment because it would be rubbish, and of course they won’t trust it’s sources, but maybe they are still going to use it as a starting point to get some ideas on what to research. After all, in Legal Research that was probably the most useful thing about CoPilot - not the actual resources it gave, but the direction it steers you in and where it pushes you to look. In terms of Law assessment, the ability to test a student’s actual work, not their use of AI, is pretty easy, because we *mostly* have problem questions. GenAI might be able to give you all the content or the law, but it will never be able to accurately apply that to the problem scenario in an assessment to the degree or standard that the assessment requires - that’s just the nature of the assessment. So when we think about incorporating or embracing or accepting that AI is part of our world and now part of our learning, it’s probably a great example of how AI can be used to help research and that’s fine, because the assessment isn’t testing whether you have memorised the statements of law, it’s testing whether you know how to apply to the facts, which takes a level of discretion, nuance and scrutiny of the facts which GenAI probably doesn’t have. What I think this means for other realms of education, particularly in school, is that assessment or just learning in general needs to focus on critical thinking and applying knowledge. A year 7 English booklet might have questions like, what happened in this chapter, or what did this character do when X? That’s a recall question that GenAI can easily answer. Instead we might ask what can be inferred about character X because of the way they did Y? What does their relationship with Z say about them? How does this event in this book link to broader societal issues? That kind of thinking is going to be CRUCIAL for educational institutions to emphasise because otherwise, we’re producing people who do not have the capacity to think critically because they’ve never really had to. These students are at the age where their brains are so malleable and if they are not being exercised or challenged to think critically, it could have detrimental effects in the future. I think that AI is reaching a point where it is no longer revolutionising learning, but instead has the capacity to destroy it if curriculums are adjusted to adapt to the existence of AI and how they can still challenge students to develop critical thinking, resilience, problem-solving - all of these skills that are not just important for school, but for the real world. As a final thought on AI, I think it is becoming more clear every day that we need guardrails in place for the advancement of AI. It keeps improving and improving and advancing and being able to do new things, but people are pushing it too far without putting guardrails in place. I think it opens up a world of potential problems that we can’t even comprehend let alone tackle. I think that the blind encouragement or inducement into integrating AI into schools for learning or teacher planning and organisation could be very detrimental without any guardrails in place.

Text: I feel both excited and a little nervous about bringing AI into legal education. Excited, because so much of law involves repetitive but important work. AI can help to read case law, summarise judgments, or scan statutes. These are all things AI can take off our hands so we can save energy for the harder parts like analysis, connecting principles. But I’m also nervous because law isn’t just about "finding an answer." It’s about reading between the lines like context, authority, ratio vs. obiter, and how a single word can change the outcome. AI often speaks with huge confidence but can be completely wrong, citing the wrong judge, misreading a precedent, or stitching things together mechanically. So for me, AI feels like an eager assistant, but I still have to be the "lead lawyer" who checks everything and takes responsibility. I don’t know yet if it will make things "easier" in the way I expect, or if it will actually make things harder in a different way. Because once AI becomes part of assignments and lectures, the expectations will probably rise too. Teachers might assume we can move faster through basic tasks and spend more time on complex analysis, deeper research, or bigger projects. It won’t be enough to hand in a simple answer anymore. We’ll need to show how we used AI, how we checked it, and what critical thinking we added on top. That could feel more demanding. I also think that teaching and learning law is already difficult. If AI is integrated, it will certainly lead to many changes, not just "another tool". Teachers have to get used to it like choosing which tools, designing new assessment criteria and recreating exercises in a more realistic way. Students also have to learn new skill. All of this takes time - at least at first. If AI is going to be a part of learning, then we should be taught how to use it effectively.
